nodes.statement_short: Necessity from the monomial formula; sufficiency by moving indices one at a time using the zero-insertion equations.

nodes.name: Necessity: zero-insertion property of monomials.
nodes.statement: For the quasi-symmetric monomial $M_{\omega}$ we have $$ M_{\omega}(t_1,\dots,t_i,0,t_{i+1},\dots,t_{r-1})= \begin{cases} 0,&\omega=(j_1,\dots,j_r);\\ M_{\omega}(t_1,\dots,t_i,t_{i+1},\dots,t_{r-1}),&\omega=(j_1,\dots,j_k),\;k<r. \end{cases} $$ So this property is true for all quasi-symmetric functions.
nodes.statement_short: Necessity: zero-insertion property of monomials.

nodes.name: Sufficiency: show monomials of the same type have equal coefficients.
nodes.statement: On the other hand, let the condition of the proposition be true. Let us prove that for a fixed composition $\omega$ any two monomials $t_{l_1}^{j_1}\dots t_{l_k}^{j_k}$ and $t_{l_1'}^{j_1}\dots t_{l_k'}^{j_k}$ have the equal coefficients $g_{l_1,\,\dots,\,l_k}^{j_1,\,\dots,\,j_k}$ and $g_{l_1',\,\dots,\,l_l'}^{j_1,\,\dots,\,j_k}$.
nodes.statement_short: Sufficiency: show monomials of the same type have equal coefficients.

nodes.name: Compare coefficients to shift an index by one.
nodes.statement: Let $l_i+1<l_{i+1}$ or $i=k$ and $l_i<r$. Consider the corresponding coefficients in the polynomial equation: $$ g(t_1,\dots,t_{l_i-1},0,t_{l_i},t_{l_i+1},\dots,t_{r-1})=g(t_1,\dots,t_{l_i-1},t_{l_i},0,t_{l_i+1},\dots,t_{r-1}). $$ On the left the monomial $t_{l_1}^{j_1}\dots t_{l_i}^{j_i}t_{l_{i+1}-1}^{j_{i+1}}\dots t_{l_k-1}^{j_k}$ has the coefficient $g_{l_1,\,\dots,\,l_i+1,\,l_{i+1},\dots,\,l_k}^{j_1,\,\dots,\,j_k}$, and on the right $g_{l_1,\,\dots,\,l_i,\,l_{i+1},\,\dots,\,l_k}^{j_1,\dots,j_k}$, so they are equal. Now we can move the index $l_i$ to the right to $l_i+1$ and in the same manner we can move $l_i$ to the left, if $l_{i-1}<l_i-1$, or $i=1$ and $l_i>1$.
nodes.statement_short: Compare coefficients to shift an index by one.

nodes.name: Move all indices to 1..k.
nodes.statement: Now let us move step by step the index $l_1$ to $1$, then the index $l_2$ to $2$, and so on. At last we obtain that $g_{l_1,\,\dots,\,l_k}^{j_1,\,\dots,\,j_k}=g_{1,\,\dots,\,k}^{j_1,\,\dots,\,j_k}$.
nodes.statement_short: Move all indices to 1..k.

nodes.name: Remark 3.4 (criterion with infinitely many variables)
nodes.statement: Similar argument shows that the same is true in the case of an infinite number of variables, if we consider all the expressions $$ a+\sum\limits_{k=1}^{\infty}\sum\limits_{1\leqslant l_1<\dots<l_k}\sum\limits_{j_1,\,\dots,\,j_k\geqslant 1}a_{ l_1,\,\dots,\,l_k}^{j_1,\,\dots,\,j_k}t_{l_1}^{j_1}\dots t_{l_k}^{j_k}. $$ of bounded degree: $2|\omega|=2(j_1+\dots+j_k)<N$ for all $\omega$. Then the infinite series $g$ of bounded degree belongs to $\mathcal{Q}sym$ if and only if $$ g(t_1,\dots,t_{i-1},0,t_{i+1},\dots)=g(t_1,\dots,t_{i-1},t_{i+1},\dots) $$ for all $i\geqslant 1$. As a corollary we obtain another proof of the fact that quasi-symmetric functions form a ring.
nodes.statement_short: Bounded-degree series is in Qsym iff deleting any variable equals setting it to 0; gives another proof Qsym is a ring.
nodes.label: cr

nodes.name: Hazewinkel's theorem (Ditters conjecture)
nodes.statement: In \cite{H} M.~Hazewinkel proved the Ditters conjecture that $\mathrm{Qsym}[t_1,t_2,\dots]$ is a free commutative algebra of polynomials over the integers.
nodes.statement_short: Qsym is a free commutative polynomial algebra over Z.

nodes.name: Rank of Qsym^{2n} is 2^{n-1}
nodes.statement: The $(2n)$-th graded component $\mathrm{Qsym}^{2n}[t_1,t_2,\dots]$ has rank $2^{n-1}$.

nodes.name: Maps V_{r+1} and E_r between finite-variable Qsym
nodes.statement: There are group homomorphisms: \begin{gather*} V_{r+1}:\mathrm{Qsym}[t_1,\dots,t_r]\to\mathrm{Qsym}[t_1,\dots,t_{r+1}]:\quad V_{r+1}M_{\omega}(t_1,\dots,t_r)=M_{\omega}(t_1,\dots,t_{r+1})\\ E_r:\mathrm{Qsym}[t_1,\dots,t_{r+1}]\to\mathrm{Qsym}[t_1,\dots,t_r]:\quad t_{r+1}\to 0; \end{gather*}

nodes.name: E_r is a ring homomorphism
nodes.statement: The mapping $E_r$ sends all the monomials $M_{\omega}$ corresponding to the compositions $(j_1,\dots,j_{r+1})$ of length $r+1$ to zero, and for the compositions $\omega$ of smaller length $E_rM_{\omega}(t_1,\dots,t_{r+1})=M_{\omega}(t_1,\dots,t_r)$. It is a ring homomorphism.

nodes.name: Projection Pi_Qsym onto quasi-symmetric polynomials
nodes.statement: Given $r>0$ there is a projection $\Pi_{\mathrm{Qsym}}:\mathbb Z[t_1,\dots,t_r]\to\mathrm{Qsym}[t_1,\dots,t_r]\otimes\mathbb Q$:\\ for $s_1<s_2<\dots<s_k$ $$ \Pi_{\mathrm{Qsym}} t_{s_1}^{j_1}\dots t_{s_k}^{j_k}=\frac{1}{{r\choose k}}\left(\sum\limits_{l_1<\dots<l_k}t_{l_1}^{j_1}\dots t_{l_k}^{j_k}\right), $$ which gives the average value over all the monomials of each type.

nodes.name: Pi_Qsym fixes quasi-symmetric monomials
nodes.statement: Then for the quasi-symmetric monomial $M_{\omega},\;\omega=(j_1,\dots,j_k)$ we have: $$ \Pi_{\mathrm{Qsym}} M_{\omega}=\sum\limits_{1\leqslant j_1<\dots<j_k\leqslant r}\frac{1}{{r\choose k}}M_{\omega}={r\choose k}\frac{1}{{r\choose k}}M_{\omega}=M_{\omega}, $$ So $\Pi_{\mathrm{Qsym}}$ is indeed a projection.

nodes.name: Remark 3.5 (number of variables as a grading)
nodes.statement: We see that in the theory of symmetric and quasi-symmetric functions there is an important additional graduation -- the number of variables in the polynomial.

nodes.name: Reversed composition omega^*
nodes.statement: For a composition $\omega=(j_1,\dots,j_k)$ let us define the composition $\omega^*=(j_k,\dots,j_1)$.

nodes.name: Involution * on Qsym
nodes.statement: The correspondence $M_{\omega}\to (M_{\omega})^*=M_{\omega^*}$ defines an involutory ring homomorphism $$ *:\mathrm{Qsym}[t_1,t_2,\dots]\to \mathrm{Qsym}[t_1,t_2,\dots]. $$

nodes.name: Remark 3.7 (coproduct of M_omega^*)
nodes.statement: Let $\tau_{\mathcal{Q}sym}\colon\mathcal{Q}sym\otimes\mathcal{Q}sym\to\mathcal{Q}sym\otimes\mathcal{Q}sym$ be the ring homomorphism that interchanges the tensor factors $\tau_{\mathcal{Q}sym}(x\otimes y)=y\otimes x$. Then $\Delta(M_{\omega}^*)=*\otimes*(\tau_{\mathcal{Q}sym}\Delta M_{\omega})$.
nodes.label: DQsym

nodes.name: Leibnitz-Hopf algebra and universal Leibnitz-Hopf algebra
nodes.statement: A {\itshape Leibnitz-Hopf algebra} over the ring $R$ is an associative Hopf algebra $\mathcal{H}$ over the ring $R$ with a fixed sequence of a finite or countable number of multiplicative generators $H_i$, $i=1,2\dots$ satisfying the comultiplication formula $$ \Delta H_n=\sum\limits_{i+j=n}H_i\otimes H_j,\quad H_0=1. $$ A {\itshape universal Leibnitz-Hopf algebra} $\mathcal{A}$ over the ring $R$ is a Leibnitz-Hopf algebra with the universal property: for any Leibnitz-Hopf algebra $\mathcal{H}$ over the ring $R$ the correspondence $A_i\to H_i$ defines a Hopf algebra homomorphism.
differentia: with a fixed sequence of a finite or countable number of multiplicative generators $H_i$, $i=1,2\dots$ satisfying the comultiplication formula

nodes.name: Free associative Leibnitz-Hopf algebra Z
nodes.statement: Consider the free associative Leibnitz-Hopf algebra over the integers $\mathcal{Z}=\mathbb Z \langle Z_1,Z_2,\dots\rangle$ in countably many generators $Z_i$.

nodes.name: Proposition 3.9 (Z tensor R is universal)
nodes.statement: $\mathcal{Z}\otimes R$ is a universal Leibnitz-Hopf algebra over the ring $R$.

nodes.name: Graded dual Hopf algebra M of Z
nodes.statement: Set $\deg Z_i=2i$. Let us denote by $\mathcal{M}$ the graded dual Hopf algebra over the integers.

nodes.name: M is the algebra of quasi-symmetric functions
nodes.statement: It is not difficult to see that $\mathcal M$ is precisely the algebra of quasi-symmetric functions over the integers.

nodes.name: Proof that M is Qsym
nodes.statement: Indeed, for any composition $\omega=(j_1,\dots,j_k)$ we can define $m_{\omega}$ by the dual basis formula $$ \langle m_{\omega},Z_{\sigma}\rangle=\delta_{\omega,\,\sigma}, $$ where $Z_{\sigma}=Z_{a_1}\dots Z_{a_l}$ for a composition $\sigma=(a_1,\dots,a_l)$. Then the elements $m_{\omega}$ are multiplied exactly as the quasi-symmetric monomials $M_{\omega}$.
nodes.statement_short: Define the dual basis m_omega and observe it multiplies like M_omega.

nodes.name: Generating series Phi(t) in Z
nodes.statement: Let us denote $$ \Phi(t)=1+Z_1t+Z_2t^2+\dots=\sum\limits_{k=0}^{\infty}Z_kt^k $$

nodes.name: Comultiplication of Phi(t) is grouplike
nodes.statement: Then the comultiplication formula is equivalent to $$ \Delta\Phi(t)=\Phi(t)\otimes\Phi(t) $$

nodes.name: Antipode, counit and unit of Z
nodes.statement: Let $\chi:\mathcal{Z}\to\mathcal{Z}$ be the {\itshape antipode}, that is a linear operator, satisfying the property $$ 1\star\chi=\mu\circ(1\otimes\chi)\circ\Delta=\eta\circ\varepsilon=\mu\circ(\chi\otimes 1)\circ\Delta=\chi\star 1, $$ where $\varepsilon:\mathcal{Z}\to\mathbb Z$, $\varepsilon(1)=1$, $\varepsilon(Z_{\sigma})=0$, $\sigma\ne\varnothing$, is a {\itshape counit}, $\eta:\mathbb Z\to\mathcal{Z}$, $\eta(a)=a\cdot 1$ is a {\itshape unite} map, and $\mu$ is a multiplication in $\mathcal{Z}$.

nodes.name: Recurrent formula for the antipode of Z
nodes.statement: Then $\Phi(t)\chi(\Phi(t))=1=\chi(\Phi(t))\Phi(t)$ and $\{\chi(Z_n)\}$ satisfy the recurrent formulas \begin{equation} \chi(Z_1)=-Z_1;\quad \chi(Z_{n+1})+\chi(Z_n)Z_1+\dots+\chi(Z_1)Z_n+Z_{n+1}=0,\;n\geqslant 1. \end{equation}

nodes.name: Antipode recursion (6)
nodes.statement: \chi(Z_1)=-Z_1;\quad \chi(Z_{n+1})+\chi(Z_n)Z_1+\dots+\chi(Z_1)Z_n+Z_{n+1}=0,\;n\geqslant 1.
nodes.label: X1

nodes.name: Explicit formula for the antipode of Z
nodes.statement: In fact, since $\Phi(t)=1+Z_1t+\dots$, we can use the previous formula to obtain \begin{gather*} \chi(\Phi(t))=\frac{1}{\Phi(t)}=\sum\limits_{i=0}^{\infty}(-1)^i\left(\Phi(t)-1\right)^i;\\ \chi(Z_n)=\sum\limits_{k=1}^n(-1)^k\sum\limits_{j_1+\dots+j_k=n}Z_{j_1}\dots Z_{j_k}\quad j_i\geqslant 1,\;n\geqslant 1 \end{gather*} This formula defines $\chi$ on generators, and therefore on the whole algebra.
nodes.statement_short: chi(Phi(t)) = 1/Phi(t), giving chi(Z_n) as a signed sum over compositions of n.

nodes.name: Opposite Hopf algebra Z^op and anti-isomorphism rho
nodes.statement: Let $\mathcal{Z}^{op}$ be the Hopf algebra opposite to $\mathcal{Z}$, i.e. $\mathcal{Z}=\mathcal{Z}^{op}$ as coalgebras, and the multiplication in $\mathcal{Z}^{op}$ is given by the rule $a\diamond b:=b\cdot a$. Then the antiisomorphism $$ \varrho\colon\mathcal{Z}\to\mathcal{Z},\quad Z_{a_1}\dots Z_{a_k}\to Z_{a_k}\dots Z_{a_1} $$ satisfies the property $\Delta\circ\varrho=(\varrho\otimes\varrho)\circ\Delta$, and defines the Hopf algebra isomorphism $\mathcal{Z}\to\mathcal{Z}^{op}$.

nodes.name: Proposition 3.11 (rho^* = *)
nodes.statement: We have $\varrho^*=*$

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 3.11
nodes.statement: Indeed, $$ \langle\varrho^*M_{\omega},Z_{\sigma}\rangle=\langle M_{\omega},\varrho Z_{\sigma}\rangle=\langle M_{\omega}, Z_{\sigma^*}\rangle=\delta_{\omega,\,\sigma^*}. $$ Therefore, $\varrho^*M_{\omega}=M_{\omega^*}=M_{\omega}^*$
nodes.statement_short: Pair with Z_sigma and use rho Z_sigma = Z_{sigma^*}.

nodes.name: Milnor module
nodes.statement: A (left) \emph{Milnor module} $M$ over the Hopf algebra $X$ is an algebra with unit $1\in R$ which is also a (left) module over $X$ satisfying \[ x(uv) = \sum x'_n(u)x''_n(v), \quad x\in X,\; u,v \in M, \;\, \Delta x = \sum x'_n \otimes x''_n. \]
differentia: which is also a (left) module over $X$ satisfying

nodes.name: Proposition 3.13 (P and RP are Milnor modules over Z)
nodes.statement: The homomorphism $\EuScript{L}_{\mathrm{R}}\colon\mathcal{Z}\to\mathcal{D}(\mathrm{R})\;\colon\; Z_k\to d_k$ defines on the rings $\mathcal{P}$ and $\mathcal{RP}$ the structures of left Milnor modules over the Leibnitz-Hopf algebra $\mathcal{Z}$. The homomorphism $\EuScript{R}_{\mathrm{R}}\colon\mathcal{Z}^{op}\to\mathcal{D}(\mathrm{R})\;\colon\; \EuScript{R}_{\mathrm{R}}=\EuScript{L}_{\mathrm{R}}\circ \varrho$ defines on the rings $\mathcal{P}$ and $\mathcal{RP}$ the structures of right Milnor modules over the Leibnitz-Hopf algebra $\mathcal{Z}$.
nodes.statement_short: Z_k -> d_k makes P and RP left (and via rho right) Milnor modules over Z.

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 3.13
nodes.statement: This follows from Proposition \ref{MM}
nodes.statement_short: Follows from the Leibniz rule for d_k (Prop 2.49).

nodes.name: Operators D_omega
nodes.statement: Let us note, that the word $Z_{\omega}=Z_{j_1}\dots Z_{j_k}$ corresponds under the homomorphism $\EuScript{L}_{\mathrm{R}}$ to the operator $D_{\omega}=d_{j_1}\dots d_{j_k}$, and under the homomorphism $\EuScript{R}_{\mathrm{R}}$ to the operator $D_{\omega^*}=d_{j_k}\dots d_{j_1}$.

nodes.name: Universal Hopf algebra U with antipode chi(H_i)=(-1)^i H_i
nodes.statement: Denote by $\mathcal{U}$ the universal Hopf algebra in the category of Leibnitz-Hopf algebras with an antipode $\chi(H_i)=(-1)^iH_i$. It is is easy to see that $\mathcal{U}=\mathcal{Z}/J_{\mathcal{U}}$, where the two-sided Hopf ideal $J_{\mathcal{U}}$ is generated by the relations \begin{equation} Z_n-Z_1Z_{n-1}+\dots+(-1)^{n-1}Z_{n-1}Z_1+(-1)^nZ_n=0,\;n\geqslant 2 \end{equation} These relations can be written in the short form as $\Phi(-t)\Phi(t)=1$. It can be shown that $\mathcal{U}\otimes\mathbb Q\simeq \mathbb Q\langle Z_1,Z_3,Z_5,\dots\rangle$, and $\mathcal{U}\xrightarrow{\mathrm{id}\otimes 1}\mathcal{U}\otimes\mathbb Q$ is an embedding.
nodes.statement_short: U = Z/J_U with J_U generated by Phi(-t)Phi(t)=1; rationally free on Z_1, Z_3, Z_5, ...

nodes.name: Corollary 3.15 (Milnor modules over U)
nodes.statement: The mappings $\EuScript{L}_{\mathrm{R}}$ and $\EuScript{R}_{\mathrm{R}}$ define on the rings $\mathcal{P}$ and $\mathcal{RP}$ the structures of left and right Milnor modules over the Leibnitz-Hopf algebra $\mathcal{U}$.

nodes.name: Proof of Corollary 3.15
nodes.statement: This follows from Proposition \ref{PM}.
nodes.statement_short: Follows from Phi(-t)Phi(t)=1 (Prop 2.52).

nodes.name: rho induces U = U^op
nodes.statement: Since $\varrho(J_{\mathcal{U}})=J_{\mathcal{U}}$, we see that $\varrho$ induces a correctly defined homomorphism $\varrho\colon\mathcal{U}\to\mathcal{U}$, which gives the isomorphism $\mathcal{U}\simeq \mathcal{U}^{op}$.

nodes.name: U^* embeds in Qsym, invariant under *
nodes.statement: Since the factor map $\mathcal{Z}\to\mathcal{Z}/J_{\mathcal{U}}$ is an epimorphism, the dual map $\mathcal{U}^*\to\mathcal{Z}^*=\mathcal{Q}sym$ is an embedding. Then the subring $\mathcal{U}^*\subset\mathcal{Q}sym$ is invariant under the involution $\varrho^*=*$.

nodes.name: Universal commutative Leibnitz-Hopf algebra C
nodes.statement: A {\itshape universal commutative Leibnitz-Hopf algebra} $\mathcal{C}=\mathbb Z[C_1,C_2,\dots]$ is a free commutative polynomial Leibnitz-Hopf algebra in generators $C_i$ of degree $2i$. We have $\mathcal{C}=\mathcal{Z}/J_{\mathcal{C}}$, where the ideal $J_{\mathcal{C}}$ is generated by the relations $Z_iZ_j-Z_jZ_i$. It is a self-dual Hopf algebra and the graded dual Hopf algebra is naturally isomorphic to the algebra of symmetric functions $\mathbb Z[\sigma_1,\sigma_2,\dots]=\mathrm{Sym}[t_1,t_2,\dots]\subset\mathrm{Qsym}[t_1,t_2,\dots]$ generated by the symmetric monomials $$ \sigma_i=M_{\omega_i}=\sum\limits_{l_1<\dots<l_i}t_{l_1}\dots t_{l_i}, $$ where $\omega_i=\underbrace{(1,\;\dots,\;1)}_{i}$. The isomorphism $\mathcal{C}\simeq \mathcal{C}^*$ is given by the correspondence $C_i\to \sigma_i$.

nodes.name: Universal commutative Hopf algebra US
nodes.statement: Denote by $\mathcal{US}$ the universal Hopf algebra in the category of commutative Leibnitz-Hopf algebras with an antipode $\chi(H_i)=(-1)^iH_i$. It is easy to see that $\mathcal{US}=\mathcal{Z}/J_{\mathcal{US}}$, where the two-sided ideal $J_{\mathcal{US}}$ is generated by the relations (\ref{Phi}), and the commutators $Z_iZ_j-Z_jZ_i$. Then the relations (\ref{Phi}) for odd $n$ are trivial, while for even $n$ we have $$ 2Z_{2k}=2\sum\limits_{i=1}^{k-1}(-1)^{i-1}Z_iZ_{2k-i}+(-1)^{k-1}Z_k^2 $$ It can be shown that $\mathcal{US}\otimes\mathbb Q\simeq \mathbb Q[Z_1,Z_3,Z_5,\dots]$.

nodes.name: Lie-Hopf algebra, universal Lie-Hopf algebra W and shuffle algebra N
nodes.statement: A {\itshape Lie-Hopf algebra} over the ring $R$ is an associative Hopf algebra $\mathfrak{L}$ with a fixed sequence of a finite or countable number of multiplicative generators $L_i$, $i=1,2\dots$ satisfying the comultiplication formula $$ \Delta L_i=1\otimes L_i+L_i\otimes 1,\quad L_0=1. $$ A {\itshape universal Lie-Hopf algebra} over the ring $R$ is a Lie-Hopf algebra $\mathcal{A}$ satisfying the universal property: for any Lie-Hopf algebra $\mathfrak{L}$ over the ring $R$ the correspondence $A_i\to L_i$ defines a Hopf algebra homomorphism $\mathcal{A}\to\mathfrak{L}$. Consider the free associative Lie-Hopf algebra $\mathcal{W}$ over the integers $\mathbb Z\langle W_1,W_2,\dots\rangle$ in countably many variables $W_i$. \begin{prop} $\mathcal{W}\otimes R$ is a universal Lie-Hopf algebra over the ring $R$. \end{prop} Let us set $\deg W_i=2i$. Then the graded dual Hopf algebra is denoted by $\mathcal{N}$. This is the so-called {\itshape shuffle algebra}.
nodes.statement_short: Hopf algebra with primitive generators L_i; W is the free one, its graded dual N is the shuffle algebra.

nodes.name: Proposition 3.19 (W tensor R is universal Lie-Hopf)
nodes.statement: $\mathcal{W}\otimes R$ is a universal Lie-Hopf algebra over the ring $R$.

nodes.name: Antipode of W
nodes.statement: The antipode $\chi$ in $\mathcal{W}$ has a very simple form $\chi(W_i)=-W_i$.

nodes.name: Lyndon words
nodes.statement: Let us denote by $[a_1,\dots,a_n]$ an element of $\mathbb N^*$, that is the word over $\mathbb N$, consisting of symbols $a_1,\dots,a_n$, $a_i\in\mathbb N$. Let us order the words from $\mathbb N^*$ lexicographically, where any symbol is larger than nothing, that is $[a_1,\dots,a_n]>[b_1,\dots,b_m]$ if and only if there is an $i$ such that $a_1=b_1,\dots,a_{i-1}=b_{i-1}, a_i>b_i, 1\leqslant i\leqslant\min\{m,n\}$, or $n>m$ and $a_1=b_1,\dots,a_m=b_m$. A {\itshape proper tail} of a word $[a_1,\dots,a_n]$ is a word of the form $[a_i,\dots,a_n]$ with $1<i\leqslant n$. (The empty word and one-symbol word have no proper tails.) A word is {\itshape Lyndon} if all its proper tails are larger than the word itself. For example, the words $[1,1,2]$, $[1,2,1,2,2]$, $[1,3,1,5]$ are Lyndon and the words $[1,1,1,1]$, $[1,2,1,2]$, $[2,1]$ are not Lyndon. The set of Lyndon words is denoted by $\mathrm{LYN}$. The same definitions make sense for any totally ordered set, for example, for the set $\{1,2\}$ or for the set of all odd positive integers.
nodes.statement_short: A word is Lyndon if all its proper tails are lexicographically larger than the word.

nodes.name: Chen-Fox-Lyndon factorization
nodes.statement: Every word $w$ in $\mathbb N^*$ factors uniquely into a decreasing concatenation product of Lyndon words $$ w=u_1*u_2*\dots*u_k,\quad u_i\in\mathrm{LYN},\;u_1\geqslant u_2\geqslant\dots\geqslant u_k $$
nodes.statement_short: Every word factors uniquely as a weakly decreasing concatenation of Lyndon words.

nodes.name: Shuffle multiplication
nodes.statement: The multiplication in the algebra $\mathcal{N}$ is the so-called {\itshape shuffle multiplication}: $$ [a_1,\dots,a_n]\times_{sh}[a_{n+1},\dots,a_{m+n}]=\sum\limits_{\sigma}[a_{\sigma(1)},\dots,a_{\sigma(n)},a_{\sigma(n+1)},\dots,a_{\sigma(n+m)}], $$ where $\sigma$ runs over all the substitutions $\sigma\in S_{m+n}$ such that $$ \sigma^{-1}(1)<\dots<\sigma^{-1}(n)\mbox{ and }\sigma^{-1}(n+1)<\dots<\sigma^{-1}(n+m). $$

nodes.name: Shuffle algebra structure theorem
nodes.statement: $\mathcal{N}\otimes \mathbb Q=\mathbb Q[\mathrm{LYN}]$, the free commutative algebra over $\mathbb Q$ in the symbols from $\mathrm{LYN}$.
nodes.statement_short: N tensor Q is the free commutative algebra on Lyndon words.

nodes.name: Shuffle products of Chen-Fox-Lyndon factors
nodes.statement: Let $w$ be a word on the natural numbers and let $w=u_1*u_2*\dots *u_m$ be its Chen-Fox-Lyndon factorization. Then all words that occur with nonzero coefficient in the shuffle product $u_1\times_{sh}u_2\times_{sh}\dots\times_{sh}u_m$ are lexicographically smaller or equal to $w$, and $w$ occurs with a nonzero coefficient in this product.
assumptions: Let $w$ be a word on the natural numbers and let $w=u_1*u_2*\dots *u_m$ be its Chen-Fox-Lyndon factorization.
conclusions: all words that occur with nonzero coefficient in the shuffle product $u_1\times_{sh}u_2\times_{sh}\dots\times_{sh}u_m$ are lexicographically smaller or equal to $w$, and $w$ occurs with a nonzero coefficient in this product.

nodes.name: Proof of the shuffle algebra structure theorem for a subset M
nodes.statement: Given this result it is easy to prove the shuffle algebra structure theorem in the case of arbitrary totally ordered subset $M=\{m_1,m_2,\dots\}\subset\mathbb N$. Let us denote by $\mathcal{W}_{M}$ the free associative Lie-Hopf algebra $\mathbb Z\langle W_{m_1},W_{m_2},\dots\rangle$, let $\mathcal{N}_{M}$ be its graded dual algebra, and $\mathrm{LYN}_M$ be the corresponding set of all Lyndon words. We need to prove that $\mathcal{N}_M\otimes\mathbb Q=\mathbb Q[\mathrm{LYN}_M]$. Let $m_1$ be the minimal number in $M$. The smallest word $[m_1]$ is Lyndon. Given a word $w$ we can assume by induction that all the words lexicographically smaller than $w$ have been written as polynomials in the elements of $\mathrm{LYN}_M$. Take the Chen-Fox-Lyndon factorization $w=u_1*u_2*\dots*u_m$ of $w$ and consider, using the preceding theorem, $$ u_1\times_{sh}u_2\times_{sh}\dots\times_{sh}u_m=aw+(\mbox{reminder}). $$ By the theorem the coefficient $a$ is nonzero and all the words in (reminder) are lexicographically smaller than $w$, hence they belong to $\mathbb Q[\mathrm{LYN}_M]$. Therefore $w\in\mathbb Q[\mathrm{LYN}_M]$. This proves generation. Since each monomial in $(2n)$-th graded component of $\mathcal{N}\otimes \mathbb Q$ has a unique Chen-Fox-Lyndon decomposition, the number of monomials in $\mathbb Q[\mathrm{LYN}_M]$ of graduation $2n$ is equal to the number of monomials of the same graduation in $\mathcal{N}_{M}\otimes\mathbb Q$, monomials in Lyndon words are linearly independent. This proves that Lyndon words are algebraically independent.
nodes.statement_short: Induction on words in lexicographic order using the CFL shuffle theorem for generation; counting monomials for independence.

nodes.name: Set up W_M, N_M and LYN_M for a subset M.
nodes.statement: Given this result it is easy to prove the shuffle algebra structure theorem in the case of arbitrary totally ordered subset $M=\{m_1,m_2,\dots\}\subset\mathbb N$. Let us denote by $\mathcal{W}_{M}$ the free associative Lie-Hopf algebra $\mathbb Z\langle W_{m_1},W_{m_2},\dots\rangle$, let $\mathcal{N}_{M}$ be its graded dual algebra, and $\mathrm{LYN}_M$ be the corresponding set of all Lyndon words. We need to prove that $\mathcal{N}_M\otimes\mathbb Q=\mathbb Q[\mathrm{LYN}_M]$.
nodes.statement_short: Set up W_M, N_M and LYN_M for a subset M.

nodes.name: Base: the smallest word is Lyndon.
nodes.statement: Let $m_1$ be the minimal number in $M$. The smallest word $[m_1]$ is Lyndon.
nodes.statement_short: Base: the smallest word is Lyndon.

nodes.name: Inductive step: CFL shuffle theorem expresses w through smaller words.
nodes.statement: Given a word $w$ we can assume by induction that all the words lexicographically smaller than $w$ have been written as polynomials in the elements of $\mathrm{LYN}_M$. Take the Chen-Fox-Lyndon factorization $w=u_1*u_2*\dots*u_m$ of $w$ and consider, using the preceding theorem, $$ u_1\times_{sh}u_2\times_{sh}\dots\times_{sh}u_m=aw+(\mbox{reminder}). $$ By the theorem the coefficient $a$ is nonzero and all the words in (reminder) are lexicographically smaller than $w$, hence they belong to $\mathbb Q[\mathrm{LYN}_M]$. Therefore $w\in\mathbb Q[\mathrm{LYN}_M]$. This proves generation.
nodes.statement_short: Inductive step: CFL shuffle theorem expresses w through smaller words.

nodes.name: Dimension count gives algebraic independence.
nodes.statement: Since each monomial in $(2n)$-th graded component of $\mathcal{N}\otimes \mathbb Q$ has a unique Chen-Fox-Lyndon decomposition, the number of monomials in $\mathbb Q[\mathrm{LYN}_M]$ of graduation $2n$ is equal to the number of monomials of the same graduation in $\mathcal{N}_{M}\otimes\mathbb Q$, monomials in Lyndon words are linearly independent. This proves that Lyndon words are algebraically independent.
nodes.statement_short: Dimension count gives algebraic independence.

nodes.name: Corollary 3.21 (duals of W_12 and W_odd are polynomial on Lyndon words)
nodes.statement: The graded dual algebras to the free associative Lie-Hopf algebras $\mathcal{W}_{12}=\mathbb Z\langle W_1,W_2\rangle$ and $\mathcal{W}_{odd}=\mathbb Z\langle W_1,W_3,W_5,\dots\rangle$ are free polynomial algebras in Lyndon words $\mathrm{LYN}_{12}$ and $\mathrm{LYN}_{odd}$ respectively.
nodes.label: Poly

nodes.name: Z tensor Q is isomorphic to W tensor Q
nodes.statement: The correspondence $$ 1+Z_1t+Z_2t^2+\dots+=\exp(W_1t+W_2t^2+\dots);\\ $$ defines an isomorphism of Hopf algebras $\mathcal{Z}\otimes\mathbb Q\simeq\mathcal{W}\otimes\mathbb Q$.

nodes.name: N is not free over the integers
nodes.statement: However it is not true that $\mathcal{N}$ is a free polynomial commutative algebra over the integers.

nodes.name: Bott-Samelson theorem
nodes.statement: By the Bott-Samelson theorem \cite{BS}, $\mathrm{H}_*(\Omega\Sigma X)$ is the free associative algebra $T(\widetilde\mathrm{H}_*(X))$ generated by $\widetilde \mathrm{H}_*(X)$.
nodes.statement_short: Homology of Omega Sigma X is the tensor algebra on reduced homology of X.

nodes.name: James splitting
nodes.statement: There is a nice combinatorial model for any topological space of the form $\Omega\Sigma X$ with $X$ connected, namely the James construction $JX$ on $X$. After one suspension this gives rise to a splitting \[ \Sigma\Omega\Sigma X \sim \Sigma JX \sim\bigvee_{n\geqslant1}\Sigma X^{(n)}, \] where $X^{(n)}$ denotes the $n$-fold smash power of $X$.

nodes.name: Example 4.1 (splitting of Omega Sigma S^2)
nodes.statement: There exists a homotopy equivalence \[ \Sigma\Omega\Sigma S^2 \to \bigvee\limits_{n\geqslant1} \Sigma(S^2)^{(n)}\simeq \Sigma \Big(\bigvee\limits_{n\geqslant1} S^{2n}\Big). \] Therefore there exists an $H$-map \, $\Omega \Sigma(\Omega\Sigma S^2) \to \Omega \Sigma \Big(\bigvee\limits_{n\geqslant1} S^{2n}\Big)$ that is a homotopy equivalence.

nodes.name: Topological realizations of the Hopf algebras
nodes.statement: We have the following Hopf algebras: \begin{itemize} \item[\textbf{I.}] \begin{enumerate} \item $\mathrm{H}_*(\mathbb CP^{\infty})$ is a divided power algebra $\mathbb Z[u_1,u_2,\dots]/I$, where the ideal $I$ is generated by the relations $u_iu_j-{i+j\choose i}u_{i+j}$, with the comultiplication \begin{equation} \Delta u_n=\sum_{k=0}^{n}u_k\otimes u_{n-k}; \end{equation} \item $\mathrm{H}^*(\mathbb CP^{\infty})=\mathbb Z[u]$ -- a polynomial ring with the comultiplication $$ \Delta u=1\otimes u+u\otimes 1; $$ \end{enumerate} \item[\textbf{II.}] \begin{enumerate} \item $\mathrm{H}_*(\Omega\Sigma\mathbb CP^{\infty})\simeq T(\tilde\mathrm{H}_*(\mathbb CP^{\infty}))=\mathbb Z\langle u_1,u_2,\dots\rangle$ with $u_i$ being non-commuting variables of degree $2i$. Thus there is an isomorphism of rings $$ \mathrm{H}_*(\Omega\Sigma\mathbb CP^{\infty})\simeq\mathcal{Z} $$ under which $u_n$ corresponds to $Z_n$. The coproduct $\Delta$ on $H_*(\Omega\Sigma\mathbb CP^{\infty})$ induced by the diagonal in $\Omega\Sigma\mathbb CP^{\infty}$ is compatible with the one in $\mathcal{Z}$: $$ \Delta u_n=\sum\limits_{i+j=n}u_i\otimes u_j $$ So there is an isomorphism of graded Hopf algebras. This gives a geometric interpretation for the antipode $\chi$ in $\mathcal{Z}$ : in $\mathrm{H}_*(\Omega\Sigma\mathbb CP^{\infty})$ it arises from the time-inversion of loops. \item $\mathrm{H}^*(\Omega\Sigma\mathbb CP^{\infty})$ is the graded dual Hopf algebra to $\mathrm{H}_*(\Omega\Sigma\mathbb CP^{\infty})$. \end{enumerate} \begin{thm*}\, [BR] There is an isomorphism of graded Hopf algebras: $$ \mathrm{H}_*(\Omega\Sigma \mathbb CP^{\infty})\simeq \mathcal{Z}=\mathbb Z \langle Z_1,Z_2,\dots\rangle,\quad \mathrm{H}^*(\Omega\Sigma \mathbb CP^{\infty})\simeq \mathcal{M}=\mathrm{Qsym}[t_1,t_2,\dots]. $$ \end{thm*} \item[\textbf{III.}] $\mathrm{H}_*(BU)\simeq \mathrm{H}^*(BU)\simeq\mathbb Z[\sigma_1,\sigma_2,\dots]\simeq\mathcal{C}$. It is a self-dual Hopf algebra of symmetric functions. In the cohomology $\sigma_i$ are represented by Chern classes. \item[\textbf{IV.}] \begin{enumerate} \item $\mathrm{H}_*(\Omega\Sigma S^2)=\mathrm{H}_*(\Omega S^3)=\mathbb Z[w]$ -- a polynomial ring with $\deg w=2$ and the comultiplication $$ \Delta w=1\otimes w+w\otimes 1; $$ \item $\mathrm{H}^*(\Omega\Sigma S^2)=\mathbb Z[u_n]/I$ is a divided power algebra. Thus $\mathrm{H}^*(\Omega\Sigma S^2)\simeq\mathrm{H}_*(\mathbb CP^{\infty})$. \end{enumerate} \item[\textbf{V.}] $\mathrm{H}_*(\Omega\Sigma(\Omega\Sigma S^2))\simeq\mathbb Z\langle w_1,w_2,\dots\rangle$. It is a free associative Hopf algebra with the comultiplication \begin{equation} \Delta w_n=\sum\limits_{k=0}^n{n\choose k}w_k\otimes w_{n-k} \end{equation} \item[\textbf{VI.}] $\mathrm{H}_*\Big(\Omega\Sigma\Big(\bigvee\limits_{n\geqslant1}S^{2n}\Big)\Big)\simeq \mathbb{Z}\langle \xi_1,\xi_2,\ldots\rangle$. It is a free associative algebra and has the structure of a graded Hopf algebra with the comultiplication \begin{equation} \Delta\xi_n = 1\otimes \xi_n + \xi_n\otimes 1. \end{equation} Therefore, $\mathrm{H}_*\Big(\Omega\Sigma\Big(\bigvee\limits_{n\geqslant1}S^{2n}\Big)\Big)$ gives a topological realization of the universal Lie-Hopf algebra $\mathcal{W}$. The homotopy equivalence \[ a \colon \Omega\Sigma\Big(\bigvee\limits_{n\geqslant1}S^{2n}\Big) \longrightarrow \Omega\Sigma(\Omega\Sigma S^2) \] induces an isomorphism of graded Hopf algebras \[ a_* \colon \mathbb{Z}\langle \xi_1,\xi_2,\ldots\rangle \longrightarrow \mathbb{Z}\langle w_1,w_2,\ldots\rangle, \] and its algebraic form is determined by the conditions: \[ \Delta a_*\xi_n = (a_* \otimes a_*)(\Delta\xi_n). \] For example, $a_*\xi_1 = w_1,\; a_*\xi_2 = w_2- w_1|w_1,\; a_*\xi_3 = w_3- 3w_2|w_1 + 2w_1|w_1|w_1$. \end{itemize}

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 5.1
nodes.statement: Let us prove the following lemma: \begin{lemma} Let $D\in\mathcal{D}(\mathrm{R})$ be an operator of graduation $2k$. Then for each space $\mathrm{R}^{2n},\;n\geqslant k$ there is a unique representation \begin{equation} D=u(d_2,d_3,\dots,d_k)+dw(d_2,d_3,\dots,d_{k-1}), \end{equation} and there is a unique representation \begin{equation} D=u'(d_2,d_3,\dots,d_k)+w'(d_2,\dots,d_{k-1})d, \end{equation} where $u,u',w,w'$ are polynomials. \end{lemma} \begin{proof} For $k=0$ and $1$ it is evident. Since $2d_2=d^2$, this is true for $k=2$. Let $k\geqslant 3$. Using the relations (\ref{PM}) we obtain $$ dd_i=(-1)^id_id+\left(d_2d_{i-1}-d_3d_{i-2}+\dots+(-1)^{i-1}d_{i-1}d_2\right)+(1+(-1)^{i+1})d_{i+1} $$ So the expressions (\ref{X5}) and (\ref{X6}) exist. Let $u(d_2,d_3,\dots,d_k)+dw(d_2,\dots,d_{k-1})=0$, where $u=\sum\limits_{|\omega|=k}a_{\omega}D_{\omega}$, and $w=\sum\limits_{|\omega|=k-1}b_{\omega}D_{\omega}$. Then for any $n$-dimensional polytope $P^n,\;n\geqslant k$ we have $$ \xi_1(u+dw)P^n=0, \quad \varepsilon_1(u+dw)P^n=0 $$ Since $u+dw$ has degree $2k$, this equality can be written as \begin{equation} \sum\limits_{|\omega|=k}a_{\omega}f_{n-k,\,n-k+j_1,\,n-k+j_1+j_2,\,\dots,\,n-j_l}(P^n)+\sum\limits_{|\omega|=k-1}b_{\omega}f_{n-k,\,n-k+1,\,n-k+1+j_1,\,\dots,\,n-j_l}(P^n). \end{equation} Using the generalized Dehn-Sommerville equations we obtain \begin{multline*} f_{n-k,\,n-k+1,\,n-k+1+j_1,\,\dots,\,n-j_l}=(-1)^{n-k-1}\left(\sum\limits_{j=0}^{n-k-1}(-1)^jf_{j,\,n-k+1,\,n-k+1+j_1,\,\dots,\,n-j_l}\right)+\\ +(1+(-1)^{n-k})f_{n-k+1,\,n-k+1+j_1,\,\dots,\,n-j_l} \end{multline*} All the sets $\{n-k,n-k+j_1,n-k+j_1+j_2,\dots,n-j_l\},\{j,n-k+1,n-k+j_1,\dots,n-j_l\}$ and $\{n-k+1,n-k+1+j_1,\dots,n-j_l\}$ for all $\omega$ are different and belong to $\Psi^n$. In the case of $\mathcal{RP}$ and $P^{k-1}$ we obtain that $n=k-1$, therefore $n-k=-1$ in the expression (\ref{FVECT}) vanishes and we obtain $$ \sum\limits_{|\omega|=k}a_{\omega}f_{j_1-1,\,j_1+j_2-1,\,\dots,\,n-j_l}(P^n)+\sum\limits_{|\omega|=k-1}b_{\omega}f_{0,\,j_1,\,\dots,\,n-j_l}(P^n). $$ Again all he sets $\{j_1-1,j_1+j_2-1,\dots,n-j_l\}, \{0,j_1,\dots,n-j_l\}$ for all $\omega$ are different and belong to $\Psi^n$. Since the vectors $\{f_{S}(Q),\,S\in\Psi^n\}, Q\in\Omega^n$ are linearly independent, we obtain that all $a_{\omega}$ and $b_{\omega}$ are equal to $0$, so the representation (\ref{X5}) is unique. We obtain that the monomials $D_{\omega}=d_{j_1}\dots d_{j_l},\;|\omega|=k,\;j_i\geqslant 2$ and $dD_{\omega}=dd_{j_1}\dots d_{j_l}\;|\omega|=k-1,\;j_i\geqslant2$ form a basis of the abelian group $\mathcal{D}(\mathrm{R}^{2n},\mathrm{R}^{2(n-k)})$. But each monomial $dD_{\omega},\;|\omega|=k,\;j_i\geqslant 2$ can be expressed as an integer combination of the monomials $D_{\omega'}$ and $D_{\omega'}d$. So the monomials $D_{\omega}$ and $D_{\omega}d$ also form a basis. This proves the second part of the lemma. \end{proof} Now let us prove the theorem. The mapping $\EuScript{L}_{\mathrm{R}}:\mathcal{Z}\to\mathcal{D}(\mathrm{R}):\; Z_i\to d_i$ is an epimorphism. Let $z\in\mathcal{Z}$ such that $\deg z=2k$ and $\EuScript{L}_{\mathrm{R}}z=0$. $$ z=\sum\limits_{|\omega|=k}a_{\omega}Z_{\omega}. $$ We know that $$ Z_1Z_{k-1}=(-1)^{k-1}Z_{k-1}Z_1+\sum\limits_{i=2}^{k-2}(-1)^iZ_iZ_{k-i}+(1+(-1)^k)Z_k-\sum\limits_{i=0}^{k}(-1)^iZ_iZ_{k-i}. $$ So $$ z=\sum\limits_{|\omega|=k,\;j_i\geqslant 2}a'_{\omega}Z_{\omega}+\sum\limits_{|\omega|=k-1,\;j_i\geqslant 2}b_{\omega}Z_{\omega}Z_1+z', $$ where $z'\in J_{\mathcal{U}}$. Since $\EuScript{L}_{\mathrm{R}}z=\EuScript{L}_{\mathrm{R}}z'=0$, we obtain $$ \sum\limits_{|\omega|=k,\;j_i\geqslant 2}a'_{\omega}D_{\omega}+\sum\limits_{|\omega|=k-1,\;j_i\geqslant 2}b_{\omega}D_{\omega}d=0, $$ Lemma \ref{basis} implies that all the coefficients $a_{\omega}'$ and $b_{\omega}$ are equal to $0$, so $z=z'\in J_{\mathcal{U}}$. This proves that $\mathcal{D}(\mathrm{R})\simeq \mathcal{Z}/J_{\mathcal{U}}$.
nodes.statement_short: Reduce any kernel element modulo J_U to a combination of D_omega and D_omega d with parts >= 2, then use Lemma 5.2 (unique normal form via Bayer-Billera independence).

nodes.name: Basis of the degree -2k operators.
nodes.statement: We obtain that the monomials $D_{\omega}=d_{j_1}\dots d_{j_l},\;|\omega|=k,\;j_i\geqslant 2$ and $dD_{\omega}=dd_{j_1}\dots d_{j_l}\;|\omega|=k-1,\;j_i\geqslant2$ form a basis of the abelian group $\mathcal{D}(\mathrm{R}^{2n},\mathrm{R}^{2(n-k)})$.
nodes.statement_short: Basis of the degree -2k operators.

nodes.name: Second normal form also a basis.
nodes.statement: But each monomial $dD_{\omega},\;|\omega|=k,\;j_i\geqslant 2$ can be expressed as an integer combination of the monomials $D_{\omega'}$ and $D_{\omega'}d$. So the monomials $D_{\omega}$ and $D_{\omega}d$ also form a basis. This proves the second part of the lemma.
nodes.statement_short: Second normal form also a basis.

nodes.name: Flag-number expansion (13)
nodes.statement: \sum\limits_{|\omega|=k}a_{\omega}f_{n-k,\,n-k+j_1,\,n-k+j_1+j_2,\,\dots,\,n-j_l}(P^n)+\sum\limits_{|\omega|=k-1}b_{\omega}f_{n-k,\,n-k+1,\,n-k+1+j_1,\,\dots,\,n-j_l}(P^n).
nodes.label: FVECT

nodes.name: Remark 5.3 (D(RP) = D(P))
nodes.statement: Now we see that the correspondence $d_k\to d_k$ defines a natural isomorphism between $\mathcal{D}(\mathcal{RP})$ and $\mathcal{D}(\mathcal{P})$. Therefore from this moment we will often use the notation $\mathcal{D}$ for both these algebras, and the notations $\EuScript{L}$, $\EuScript{R}$ for the homomorphisms $\EuScript{L}_{\mathrm{R}}$ and $\EuScript{R}_{\mathrm{R}}$.

nodes.name: Corollary 5.4 (D is a Leibnitz-Hopf algebra isomorphic to U)
nodes.statement: The comultiplication $d_k\to \sum\limits_{i+j=k}d_i\otimes d_j$ defines on $\mathcal{D}$ the structure of a Leibnitz-Hopf algebra over the ring $\mathbb Z$. This Hopf algebra $\mathcal{D}$ is isomorphic to the Hopf algebra $\mathcal{U}$, universal in the category of Leibnitz-Hopf algebras with the antipode $\chi(U_i)=(-1)^iU_i$. Both $\mathcal{P}$ and $\mathcal{RP}$ have natural left Milnor module structures over $\mathcal{D}$

nodes.name: D_omega vanishes on R^[2n] for |omega|>n
nodes.statement: It is evident that $\left.D_{\omega}\right|_{\mathrm{R}^{[2n]}}=0$ for $|\omega|>n$.

nodes.name: Corollary 5.5 (D(R^[2n]) = D(R)/J_n)
nodes.statement: We have $$ \mathcal{D}(\mathrm{R}^{[2n]})=\mathcal{D}(\mathrm{R})/J_n $$ where the ideal $J_n$ is generated by all the operators $D_{\omega},\;|\omega|>n$.

nodes.name: Proof of Corollary 5.5
nodes.statement: As in the proof of Theorem \ref{D} using Lemma \ref{basis} it is easy to show that $\mathcal{D}(\mathrm{R}^{[2n]})\simeq\mathcal{Z}/J_{\mathcal{D}(\mathrm{R}^{[2n]})}$, where the ideal $J_{\mathcal{D}(\mathrm{R}^{[2n]})}$ is generated by the the relations $\Phi(-t)\Phi(t)=1$ and $Z_{\omega}=0$ for $|\omega|>n$.
nodes.statement_short: As in Theorem 5.1 using Lemma 5.2.

nodes.name: Corollary 5.6 (d_2, d_3, ... algebraically independent)
nodes.statement: The operators $d_2,d_3,d_4,\dots$ are algebraically independent.

nodes.name: Corollary 5.7 (rank of D^{2n} is Fibonacci c_{n-1})
nodes.statement: Rank of the $(2n)$-th graded component of the ring $\mathcal{D}$ is equal to the $(n-1)$-th Fibonacci number $c_{n-1}$.
nodes.label: Fib

nodes.name: Proof of Corollary 5.7
nodes.statement: At first, let us calculate rank $\mathrm{rk}_n$ of the $(2n)$-th graded component of the ring $\mathbb Z\langle d_2,d_3,d_4,\dots\rangle$. $$ \mathrm{rk}_0=1,\;\mathrm{rk}_1=0,\;\mathrm{rk}_2=1,\;\mathrm{rk}_3=1,\;\mathrm{rk}_4=2,\;\mathrm{rk}_5=3,\dots $$ It is easy to see that there is a recursive relation $$ \mathrm{rk}_{n+1}=\mathrm{rk}_{n-1}+\mathrm{rk}_{n-2}+\dots+\mathrm{rk}_2+1,\;n\geqslant 3 $$ Then $\mathrm{rk}_{n+1}=\mathrm{rk}_{n-1}+\mathrm{rk}_n$. Since $\mathrm{rk}_2=\mathrm{rk}_3=1$, we obtain $\mathrm{rk}_n=c_{n-2},\; n\geqslant 2$. At last, rank of the $(2n)$-th graded component of the ring $\mathcal{D}$ is equal to $\mathrm{rk}_{n-1}+\mathrm{rk}_n=c_{n-3}+c_{n-2}=c_{n-1}$ for $n\geqslant 3$. It is easy to see that for $n=1$ and $2$ it is also true.
nodes.statement_short: Count monomials in d_2, d_3, ... by a Fibonacci recursion and add those times d.

nodes.name: Ranks of Z<d_2,d_3,...> in small degrees.
nodes.statement: At first, let us calculate rank $\mathrm{rk}_n$ of the $(2n)$-th graded component of the ring $\mathbb Z\langle d_2,d_3,d_4,\dots\rangle$. $$ \mathrm{rk}_0=1,\;\mathrm{rk}_1=0,\;\mathrm{rk}_2=1,\;\mathrm{rk}_3=1,\;\mathrm{rk}_4=2,\;\mathrm{rk}_5=3,\dots $$
nodes.statement_short: Ranks of Z<d_2,d_3,...> in small degrees.

nodes.name: Fibonacci recursion for rk_n.
nodes.statement: It is easy to see that there is a recursive relation $$ \mathrm{rk}_{n+1}=\mathrm{rk}_{n-1}+\mathrm{rk}_{n-2}+\dots+\mathrm{rk}_2+1,\;n\geqslant 3 $$ Then $\mathrm{rk}_{n+1}=\mathrm{rk}_{n-1}+\mathrm{rk}_n$. Since $\mathrm{rk}_2=\mathrm{rk}_3=1$, we obtain $\mathrm{rk}_n=c_{n-2},\; n\geqslant 2$.
nodes.statement_short: Fibonacci recursion for rk_n.

nodes.name: Rank of D^{2n} is rk_{n-1}+rk_n=c_{n-1}.
nodes.statement: At last, rank of the $(2n)$-th graded component of the ring $\mathcal{D}$ is equal to $\mathrm{rk}_{n-1}+\mathrm{rk}_n=c_{n-3}+c_{n-2}=c_{n-1}$ for $n\geqslant 3$. It is easy to see that for $n=1$ and $2$ it is also true.
nodes.statement_short: Rank of D^{2n} is rk_{n-1}+rk_n=c_{n-1}.

nodes.name: Proposition 5.8 (D tensor Q is free on odd d's)
nodes.statement: $$ \mathcal{D}\otimes\mathbb Q=\mathbb Q\langle d_1,d_3,d_5,\dots\rangle, $$ The inclusion $\mathcal{D}\subset\mathcal{D}\otimes\mathbb Q$ is an embedding, and the operators $d_{2k}$ are expressed in terms of the operators $d_1,d_3,\dots,d_{2k-1}$ by the formulas \begin{equation} d_{2k}=\sum\limits_{i=1}^{k}(-1)^{i-1}\frac{{2i-2\choose i-1}}{i2^{2i-1}}\left(\sum\limits_{j_1+j_2+\dots+j_{2i}=i+k,\,j_l\geqslant 1}d_{2j_1-1}\dots d_{2j_{2i}-1}\right). \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Rationally D is the free associative algebra on d_1,d_3,d_5,..., with d_{2k} given by formula (14).

nodes.name: Even face operators via odd ones (14)
nodes.statement: d_{2k}=\sum\limits_{i=1}^{k}(-1)^{i-1}\frac{{2i-2\choose i-1}}{i2^{2i-1}}\left(\sum\limits_{j_1+j_2+\dots+j_{2i}=i+k,\,j_l\geqslant 1}d_{2j_1-1}\dots d_{2j_{2i}-1}\right).
nodes.label: X7

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 5.8
nodes.statement: Let us denote $$ a(t)=\sum\limits_{k\geqslant 0}d_{2k}t^{2k},\quad b(t)=\sum\limits_{k\geqslant 0}d_{2k+1}t^{2k+1}. $$ Then \begin{gather*} \Phi(t)=a(t)+b(t)\;\quad\Phi(-t)=a(t)-b(t);\\ a(t)b(t)=\frac{\Phi(t)+\Phi(-t)}{2}\cdot\frac{\Phi(t)-\Phi(-t)}{2}=\frac{\Phi(t)^2-\Phi(-t)^2}{4}=b(t)a(t). \end{gather*} Then the relation $\Phi(-t)\Phi(t)=1$ is equivalent to the relations \begin{gather*} a(t)^2-b(t)^2=1;\\ a(t)b(t)=b(t)a(t). \end{gather*} Therefore $a(t)=\sqrt{1+b(t)^2}$ and the formula (\ref{X7}) is valid. Consequently all the operators $d_{2k}$ are expressed as polynomials in $d_1,d_3,\dots$ with rational coefficients. For example, $$ d_2=\frac{d^2}{2},\quad d_4=\frac{dd_3+d_3d}{2}-\frac{d^4}{8}. $$ This means that the algebra $\mathcal{D}\otimes\mathbb Q$ is generated by $d_1,d_3,d_5,\dots$. On the other hand, let us calculate the number of the monomials $d_{2j_1-1}\dots d_{2j_k-1}$ with $(2j_1-1)+\dots+(2j_k-1)=n$. Denote this number by $l_n$. Then $$ l_0=1,\;l_1=1,\;l_2=1,\;l_3=2,\;l_4=3,\dots, $$ and there is a recursive formula $l_{n+1}=l_{n}+l_{n-2}+l_{n-4}+\dots$ for $n\geqslant 2$. Hence $l_{n+1}=l_n+l_{n-1}$ for $n\geqslant 2$, and $l_n=c_{n-1}$ for $n\geqslant 1$. We see that the number of monomials of degree $2n$ is equal to dimension of the $(2n)$-th graded component according to Corollary \ref{Fib}. This implies that they are linearly independent over the rationals. Therefore $d_1,d_3,d_5,\dots$ are algebraically independent. At last, the inclusion $\mathcal{D}\subset \mathcal{D}\otimes\mathbb Q$ is an embedding, since $\mathcal{D}$ is torsion-free.
nodes.statement_short: Split Phi into even and odd parts: a^2-b^2=1 gives a=sqrt(1+b^2); count monomials to get independence.

nodes.name: Even and odd parts a(t), b(t) of Phi(t).
nodes.statement: Let us denote $$ a(t)=\sum\limits_{k\geqslant 0}d_{2k}t^{2k},\quad b(t)=\sum\limits_{k\geqslant 0}d_{2k+1}t^{2k+1}. $$ Then \begin{gather*} \Phi(t)=a(t)+b(t)\;\quad\Phi(-t)=a(t)-b(t);\\ a(t)b(t)=\frac{\Phi(t)+\Phi(-t)}{2}\cdot\frac{\Phi(t)-\Phi(-t)}{2}=\frac{\Phi(t)^2-\Phi(-t)^2}{4}=b(t)a(t). \end{gather*}
nodes.statement_short: Even and odd parts a(t), b(t) of Phi(t).

nodes.name: a = sqrt(1+b^2) gives formula (14).
nodes.statement: Then the relation $\Phi(-t)\Phi(t)=1$ is equivalent to the relations \begin{gather*} a(t)^2-b(t)^2=1;\\ a(t)b(t)=b(t)a(t). \end{gather*} Therefore $a(t)=\sqrt{1+b(t)^2}$ and the formula (\ref{X7}) is valid.
nodes.statement_short: a = sqrt(1+b^2) gives formula (14).

nodes.name: Generation by odd operators.
nodes.statement: Consequently all the operators $d_{2k}$ are expressed as polynomials in $d_1,d_3,\dots$ with rational coefficients. For example, $$ d_2=\frac{d^2}{2},\quad d_4=\frac{dd_3+d_3d}{2}-\frac{d^4}{8}. $$ This means that the algebra $\mathcal{D}\otimes\mathbb Q$ is generated by $d_1,d_3,d_5,\dots$.
nodes.statement_short: Generation by odd operators.

nodes.name: Count odd monomials: Fibonacci numbers.
nodes.statement: On the other hand, let us calculate the number of the monomials $d_{2j_1-1}\dots d_{2j_k-1}$ with $(2j_1-1)+\dots+(2j_k-1)=n$. Denote this number by $l_n$. Then $$ l_0=1,\;l_1=1,\;l_2=1,\;l_3=2,\;l_4=3,\dots, $$ and there is a recursive formula $l_{n+1}=l_{n}+l_{n-2}+l_{n-4}+\dots$ for $n\geqslant 2$. Hence $l_{n+1}=l_n+l_{n-1}$ for $n\geqslant 2$, and $l_n=c_{n-1}$ for $n\geqslant 1$.
nodes.statement_short: Count odd monomials: Fibonacci numbers.

nodes.name: Compare with Corollary 5.7 for independence.
nodes.statement: We see that the number of monomials of degree $2n$ is equal to dimension of the $(2n)$-th graded component according to Corollary \ref{Fib}. This implies that they are linearly independent over the rationals. Therefore $d_1,d_3,d_5,\dots$ are algebraically independent.
nodes.statement_short: Compare with Corollary 5.7 for independence.

nodes.name: Torsion-freeness gives the embedding.
nodes.statement: At last, the inclusion $\mathcal{D}\subset \mathcal{D}\otimes\mathbb Q$ is an embedding, since $\mathcal{D}$ is torsion-free.
nodes.statement_short: Torsion-freeness gives the embedding.

nodes.name: Logarithmic operators s_k
nodes.statement: Let us define operators $s_k$ by the formula $$ s(t)=s_1t+s_2t^2+s_3t^3+\dots=\log\Phi(t). $$

nodes.name: Even s_k vanish
nodes.statement: Then $s_1=d_1,\;s_2=0,\;s_3=d_3-\frac{d^3}{6}$, and so on. The relation $\Phi(-t)\Phi(t)=1$ turns into the relation $s(-t)+s(t)=0$. Thus $s_{2k}=0$ for all $k$.

nodes.name: Odd s_k are primitive derivations
nodes.statement: Also we have $\Delta s(t)=1\otimes s(t)+s(t)\otimes 1$, so each operator $s_{2k-1}$ is a derivation.

nodes.name: Proposition 5.10 (D tensor Q free Lie-Hopf on s_odd)
nodes.statement: There is an isomorphism of Hopf algebras $$ \mathcal{D}\otimes\mathbb Q=\mathbb Q\langle s_1,s_3,s_5,\dots\rangle, $$ where $\mathbb Q\langle s_1,s_3,s_5,\dots\rangle$ is a free Lie-Hopf algebra in the generators of degree $\deg s_{2k-1}=2(2k-1)$, $k\geqslant 1$, the comultiplication $\Delta s_{2k-1}=1\otimes s_{2k-1}+s_{2k-1}\otimes 1$, and the antipode $\chi(s_{2k-1})=-s_{2k-1}$
nodes.label: S

nodes.name: Phi is a ring homomorphism
nodes.statement: The mapping $\Phi:\mathcal{P}\to\mathcal{P}[t]$ is a ring homomorphism.

nodes.name: Iterated homomorphisms Phi_n
nodes.statement: Thus for each $n\geqslant 0$ we can define the ring homomorphism $\Phi_n:\mathcal{P}\to\mathcal{P}[[t_1,\dots,t_n]]$ as a composition: $$ \Phi_n(t_1,\dots,t_n)P=\Phi(t_n)\dots\Phi(t_1)P. $$

nodes.name: Quasi-symmetric function f_r(alpha,t_1,...,t_r)
nodes.statement: Let $P^n$ be an $n$-dimensional polytope. Let us define a quasi-symmetric function $$ f_r(\alpha,t_1,\dots,t_r)(P^n)=\xi_{\alpha}\Phi(t_r)\dots\Phi(t_1)P^n=\alpha^n+\sum\limits_{k=1}^{\min\{r,n\}}\sum\limits_{0\leqslant a_1<\dots<a_k\leqslant n-1}f_{a_1,\,\dots,\,a_k}\alpha^{a_1}M_{(n-a_k,\,\dots,\,a_2-a_1)}. $$
nodes.statement_short: f_r(P^n) = xi_alpha Phi(t_r)...Phi(t_1) P^n, a generating function of flag numbers in quasi-symmetric monomials.

nodes.name: f_1 is the homogeneous f-polynomial
nodes.statement: For $n=1$ we obtain $f_1(\alpha,t_1)(P^n)=\alpha^n+f_{n-1}\alpha^{n-1}t_1+\dots+f_0t_1^n$ is a homogeneous $f$-polynomial in two variables (\cite{Buch}). So the polynomial $f_n$ is a generalization of the $f$-polynomial.

nodes.name: Generalized f-polynomial f
nodes.statement: Consider the increasing sequence of rings $$ \mathbb Z[\alpha]\subset \mathbb Z[\alpha,t_1]\subset\mathbb Z[\alpha,t_1,t_2]\subset\dots $$ with the restriction maps $E_r:\mathbb Z[\alpha,t_1,\dots,t_{r+1}]\to\mathbb Z[\alpha,t_1,\dots,t_r]$ $$ (E_rg)(\alpha,t_1,\dots,t_r)=g(\alpha,t_1,\dots,t_r,0). $$ Since $f_{r+1}(\alpha,t_1,\dots,t_r,0)(P^n)=f_r(\alpha,t_1,\dots,t_r)(P^n)$, we obtain the ring homomorphism \begin{gather*} f:\mathcal{P}\to\mathrm{Qsym}[t_1,t_2,\dots][\alpha]\subset\varprojlim\limits_r\mathbb Z[\alpha,t_1,\dots,t_r]:\\ f(\alpha,t_1,t_2,\dots)(P^n)=\alpha^n+\sum\limits_{k=1}^{n}\sum\limits_{0\leqslant a_1<\dots<a_k\leqslant n-1}f_{a_1,\,\dots,\,a_k}\alpha^{a_1}M_{(n-a_k,\,\dots,\,a_2-a_1)}. \end{gather*}
nodes.statement_short: Inverse limit of the f_r gives the ring homomorphism f: P -> Qsym[alpha] encoding all flag numbers.

nodes.name: Composition omega(S) of a set S
nodes.statement: For a set $S=\{a_1,\dots,a_k\}\subset \{0,1,\dots,n-1\}$ let us denote by $\omega(S)$ the composition $(n-a_k,a_k-a_{k-1},\dots,a_2-a_1)$ of the number $n-a_1$.

nodes.name: f in terms of omega(S)
nodes.statement: Then we can write $$ f(P^n)=\sum\limits_{k\geqslant 0}\sum\limits_{S:\;l(S)=k}f_{S}\;\alpha^{a_1}M_{\omega(S)} $$

nodes.name: Restriction to r variables is injective for n <= r
nodes.statement: It follows from the formula, that the restriction $$ f(\alpha,t_1,\dots,t_r,t_{r+1},\dots)\to f(\alpha,t_1,\dots,t_r,0,0,\dots)=f_r(\alpha,t_1,\dots,t_r) $$ is injective on the space of all $n$-dimensional polytopes, $n\leqslant r$.

nodes.name: Theorem 6.3 (image of P^{2n} under f_r)
nodes.statement: The image of the space $\mathcal{P}^{2n}$ generated by all $n$-dimensional polytopes in the ring\linebreak $\mathrm{Qsym}[t_1,\dots,t_r][\alpha],\;r\geqslant n$ under the mapping $f_r$ consists of all the homogeneous polynomials $g$ of degree $2n$ satisfying the equations \begin{enumerate} \item \begin{align*} g(\alpha,t_1,-t_1,t_3,\dots,t_r)&=g(\alpha,0,0,t_3,\dots,t_r);\\ g(\alpha,t_1,t_2,-t_2,t_4,\dots,t_r)&=g(\alpha,t_1,0,0,t_4\dots,t_r);\\ \dots\\ g(\alpha,t_1,\dots,t_{r-2},t_{r-1},-t_{r-1})&=g(\alpha,t_1,\dots,t_{r-2},0,0); \end{align*} \item $$ g(-\alpha,t_1,\dots,t_{r-1},\alpha)=g(\alpha,t_1,\dots,t_{r-1},0); $$ \end{enumerate} These equations are equivalent to the Bayer-Billera (generalized Dehn-Sommerville) relations.
nodes.statement_short: f_r(P^{2n}), r>=n, is exactly the set of degree-2n polynomials satisfying the two families of functional equations, equivalent to Bayer-Billera relations.
nodes.label: f
