nodes.name: Proposition 6.7 (f_r collapses to f_1 iff P is simple)
nodes.statement: Let $r\geqslant 2$, and let $P^n$ be an $n$-dimensional polytope. Then $$ f_r(\alpha,t_1,\dots,t_r)(P^n)=f_1(\alpha,t_1+\dots+t_r)(P^n) $$ if and only if $P^n$ is simple. Here $f_1(\alpha,t)$ is a usual homogeneous $f$-polynomial in two variables.
assumptions: Let $r\geqslant 2$, and let $P^n$ be an $n$-dimensional polytope.
conclusions: if and only if $P^n$ is simple.

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 6.7
nodes.statement: On the ring of simple polytopes $ \left.d_k\right|_{\mathcal{P}_s}=\left.\frac{d^k}{k!}\right|_{\mathcal{P}_s}, $ so $\Phi(t)=e^{td}$. Then $\Phi(t_r)\Phi(t_{r-1})\dots\Phi(t_1)=\Phi(t_1+\dots+t_r)$, therefore $f_r(\alpha,t_1,\dots,t_r)(P^n)=f_1(\alpha,t_1+\dots+t_r)(P^n)$. On the other hand, let $f_r(\alpha,t_1,\dots,t_r)(P^n)=f_1(\alpha,t_1+\dots+t_r)(P^n)$. Then $f_2(\alpha,t_1,t_2)(P^n)=f_1(\alpha,t_1+t_2)(P^n)$. So $$ \alpha^n+\sum\limits_{i=0}^{n-1}f_i\alpha^i(t_1^{n-i}+t_2^{n-i})+\sum\limits_{0\leqslant i<j\leqslant n-1}f_{ij}\,\alpha^it_1^{n-j}t_2^{j-i}=\alpha^n+\sum\limits_{i=0}^{n-1}f_i\alpha^i(t_1+t_2)^{n-i} $$ In particular, $f_{01}=nf_0$, since the coefficients of the monomial $t_1^{n-1}t_2$ on the left and on the right are equal. Hence $2f_1=f_{01}=nf_0$. This implies that the polytope $P^n$ is simple.
nodes.statement_short: For simple polytopes Phi(t)=e^{td}; conversely compare the t_1^{n-1}t_2 coefficients to get 2f_1=nf_0.

nodes.name: Simple case: Phi is exponential.
nodes.statement: On the ring of simple polytopes $ \left.d_k\right|_{\mathcal{P}_s}=\left.\frac{d^k}{k!}\right|_{\mathcal{P}_s}, $ so $\Phi(t)=e^{td}$. Then $\Phi(t_r)\Phi(t_{r-1})\dots\Phi(t_1)=\Phi(t_1+\dots+t_r)$, therefore $f_r(\alpha,t_1,\dots,t_r)(P^n)=f_1(\alpha,t_1+\dots+t_r)(P^n)$.
nodes.statement_short: Simple case: Phi is exponential.

nodes.name: Assume equality and specialize to r=2.
nodes.statement: On the other hand, let $f_r(\alpha,t_1,\dots,t_r)(P^n)=f_1(\alpha,t_1+\dots+t_r)(P^n)$. Then $f_2(\alpha,t_1,t_2)(P^n)=f_1(\alpha,t_1+t_2)(P^n)$. So $$ \alpha^n+\sum\limits_{i=0}^{n-1}f_i\alpha^i(t_1^{n-i}+t_2^{n-i})+\sum\limits_{0\leqslant i<j\leqslant n-1}f_{ij}\,\alpha^it_1^{n-j}t_2^{j-i}=\alpha^n+\sum\limits_{i=0}^{n-1}f_i\alpha^i(t_1+t_2)^{n-i} $$
nodes.statement_short: Assume equality and specialize to r=2.

nodes.name: Coefficient comparison gives 2f_1=nf_0, so P is simple.
nodes.statement: In particular, $f_{01}=nf_0$, since the coefficients of the monomial $t_1^{n-1}t_2$ on the left and on the right are equal. Hence $2f_1=f_{01}=nf_0$. This implies that the polytope $P^n$ is simple.
nodes.statement_short: Coefficient comparison gives 2f_1=nf_0, so P is simple.

nodes.name: Remark 6.8 (infinitely many variables)
nodes.statement: Letting $r$ tend to infinity we obtain that $f(\alpha,t_1,t_2,\dots)(P^n)=f_1(\alpha,t_1+t_2+\dots)(P^n)$ if and only if $P^n$ is simple.

nodes.name: Simple case: the alpha-equation is the Dehn-Sommerville relations
nodes.statement: In the case of simple polytopes the equations of the first type are trivial, but the equation of the second type has the form: $$ f_1(-\alpha,t_1+\dots+t_{r-1}+\alpha)=f_1(\alpha,t_1+\dots+t_{r-1}) $$ If we denote $t=t_1+\dots+t_{r-1}$, then $f_1(-\alpha,\alpha+t)=f_1(\alpha,t)$. This equation is equivalent to the Dehn-Sommerville relations (after the change of variables $h(\alpha,t)=f_1(\alpha-t,t)$ it is equivalent to the fact that $h(\alpha,t)=h(t,\alpha)$)

nodes.name: Proposition 6.9 (f of d_k P via derivatives)
nodes.statement: For any polytope $P^n\in\mathcal{P}$ we have $$ f(\alpha,t_1,t_2,\dots)(d_kP^n)=\frac{1}{k!}\left.\frac{\partial^k}{\partial t^k}\right|_{t=0}f(\alpha,t,t_1,t_2,\dots)(P^n) $$
nodes.statement_short: f(d_kP) is the k-th Taylor coefficient in an added variable t of f(alpha,t,t_1,...)(P).
nodes.label: dk

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 6.9
nodes.statement: Indeed, both expressions belong to $\mathcal{Q}sym[\alpha]$, and they are uniquely defined by their restrictions to $n$ variables. Then we have \begin{multline*} \left.\left(\left.\frac{1}{k!}\frac{\partial^k}{\partial t^k}\right|_{t=0}f_{n+1}(\alpha,t,t_1,t_2,\dots)(P^n)\right)\right|_{t_{n+1}=t_{n+2}=\dots=0}=\\ \frac{1}{k!}\left.\frac{\partial^k}{\partial t^k}\right|_{t=0}f_{n+1}(\alpha,t,t_1,t_2,\dots,t_n)(P^n)=\frac{1}{k!}\left.\frac{\partial^k}{\partial t^k}\right|_{t=0}\xi_{\alpha}\Phi(t_n)\dots\Phi(t_1)\Phi(t)P^n=\xi_{\alpha}\Phi(t_n)\dots\Phi(t_1)d_kP^n=\\ f_n(\alpha,t_1,t_2,\dots,t_n)(d_kP^n)=\left.f(\alpha,t_1,t_2,\dots)(d_kP^n)\right|_{t_{n+1}=t_{n+2}=\dots=0} \end{multline*}
nodes.statement_short: Compare restrictions to n variables using f_r = xi_alpha Phi(t_r)...Phi(t_1).

nodes.name: Corollary 6.10 (expansion of f in an extra variable)
nodes.statement: \begin{gather*} f(\alpha,t,t_1,t_2,\dots)(P^n)=f(\alpha,t_1,t_2,\dots)(P^n)+f(\alpha,t_1,t_2,\dots)(dP^n)t+\\ +f(\alpha,t_1,t_2,\dots)(d_2P^n)t^2+\dots+f(\alpha,t_1,t_2,\dots)(d_nP^n)t^n\\ f_{r+1}(\alpha,t,t_1,\dots,t_r)(P^n)=f_r(\alpha,t_1,\dots,t_r)(P^n)+f_r(\alpha,t_1,\dots,t_r)(dP^n)t+\\ +f_r(\alpha,t_1,\dots,t_r)(d_2P^n)t^2+\dots+f_r(\alpha,t_1,\dots,t_r)(d_nP^n)t^n,\;r\geqslant 0; \end{gather*}
nodes.label: eqn

nodes.name: Proof of Corollary 6.10
nodes.statement: The first equality follows from Proposition \ref{dk}. In fact, both equalities can be proved directly: \begin{multline*} f_{r+1}(\alpha,t,t_1,\dots,t_r)(P^n)=\xi_{\alpha}\Phi(t_r)\dots\Phi(t_1)\Phi(t)P^n=\sum\limits_{k=0}^n\left(\xi_{\alpha}\Phi(t_r)\dots\Phi(t_1)d_kP^n\right)t^k=\\ =\sum\limits_{k=0}^{n}f_r(\alpha,t_1,\dots,t_r)(d_kP^n)t^k. \end{multline*} Letting $r$ tend to infinity we obtain the first equality.
nodes.statement_short: From Proposition 6.9, or directly by expanding Phi(t).

nodes.name: First equality from Proposition 6.9.
nodes.statement: The first equality follows from Proposition \ref{dk}.
nodes.statement_short: First equality from Proposition 6.9.

nodes.name: Direct expansion of Phi(t).
nodes.statement: In fact, both equalities can be proved directly: \begin{multline*} f_{r+1}(\alpha,t,t_1,\dots,t_r)(P^n)=\xi_{\alpha}\Phi(t_r)\dots\Phi(t_1)\Phi(t)P^n=\sum\limits_{k=0}^n\left(\xi_{\alpha}\Phi(t_r)\dots\Phi(t_1)d_kP^n\right)t^k=\\ =\sum\limits_{k=0}^{n}f_r(\alpha,t_1,\dots,t_r)(d_kP^n)t^k. \end{multline*}
nodes.statement_short: Direct expansion of Phi(t).

nodes.name: Pass to the limit.
nodes.statement: Letting $r$ tend to infinity we obtain the first equality.
nodes.statement_short: Pass to the limit.

nodes.name: f intertwines Phi with the variable-insertion map T
nodes.statement: The first equality of Corollary \ref{eqn} is equivalent to the condition $f(\alpha,t_1,t_2,\dots)(\Phi(t)P^n)=f(\alpha,t,t_1,t_2,\dots)(P^n)$. Thus we see that the following diagram commutes $$ \begin{CD} \mathcal{P} @>f>>\mathrm{Qsym}[t_1,t_2,\dots][\alpha]\\ @V{\Phi}VV @VTVV\\ \mathcal{P}[t]@>f>>\mathrm{Qsym}[t,t_1,t_2,\dots][\alpha] \end{CD} $$ where $f(t)=t$, and $T:\mathrm{Qsym}[t_1,t_2\dots][\alpha]\to\mathrm{Qsym}[t,t_1,t_2,\dots][\alpha]$ is a ring homomorphism: $$ Tg(\alpha,t_1,t_2\dots)=g(\alpha,t,t_1,t_2,\dots),\quad g\in\mathrm{Qsym}[t_1,t_2,\dots][\alpha]. $$
nodes.statement_short: f(Phi(t)P) = f(alpha,t,t_1,...)(P): f intertwines Phi and the shift T.

nodes.name: Remark 6.11 (finite-variable version)
nodes.statement: Note that $f_r(\alpha,t_1,\dots,t_r)(\Phi(t)P^n)=f_{r+1}(\alpha,t,t_1,\dots,t_r)(P^n)$ for all $r\geqslant 0$. Consider the ring homomorphism $T_{r+1}:\mathrm{Qsym}[t_1,\dots,t_r][\alpha]\to\mathrm{Qsym}[t,t_1,\dots,t_r][\alpha]$ defined as $$ T_{r+1}(\alpha)=\alpha,\quad T_{r+1}M_{\omega}(t_1,\dots,t_r)=M_{\omega}(t,t_1,\dots,t_r) $$ Then the corresponding diagram $f_r(\alpha,t_1,\dots,t_r)(\Phi(t)P^n)=(T_{r+1}f_r)(\alpha,t,t_1,\dots,t_r)$ commutes only for $r\geqslant n$.

nodes.name: Theorem 6.12 (characterization of the generalized f-polynomial)
nodes.statement: Let $\psi:\mathcal{P}\to\mathrm{Qsym}[t_1,t_2,\dots][\alpha]$ be a linear map such that \begin{enumerate} \item $\psi(\alpha,0,0,\dots)(P^n)=\alpha^n$; \item The following diagram commutes: $$ \begin{CD} \mathcal{P} @>\psi>>\mathrm{Qsym}[t_1,t_2,\dots][\alpha]\\ @V{\Phi}VV @VTVV\\ \mathcal{P}[t]@>\psi>>\mathrm{Qsym}[t,t_1,t_2,\dots][\alpha] \end{CD} $$ \end{enumerate} Then $\psi=f$.
nodes.statement_short: A linear map P -> Qsym[alpha] with psi(alpha,0,...)(P^n)=alpha^n intertwining Phi and T must equal f.

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 6.12
nodes.statement: The first condition implies that $\psi(\alpha,0,0,\dots)(p)=\xi_{\alpha}p$ for any $p\in\mathcal{P}$. Let $\psi(P^n)=\alpha^n+\sum\limits_{\omega}\psi_{\omega}(\alpha)M_{\omega}$, and let $\omega=(j_1,\dots,j_k)$. Since $\psi(\alpha,t,t_1,t_2,\dots)(P^n)=\psi(\alpha,t_1,t_2,\dots)(\Phi(t)P^n)$, we have $$ \psi(\alpha,y_1,y_2,\dots,y_k,t_1,t_2,\dots)(P^n)=\psi(\alpha,t_1,t_2,\dots)(\Phi(y_k)\dots\Phi(y_1)P^n) $$ Therefore, $$ \psi(\alpha,y_1,\dots,y_k,0,0,\dots)=\psi(\alpha,0,0,\dots)(\Phi(y_k)\dots\Phi(y_1)P^n)=\xi_{\alpha}\Phi(y_k)\dots\Phi(y_1)P^n=f(\alpha,y_1,\dots,y_k,0,0,\dots) $$ Hence $\psi_{\omega}(\alpha)=f_{S(\omega)}\alpha^{n-|\omega|}$, where $S(\omega)=\{n-|\omega|,n-|\omega|+j_k,\dots,n-j_1\}$. This is valid for all $\omega$, so $\psi=f$.
nodes.statement_short: Iterate the intertwining relation and set the remaining variables to 0 to recover all coefficients.

nodes.name: Condition 1 gives psi(alpha,0,...)=xi_alpha.
nodes.statement: The first condition implies that $\psi(\alpha,0,0,\dots)(p)=\xi_{\alpha}p$ for any $p\in\mathcal{P}$.
nodes.statement_short: Condition 1 gives psi(alpha,0,...)=xi_alpha.

nodes.name: Iterate the diagram to compare with f.
nodes.statement: Let $\psi(P^n)=\alpha^n+\sum\limits_{\omega}\psi_{\omega}(\alpha)M_{\omega}$, and let $\omega=(j_1,\dots,j_k)$. Since $\psi(\alpha,t,t_1,t_2,\dots)(P^n)=\psi(\alpha,t_1,t_2,\dots)(\Phi(t)P^n)$, we have $$ \psi(\alpha,y_1,y_2,\dots,y_k,t_1,t_2,\dots)(P^n)=\psi(\alpha,t_1,t_2,\dots)(\Phi(y_k)\dots\Phi(y_1)P^n) $$ Therefore, $$ \psi(\alpha,y_1,\dots,y_k,0,0,\dots)=\psi(\alpha,0,0,\dots)(\Phi(y_k)\dots\Phi(y_1)P^n)=\xi_{\alpha}\Phi(y_k)\dots\Phi(y_1)P^n=f(\alpha,y_1,\dots,y_k,0,0,\dots) $$
nodes.statement_short: Iterate the diagram to compare with f.

nodes.name: All coefficients agree.
nodes.statement: Hence $\psi_{\omega}(\alpha)=f_{S(\omega)}\alpha^{n-|\omega|}$, where $S(\omega)=\{n-|\omega|,n-|\omega|+j_k,\dots,n-j_1\}$. This is valid for all $\omega$, so $\psi=f$.
nodes.statement_short: All coefficients agree.

nodes.name: Remark 6.13 (T is an isomorphism; image of Phi)
nodes.statement: Let us mention that the mapping $T$ is an isomorphism $\mathrm{Qsym}[t_1,t_2,\dots][\alpha]\to\mathrm{Qsym}[t,t_1,t_2,\dots][\alpha]$, while $\Phi$ is an injection and its image is described by the condition: $p(t)\in\Phi(\mathcal{P})$ is and only if $\Phi(-t)p(t)\in\mathcal{P}$.

nodes.name: Image of simple polytopes lies in Z[alpha, sigma_1]
nodes.statement: On the ring of simple polytopes we have $f(\alpha,t_1,t_2,\dots)(p)=f_1(\alpha,t_1+t_2+\dots)(p)=f_1(\alpha,\sigma_1)(p)$, so the image of $\mathcal P_s$ belongs to $\mathbb Z[\alpha,\sigma_1]$. On the other hand, $\Phi(t)=e^{td}$, so we have the condition $f_1(\alpha,t_1)(e^{td}p)=f_1(\alpha,t+t_1)(p)$.

nodes.name: Proposition 6.14 (characterization of the f-polynomial of simple polytopes)
nodes.statement: Let $\psi:\mathcal{P}_s\to\mathbb Z[\alpha,t]$ be a linear mapping such that \begin{enumerate} \item $\psi(\alpha,0)(P^n)=\alpha^n$; \item One of the following equivalent conditions holds: \begin{enumerate} \item $\psi(\alpha,t_1)(e^{td}p)=\psi(\alpha,t+t_1)(p)$; \item $\psi(\alpha,t)(dp)=\frac{\partial}{\partial t}\psi(\alpha,t)(p)$. \end{enumerate} \end{enumerate} Then $\psi=f_1$.
nodes.statement_short: On simple polytopes a linear map with psi(alpha,0)=alpha^n that intertwines e^{td} (or d with d/dt) is f_1.
nodes.label: Simple

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 6.14
nodes.statement: Let conditions $1$ and $2a$ hold. Then $$ \psi(\alpha,t+t_1)(p)=\psi(\alpha,t_1)(e^{td}p)=\psi(\alpha,0)(e^{(t+t_1)d}p)=\xi_{\alpha}\Phi(t+t_1)p=f_1(\alpha,t_1+t)(p). $$ It remains to prove that conditions $2a$ and $2b$ are equivalent. Indeed, if $\psi(\alpha,t_1)(e^{td}p)=\psi(\alpha,t+t_1)(p)$, then $\psi(\alpha,t)(p)=\psi(\alpha,0)(e^{td}p)$, therefore $$ \frac{\partial}{\partial t}\psi(\alpha,t)(p)=\frac{\partial}{\partial t}\psi(\alpha,0)(e^{td}p)=\psi(\alpha,0)(e^{td}dp)=\psi(\alpha,t)(dp). $$ Now let $\psi(\alpha,t)(dp)=\frac{\partial}{\partial t}\psi(\alpha,t)(p)$. Then $$ \frac{\partial}{\partial t}\psi(\alpha,t_1)(e^{td}p)=\psi(\alpha,t_1)(d(e^{td}p))=\frac{\partial}{\partial t_1}\psi(\alpha,t_1)(e^{td}p) $$ Hence $\left(\frac{\partial}{\partial t}-\frac{\partial}{\partial t_1}\right)\psi(\alpha,t_1)(e^{td}p)=0$, so $\psi(\alpha,t_1)(e^{td}p)$ depends on $\alpha$ and $t+t_1$. Thus $\psi(\alpha,t_1)(e^{td}p)=\psi(\alpha,t+t_1)(e^{0d}p)=\psi(\alpha,t+t_1)(p)$.
nodes.statement_short: Under 1 and 2a, psi(alpha,t+t_1)=xi_alpha Phi(t+t_1); 2a and 2b are equivalent via a first-order PDE in t and t_1.

nodes.name: Conditions 1 and 2a give psi=f_1.
nodes.statement: Let conditions $1$ and $2a$ hold. Then $$ \psi(\alpha,t+t_1)(p)=\psi(\alpha,t_1)(e^{td}p)=\psi(\alpha,0)(e^{(t+t_1)d}p)=\xi_{\alpha}\Phi(t+t_1)p=f_1(\alpha,t_1+t)(p). $$
nodes.statement_short: Conditions 1 and 2a give psi=f_1.

nodes.name: Reduce to equivalence of 2a and 2b.
nodes.statement: It remains to prove that conditions $2a$ and $2b$ are equivalent.
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to equivalence of 2a and 2b.

nodes.name: 2a implies 2b by differentiation.
nodes.statement: Indeed, if $\psi(\alpha,t_1)(e^{td}p)=\psi(\alpha,t+t_1)(p)$, then $\psi(\alpha,t)(p)=\psi(\alpha,0)(e^{td}p)$, therefore $$ \frac{\partial}{\partial t}\psi(\alpha,t)(p)=\frac{\partial}{\partial t}\psi(\alpha,0)(e^{td}p)=\psi(\alpha,0)(e^{td}dp)=\psi(\alpha,t)(dp). $$
nodes.statement_short: 2a implies 2b by differentiation.

nodes.name: 2b gives a transport equation.
nodes.statement: Now let $\psi(\alpha,t)(dp)=\frac{\partial}{\partial t}\psi(\alpha,t)(p)$. Then $$ \frac{\partial}{\partial t}\psi(\alpha,t_1)(e^{td}p)=\psi(\alpha,t_1)(d(e^{td}p))=\frac{\partial}{\partial t_1}\psi(\alpha,t_1)(e^{td}p) $$ Hence $\left(\frac{\partial}{\partial t}-\frac{\partial}{\partial t_1}\right)\psi(\alpha,t_1)(e^{td}p)=0$, so $\psi(\alpha,t_1)(e^{td}p)$ depends on $\alpha$ and $t+t_1$.
nodes.statement_short: 2b gives a transport equation.

nodes.name: Hence 2a.
nodes.statement: Thus $\psi(\alpha,t_1)(e^{td}p)=\psi(\alpha,t+t_1)(e^{0d}p)=\psi(\alpha,t+t_1)(p)$.
nodes.statement_short: Hence 2a.

nodes.name: Graded dual Hopf algebra D^*
nodes.statement: Let us denote by $\mathcal{D}^*$ the graded dual Hopf algebra to $\mathcal{D}$.

nodes.name: Two embeddings of D^* into Qsym
nodes.statement: The mappings $\EuScript{L}\colon\mathcal{Z}\to\mathcal{D}$, $\EuScript{R}\colon\mathcal{Z}^{op}\to\mathcal{D}$, $Z_i\to d_i$ are surjections, so the dual mappings are injections. So the ring homomorphisms $\EuScript{L}^*$, and $\EuScript{R}^*=\varrho^*\circ\EuScript{L}^*$ define two embeddings $\mathcal{D}^*\subset\mathcal{Q}sym$, which are related by the involution $\varrho^*=*$.

nodes.name: L^* is a Hopf embedding, R^* twisted
nodes.statement: In fact, $\EuScript{L}^*$ defines an embedding $\mathcal{D}^*\subset\mathcal{Q}sym$ as a Hopf subalgebra, while for $\EuScript{R}^*$ we have $$ \Delta\circ\EuScript{R}^*=\tau_{\mathcal{Q}sym}\circ(\EuScript{R}^*\otimes\EuScript{R}^*)\circ\Delta, $$ where $\tau_{\mathcal{Q}sym}$ is a homomorphism $\mathcal{Q}sym\otimes\mathcal{Q}sym\to\mathcal{Q}sym\otimes\mathcal{Q}sym$ that interchanges the tensor factors: $\tau_{\mathcal{Q}sym}(x\otimes y)=y\otimes x$.

nodes.name: Restricted homomorphisms R_r^*
nodes.statement: For each $r$ let us define the ring homomorphism $\EuScript{R}_r^*:\mathcal{D}^*\to\mathrm{Qsym}[t_1,\dots,t_r]$ by the formula $$ \EuScript{R}^*_r(\psi)=\EuScript{R}^*(\psi)(t_1,\dots,t_r,0,0,\dots) $$

nodes.name: R_r^* is injective in degrees 2n <= 2r
nodes.statement: Since the restriction $\mathcal{Q}sym\to\mathrm{Qsym}[t_1,\dots,t_r]$ is injective for any graduation $(2n)$, $n\leqslant r$, we see that $\EuScript{R}_r^*$ is injective for graduations $(2n)$, $n\leqslant r$, of $\mathcal{D}^*$.

nodes.name: Theorem 7.3 (image of D^* in Qsym[t_1..t_r])
nodes.statement: Let $r\geqslant n$. Then the image of the $(2n)$-th, $n\geqslant 1$, graded component of the ring $\mathcal{D}^*$ in the ring $\mathrm{Qsym}[t_1,\dots,t_r]$ under the map $\EuScript{R}_r^*$ consists of all the homogeneous polynomials of degree $2n$ satisfying the relations: \begin{gather*} g(t_1,-t_1,t_3,\dots,t_r)=g(0,0,t_3,\dots,t_r);\\ g(t_1,t_2,-t_2,t_4,\dots,t_r)=g(t_1,0,0,t_4,\dots,t_r);\\ \dots\\ g(t_1,\dots,t_{r-2},t_{r-1},-t_{r-1})=g(t_1,\dots,t_{r-2},0,0). \end{gather*}
nodes.statement_short: R_r^*(D^*_{2n}), r>=n, consists exactly of the degree-2n quasi-symmetric polynomials invariant under t_i,-t_i -> 0,0.
nodes.label: D*

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 7.3
nodes.statement: The ring $\EuScript{R}^*(\mathcal{D}^*)\subset\mathcal Z^*$ consists of all the linear functions $\psi\in\mathcal{Z}^*$ satisfying the property: \begin{equation} \langle \psi, z_1\Phi(t)\Phi(-t)z_2\rangle=\langle\psi, z_1z_2\rangle \end{equation} for all $z_1,z_2\in\mathcal{Z}$, that is the coefficients of all $t^k,\;k\geqslant 1$, on the left are equal to $0$. We have $$ \EuScript{R}^*(\psi)=\sum\limits_{\omega}\langle\EuScript{R}^*(\psi),Z_{\omega}\rangle=\sum\limits_{\omega}\langle\psi,\EuScript{R}Z_{\omega}\rangle M_{\omega} $$ Therefore, \begin{multline*} \EuScript{R}^*_r(\psi)=\sum\limits_{k=0}^r\sum\limits_{(j_1,\,\dots,\,j_k)}\langle\psi,d_{j_k}\dots d_{j_1}\rangle M_{(j_1,\,\dots,\,j_k)}(t_1,\dots,t_r)=\\ =\sum\limits_{k=0}^r\sum\limits_{(j_1,\,\dots,\,j_k)}\langle\psi,d_{j_k}\dots d_{j_1}\rangle\sum\limits_{1\leqslant l_1<\dots< l_k\leqslant r}t_{l_1}^{j_1}\dots t_{l_k}^{j_k}=\\ =\sum\limits_{k=0}^r\sum\limits_{(j_1,\,\dots,\,j_k)}\sum\limits_{1\leqslant l_1<\dots<l_k\leqslant r}\langle\psi,d_{j_k}t_{l_k}^{j_k}\dots d_{j_1} t_{l_1}^{j_1}\rangle=\langle\psi, \Phi(t_r)\dots\Phi(t_1)\rangle \end{multline*} Then \begin{multline*} \EuScript{R}^*_r(\psi)(t_1,\dots,t_i,-t_i,\dots,t_r)=\langle\psi, \Phi(t_r)\dots\Phi(-t_i)\Phi(t_i)\dots\Phi(t_1)\rangle=\\ \langle\psi, \Phi(t_r)\dots\Phi(0)\Phi(0)\dots\Phi(t_1)\rangle=\EuScript{R}^*_r(\psi)(t_1,\dots,0,0,\dots,t_r) \end{multline*} On the other hand, let $g\in\mathrm{Qsym}[t_1,\dots,t_r]$ be a homogeneous polynomial of degree $2n$ satisfying all the relations of the theorem. Consider a unique homogeneous function $\psi\in\mathcal{M}$ such that $\deg\psi=2n$, and $\psi(t_1,\dots,t_r,0,0,\dots)=g$. Let us prove that $\psi$ belongs to the image of $\mathcal{D}^*$ under the embedding $\EuScript{R}^*$. It is sufficient to prove the relation (\ref{DRel}) in the case when $z_1,z_2$ are monomials. Since $$ \Phi(t)\Phi(-t)=1+(Z_1-Z_1)t+(2Z_2-Z_1^2)t^2+\dots=1+(2Z_2-Z_1^2)t^2+\dots,\mbox{ and }\deg\psi=2n, $$ the cases $\deg z_1+\deg z_2=2n$ and $2(n-1)$ are trivial. Let $$ z_1=Z_{\omega},\;z_2=Z_{\omega'},\;\omega=(j_1,\dots,j_l),\;\omega'=(j_1',\dots,j_{l'}'),\;|\omega|+|\omega'|=n-k,\;k\geqslant 2.$$ Then the only equality we need to prove is $$ \langle \psi, Z_{\omega}\left(\sum\limits_{i=0}^{k}(-1)^iZ_{k-i}Z_i\right)Z_{\omega'}\rangle=0 $$ Let us consider the equality $$ g(t_1,\dots,t_l,t_{l+1},-t_{l+1},t_{l+3},\dots,t_{l+2+l'},\dots,t_r)=g(t_1,\dots,t_l,0,0,t_{l+3},\dots,t_{l+2+l'},\dots,t_r). $$ The coefficient of the monomial $t_1^{j_1}\dots t_l^{j_l}t_{l+1}^{k}t_{l+3}^{j_1'}\dots t_{l+2+l'}^{j_{l'}'}$ on the left is exactly $$ \sum\limits_{i=0}^k(-1)^i\langle\psi, Z_{\omega}Z_{k-i}Z_iZ_{\omega'}\rangle=\langle\psi, Z_{\omega}\left(\sum\limits_{i=0}^{k}(-1)^iZ_{k-i}Z_i\right)Z_{\omega'}\rangle, $$ and on the right it is equal to $0$. So $\langle\psi, Z_{\omega}\Phi(t)\Phi(-t)Z_{\omega'}\rangle=0$ for all $\omega,\;\omega'$, therefore, $\psi\in\EuScript{R}^*(\mathcal{D}^*)$.
nodes.statement_short: R_r^*(psi) = <psi, Phi(t_r)...Phi(t_1)>; necessity from Phi(-t)Phi(t)=1, sufficiency by matching monomial coefficients with relation (15).

nodes.name: Characterize R^*(D^*) by relation (15).
nodes.statement: The ring $\EuScript{R}^*(\mathcal{D}^*)\subset\mathcal Z^*$ consists of all the linear functions $\psi\in\mathcal{Z}^*$ satisfying the property: \begin{equation} \langle \psi, z_1\Phi(t)\Phi(-t)z_2\rangle=\langle\psi, z_1z_2\rangle \end{equation} for all $z_1,z_2\in\mathcal{Z}$, that is the coefficients of all $t^k,\;k\geqslant 1$, on the left are equal to $0$.
nodes.statement_short: Characterize R^*(D^*) by relation (15).

nodes.name: R_r^*(psi) as a pairing with Phi(t_r)...Phi(t_1).
nodes.statement: We have $$ \EuScript{R}^*(\psi)=\sum\limits_{\omega}\langle\EuScript{R}^*(\psi),Z_{\omega}\rangle=\sum\limits_{\omega}\langle\psi,\EuScript{R}Z_{\omega}\rangle M_{\omega} $$ Therefore, \begin{multline*} \EuScript{R}^*_r(\psi)=\sum\limits_{k=0}^r\sum\limits_{(j_1,\,\dots,\,j_k)}\langle\psi,d_{j_k}\dots d_{j_1}\rangle M_{(j_1,\,\dots,\,j_k)}(t_1,\dots,t_r)=\\ =\sum\limits_{k=0}^r\sum\limits_{(j_1,\,\dots,\,j_k)}\langle\psi,d_{j_k}\dots d_{j_1}\rangle\sum\limits_{1\leqslant l_1<\dots< l_k\leqslant r}t_{l_1}^{j_1}\dots t_{l_k}^{j_k}=\\ =\sum\limits_{k=0}^r\sum\limits_{(j_1,\,\dots,\,j_k)}\sum\limits_{1\leqslant l_1<\dots<l_k\leqslant r}\langle\psi,d_{j_k}t_{l_k}^{j_k}\dots d_{j_1} t_{l_1}^{j_1}\rangle=\langle\psi, \Phi(t_r)\dots\Phi(t_1)\rangle \end{multline*}
nodes.statement_short: R_r^*(psi) as a pairing with Phi(t_r)...Phi(t_1).

nodes.name: Necessity from Phi(-t)Phi(t)=1.
nodes.statement: Then \begin{multline*} \EuScript{R}^*_r(\psi)(t_1,\dots,t_i,-t_i,\dots,t_r)=\langle\psi, \Phi(t_r)\dots\Phi(-t_i)\Phi(t_i)\dots\Phi(t_1)\rangle=\\ \langle\psi, \Phi(t_r)\dots\Phi(0)\Phi(0)\dots\Phi(t_1)\rangle=\EuScript{R}^*_r(\psi)(t_1,\dots,0,0,\dots,t_r) \end{multline*}
nodes.statement_short: Necessity from Phi(-t)Phi(t)=1.

nodes.name: Lift g to psi in M.
nodes.statement: On the other hand, let $g\in\mathrm{Qsym}[t_1,\dots,t_r]$ be a homogeneous polynomial of degree $2n$ satisfying all the relations of the theorem. Consider a unique homogeneous function $\psi\in\mathcal{M}$ such that $\deg\psi=2n$, and $\psi(t_1,\dots,t_r,0,0,\dots)=g$.
nodes.statement_short: Lift g to psi in M.

nodes.name: Goal psi in R^*(D^*); reduce to monomial z_1, z_2.
nodes.statement: Let us prove that $\psi$ belongs to the image of $\mathcal{D}^*$ under the embedding $\EuScript{R}^*$. It is sufficient to prove the relation (\ref{DRel}) in the case when $z_1,z_2$ are monomials.
nodes.statement_short: Goal psi in R^*(D^*); reduce to monomial z_1, z_2.

nodes.name: Only nontrivial degrees remain.
nodes.statement: Since $$ \Phi(t)\Phi(-t)=1+(Z_1-Z_1)t+(2Z_2-Z_1^2)t^2+\dots=1+(2Z_2-Z_1^2)t^2+\dots,\mbox{ and }\deg\psi=2n, $$ the cases $\deg z_1+\deg z_2=2n$ and $2(n-1)$ are trivial. Let $$ z_1=Z_{\omega},\;z_2=Z_{\omega'},\;\omega=(j_1,\dots,j_l),\;\omega'=(j_1',\dots,j_{l'}'),\;|\omega|+|\omega'|=n-k,\;k\geqslant 2.$$ Then the only equality we need to prove is $$ \langle \psi, Z_{\omega}\left(\sum\limits_{i=0}^{k}(-1)^iZ_{k-i}Z_i\right)Z_{\omega'}\rangle=0 $$
nodes.statement_short: Only nontrivial degrees remain.

nodes.name: Coefficient comparison gives the relation.
nodes.statement: Let us consider the equality $$ g(t_1,\dots,t_l,t_{l+1},-t_{l+1},t_{l+3},\dots,t_{l+2+l'},\dots,t_r)=g(t_1,\dots,t_l,0,0,t_{l+3},\dots,t_{l+2+l'},\dots,t_r). $$ The coefficient of the monomial $t_1^{j_1}\dots t_l^{j_l}t_{l+1}^{k}t_{l+3}^{j_1'}\dots t_{l+2+l'}^{j_{l'}'}$ on the left is exactly $$ \sum\limits_{i=0}^k(-1)^i\langle\psi, Z_{\omega}Z_{k-i}Z_iZ_{\omega'}\rangle=\langle\psi, Z_{\omega}\left(\sum\limits_{i=0}^{k}(-1)^iZ_{k-i}Z_i\right)Z_{\omega'}\rangle, $$ and on the right it is equal to $0$. So $\langle\psi, Z_{\omega}\Phi(t)\Phi(-t)Z_{\omega'}\rangle=0$ for all $\omega,\;\omega'$, therefore, $\psi\in\EuScript{R}^*(\mathcal{D}^*)$.
nodes.statement_short: Coefficient comparison gives the relation.

nodes.name: Defining relation of R^*(D^*) (15)
nodes.statement: \langle \psi, z_1\Phi(t)\Phi(-t)z_2\rangle=\langle\psi, z_1z_2\rangle
nodes.label: DRel

nodes.name: Operations Theta_k
nodes.statement: Let us define the operations $\Theta_k:\mathbb Z[t_1,t_2,\dots]\to\mathbb Z[t,t_1,t_2,\dots]$ as $$ \Theta_kg(t_1,t_2,\dots)=g(t_1,\dots,t_{k-1},t,-t,t_k,t_{k+1},\dots) $$

nodes.name: Corollary 7.5 (R^*(D^*) = Theta-invariant quasi-symmetric functions)
nodes.statement: The ring $\EuScript{R}^*(\mathcal{D}^*)\subset\mathcal{Q}sym$ is defined by the equations $$ g\in\EuScript{R}^*(\mathcal{D}^*)\mbox{ if and only if }\;\Theta_kg=g \mbox{ for all } k\geqslant 1. $$
nodes.label: tD*

nodes.name: Proof of Corollary 7.5
nodes.statement: Let $g$ be a homogenous quasi-symmetric function of degree $2n$ representing the function $\psi\in\mathcal{D}^*$. Since $g$ has bounded degree, each monomial of $g(t_1,\dots,t_{k-1},t,-t,t_k,t_{k+1},\dots)$ appears with the same coefficient in the polynomial $g_{r+2}(t_1,\dots,t_{k-1},t,-t,t_k,\dots,t_r)=g(t_1,\dots,t_{k-1},t,-t,t_k,\dots,t_r,0,0,\dots)$, when $r$ is large enough. Then Theorem \ref{D*} implies that $$ g_{r+2}(t_1,\dots,t_{k-1},t,-t,t_k,\dots,t_r)=g_{r+2}(t_1,\dots,t_{k-1},0,0,t_k,\dots,t_r). $$ Therefore each monomial containing $t$ has coefficient $0$, so $g(t_1,\dots,t_{k-1},t,-t,t_k,\dots)$ does not depend on $t$. So we can set $t=0$ to obtain $$ g(t_1,\dots,t_{k-1},t,-t,t_k,\dots)=g(t_1,\dots,t_{k-1},0,0,t_k,\dots)=g(t_1,\dots,t_{k-1},t_k,\dots) $$ On the other hand, let $g\in\mathcal{Q}sym^{2n}$ be a quasi-symmetric function such that $\Theta_kg=g$ for all $k\geqslant 1$. Then for $g_n(t_1,\dots,t_n)=g(t_1,\dots,t_n,0,0,\dots)$ we have \begin{multline*} g_n(t_1,\dots,t_{i-1},t_i,-t_i,t_{i+2},\dots,t_n)=g(t_1,\dots,t_{i-1},t_i,-t_i,t_{i+2},\dots,t_n,0,0,\dots)=\\ =g(t_1,\dots,t_{i-1},t_{i+2},\dots,t_n,0,0,\dots)=g_n(t_1,\dots,t_{i-1},t_{i+2},\dots,t_n,0,0)=g_n(t_1,\dots,t_{i-1},0,0,t_{i+2},\dots,t_n) \end{multline*} for $1\leqslant i\leqslant n-1$. Then Theorem \ref{D*} implies that $g_n=\EuScript{R}_n^*(\psi)$ for some function $\psi\in\mathcal{D}^*$ of degree $2n$. Since the restriction $g(t_1,t_2,\dots)\to g(t_1,\dots,t_n,0,0,\dots)$ is injective for graduation $2n$, we have $g=\EuScript{R}^*\psi$.
nodes.statement_short: Pass between finitely many and infinitely many variables using Theorem 7.3.

nodes.name: Reduce to finitely many variables.
nodes.statement: Let $g$ be a homogenous quasi-symmetric function of degree $2n$ representing the function $\psi\in\mathcal{D}^*$. Since $g$ has bounded degree, each monomial of $g(t_1,\dots,t_{k-1},t,-t,t_k,t_{k+1},\dots)$ appears with the same coefficient in the polynomial $g_{r+2}(t_1,\dots,t_{k-1},t,-t,t_k,\dots,t_r)=g(t_1,\dots,t_{k-1},t,-t,t_k,\dots,t_r,0,0,\dots)$, when $r$ is large enough.
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to finitely many variables.

nodes.name: Theorem 7.3 gives Theta_k g = g.
nodes.statement: Then Theorem \ref{D*} implies that $$ g_{r+2}(t_1,\dots,t_{k-1},t,-t,t_k,\dots,t_r)=g_{r+2}(t_1,\dots,t_{k-1},0,0,t_k,\dots,t_r). $$ Therefore each monomial containing $t$ has coefficient $0$, so $g(t_1,\dots,t_{k-1},t,-t,t_k,\dots)$ does not depend on $t$. So we can set $t=0$ to obtain $$ g(t_1,\dots,t_{k-1},t,-t,t_k,\dots)=g(t_1,\dots,t_{k-1},0,0,t_k,\dots)=g(t_1,\dots,t_{k-1},t_k,\dots) $$
nodes.statement_short: Theorem 7.3 gives Theta_k g = g.

nodes.name: Converse: restrictions satisfy the relations.
nodes.statement: On the other hand, let $g\in\mathcal{Q}sym^{2n}$ be a quasi-symmetric function such that $\Theta_kg=g$ for all $k\geqslant 1$. Then for $g_n(t_1,\dots,t_n)=g(t_1,\dots,t_n,0,0,\dots)$ we have \begin{multline*} g_n(t_1,\dots,t_{i-1},t_i,-t_i,t_{i+2},\dots,t_n)=g(t_1,\dots,t_{i-1},t_i,-t_i,t_{i+2},\dots,t_n,0,0,\dots)=\\ =g(t_1,\dots,t_{i-1},t_{i+2},\dots,t_n,0,0,\dots)=g_n(t_1,\dots,t_{i-1},t_{i+2},\dots,t_n,0,0)=g_n(t_1,\dots,t_{i-1},0,0,t_{i+2},\dots,t_n) \end{multline*} for $1\leqslant i\leqslant n-1$.
nodes.statement_short: Converse: restrictions satisfy the relations.

nodes.name: Injectivity of restriction finishes.
nodes.statement: Then Theorem \ref{D*} implies that $g_n=\EuScript{R}_n^*(\psi)$ for some function $\psi\in\mathcal{D}^*$ of degree $2n$. Since the restriction $g(t_1,t_2,\dots)\to g(t_1,\dots,t_n,0,0,\dots)$ is injective for graduation $2n$, we have $g=\EuScript{R}^*\psi$.
nodes.statement_short: Injectivity of restriction finishes.

nodes.name: Remark 7.6 (same for L^*)
nodes.statement: Since $\EuScript{R}^*=\varrho^*\circ\EuScript{L}^*$, and the subring $\EuScript{R}^*(\mathcal{D}^*)\subset\mathcal{Q}sym$ is invariant under the involution $\varrho^*=*$, Theorem \ref{D*} and Corollary \ref{tD*} remain valid for the mapping $\EuScript{L}^*$.

nodes.name: Proposition 7.7 (D^* tensor Q = Q[LYN_odd])
nodes.statement: $\mathcal{D}^*\otimes\mathbb Q$ is a free polynomial algebra $$ \mathcal{D}^*\otimes\mathbb Q\simeq\mathbb Q[\mathrm{LYN}_{odd}], $$ where $\mathrm{LYN}_{odd}$ are Lyndon words consisting of odd positive integers. Rank of the $(2n)$-th graded component of $\mathcal{D}^*\otimes\mathbb Q$ is equal to the $(n-1)$-th Fibonacci number $c_{n-1}$.
nodes.statement_short: Rationally D^* is the free polynomial algebra on Lyndon words in odd letters, with Fibonacci ranks c_{n-1}.
nodes.label: DFM

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 7.7
nodes.statement: This follows from Proposition \ref{S}, Corollary \ref{Poly} to the shuffle algebra structure theorem, and Corollary \ref{Fib}.
nodes.statement_short: Combine Prop 5.10, Cor 3.21 and Cor 5.7.

nodes.name: Graded ring D^*[alpha]
nodes.statement: Let $\mathcal{D}^*[\alpha]$ be a graded ring of polynomials in variable $\alpha$, where $\deg \alpha=2$, and for the element $\psi_i$ of graduation $2i$ the element $\psi_i\alpha^j$ has graduation $2(i+j)$.

nodes.name: Map varphi_alpha: P -> D^*[alpha]
nodes.statement: Let us consider the mapping $\varphi_{\alpha}\colon\mathcal{P}\to\mathcal{D}^*[\alpha]$, defined by the formula $$ \langle\varphi_{\alpha}(P),D\rangle=\xi_{\alpha}(DP) $$ for $D\in\mathcal{D}$.

nodes.name: varphi_alpha is a ring homomorphism
nodes.statement: Then $$ \langle\varphi_{\alpha}(P\times Q),D\rangle=\xi_{\alpha}\left(D(P\times Q)\right)=\xi_{\alpha}\left(\sum\limits_{i}D'_i P\times D''_i Q\right)=\sum\limits_{i}\left(\xi_{\alpha}D_i'P\right)\left(\xi_{\alpha}D_i''Q\right)= \langle\varphi_{\alpha}(P)\,\cdot\,\varphi_{\alpha}(Q),D\rangle, $$ where $\Delta(D)=\sum\limits_{i}D_i'\otimes D_i''$. So $\varphi_{\alpha}$ is a ring homomorphism.

nodes.name: Proposition 7.8 (R^* o varphi_alpha = f)
nodes.statement: We have $\EuScript{R}^*\circ\varphi_{\alpha}=f$, where $f$ is the generalized $f$-polynomial.

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 7.8
nodes.statement: Indeed, \begin{multline*} \EuScript{R}^*\circ\varphi_{\alpha}(P)=\sum\limits_{\omega}\langle \EuScript{R}^*\circ\varphi_{\alpha}(P), Z_{\omega}\rangle\, M_{\omega}=\sum\limits_{\omega}\langle\varphi_{\alpha}(P),\EuScript{R}Z_{\omega}\rangle\, M_{\omega}=\\ =\sum\limits_{\omega}\langle\varphi_{\alpha}(P), D_{\omega^*}\rangle\, M_{\omega}=\sum\limits_{\omega}\xi_{\alpha}(D_{\omega}P)\,M_{\omega^*}=f(P) \end{multline*}
nodes.statement_short: Expand in the dual basis M_omega.

nodes.name: Proposition 7.9 (image of P^{2n} under varphi_alpha)
nodes.statement: The image of the space $\mathcal{P}^{2n}$ under the mapping $\varphi_{\alpha}:\mathcal{P}\to\mathcal{D}^*[\alpha]$ consists of all homogeneous functions $\psi(\alpha)$ of degree $2n$ such that \begin{equation} \langle\psi(-\alpha),\Phi(\alpha)D\rangle=\langle\psi(\alpha),D\rangle \end{equation} for all $D\in\mathcal{D}$.
nodes.statement_short: varphi_alpha(P^{2n}) consists of degree-2n psi(alpha) with <psi(-alpha), Phi(alpha)D> = <psi(alpha), D>.

nodes.name: Image condition (16)
nodes.statement: \langle\psi(-\alpha),\Phi(\alpha)D\rangle=\langle\psi(\alpha),D\rangle
nodes.label: X8

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 7.9
nodes.statement: According to Proposition \ref{Euler} we have $\xi_{-\alpha}\Phi(\alpha)=\xi_{\alpha}$, so if $\psi(\alpha)=\varphi_{\alpha}(p)$, then $$ \langle\psi(-\alpha),\Phi(\alpha)D\rangle=\xi_{-\alpha}\Phi(\alpha)Dp=\xi_{\alpha}Dp=\langle\psi(\alpha),D\rangle. $$ On the other hand, let condition (\ref{X8}) hold. Then the polynomial $g(\alpha,t_1,\dots,t_n)=\EuScript{R}^*_n\psi(\alpha)$ satisfies the relation \begin{multline*} g(-\alpha,t_1,\dots,t_{n-1},\alpha)=\langle\psi(-\alpha),\Phi(\alpha)\Phi(t_{n-1})\dots\Phi(t_1)\rangle=\\ =\langle\psi(\alpha),\Phi(0)\Phi(t_{n-1})\dots\Phi(t_1)\rangle=g(\alpha,t_1,\dots,t_{n-1},0). \end{multline*} Theorem \ref{D*} implies that the polynomial $g$ satisfies all the relations of Theorem \ref{f}, so $g=f_n(p^n)$ for some $p^n\in\mathcal{P}^{2n}$. We have $\EuScript{R}^*_n\psi(\alpha)=g=f_n(p^n)=\EuScript{R}^*_n\varphi_{\alpha}(p^n)$. Since the restriction $\EuScript{R}^*\to \EuScript{R}^*_n$ is injective on the $(2j)$-th graded component of the ring\; $\mathcal{D}^*$ for $j\leqslant n$, and $\EuScript{R}^*$ is an embedding, we obtain that $\psi(\alpha)=\varphi_{\alpha}(p^n)$.
nodes.statement_short: Necessity from Prop 2.53; sufficiency via Theorems 7.3 and 6.3.

nodes.name: Necessity from Proposition 2.53.
nodes.statement: According to Proposition \ref{Euler} we have $\xi_{-\alpha}\Phi(\alpha)=\xi_{\alpha}$, so if $\psi(\alpha)=\varphi_{\alpha}(p)$, then $$ \langle\psi(-\alpha),\Phi(\alpha)D\rangle=\xi_{-\alpha}\Phi(\alpha)Dp=\xi_{\alpha}Dp=\langle\psi(\alpha),D\rangle. $$
nodes.statement_short: Necessity from Proposition 2.53.

nodes.name: g = R_n^* psi satisfies the alpha-equation.
nodes.statement: On the other hand, let condition (\ref{X8}) hold. Then the polynomial $g(\alpha,t_1,\dots,t_n)=\EuScript{R}^*_n\psi(\alpha)$ satisfies the relation \begin{multline*} g(-\alpha,t_1,\dots,t_{n-1},\alpha)=\langle\psi(-\alpha),\Phi(\alpha)\Phi(t_{n-1})\dots\Phi(t_1)\rangle=\\ =\langle\psi(\alpha),\Phi(0)\Phi(t_{n-1})\dots\Phi(t_1)\rangle=g(\alpha,t_1,\dots,t_{n-1},0). \end{multline*}
nodes.statement_short: g = R_n^* psi satisfies the alpha-equation.

nodes.name: Theorems 7.3 and 6.3 give g = f_n(p^n).
nodes.statement: Theorem \ref{D*} implies that the polynomial $g$ satisfies all the relations of Theorem \ref{f}, so $g=f_n(p^n)$ for some $p^n\in\mathcal{P}^{2n}$. We have $\EuScript{R}^*_n\psi(\alpha)=g=f_n(p^n)=\EuScript{R}^*_n\varphi_{\alpha}(p^n)$.
nodes.statement_short: Theorems 7.3 and 6.3 give g = f_n(p^n).

nodes.name: Injectivity concludes.
nodes.statement: Since the restriction $\EuScript{R}^*\to \EuScript{R}^*_n$ is injective on the $(2j)$-th graded component of the ring\; $\mathcal{D}^*$ for $j\leqslant n$, and $\EuScript{R}^*$ is an embedding, we obtain that $\psi(\alpha)=\varphi_{\alpha}(p^n)$.
nodes.statement_short: Injectivity concludes.

nodes.name: Right action of D on D^*
nodes.statement: There is a right action of the ring $\mathcal{D}$ on its graded dual $\mathcal{D}^*$: $$ (\psi,D)\to\psi D\colon\quad \langle \psi D, D'\rangle=\langle \psi, DD'\rangle. $$ If $\deg\psi=2n$ and $\deg D=2k$, then $\deg\psi D=2(n-k)$. Similarly, there is an action of $\mathcal{D}[[\alpha]]$ on $\mathcal{D}^*[[\alpha]]$.

nodes.name: Proof of Corollary 7.10
nodes.statement: Then condition (\ref{X8}) means that $\psi(-\alpha)\Phi(\alpha)=\psi(\alpha)$. Since for any homogeneous function $\psi(\alpha)$ of degree $2n$ the function $\psi(\alpha)\Phi(\alpha)$ still has degree $2n$, we obtain the corollary.
nodes.statement_short: Rewrite (16) using the right action as psi(-alpha)Phi(alpha)=psi(alpha); degree is preserved.

nodes.name: Corollary 7.10 (image of varphi_alpha)
nodes.statement: Let $\psi(\alpha)\in\mathcal{D}^*[\alpha]$. Then \begin{equation} \psi(\alpha)\in \varphi_{\alpha}(\mathcal{P})\Leftrightarrow \psi(-\alpha)\Phi(\alpha)=\psi(\alpha). \end{equation}
nodes.label: Im

nodes.name: Image criterion (17)
nodes.statement: \psi(\alpha)\in \varphi_{\alpha}(\mathcal{P})\Leftrightarrow \psi(-\alpha)\Phi(\alpha)=\psi(\alpha).
nodes.label: X9

nodes.name: Even/odd parts u(alpha), w(alpha) of psi(alpha)
nodes.statement: Let $\psi(\alpha)=\psi_0+\psi_1\alpha+\dots+\psi_n\alpha^n$, $u(\alpha)=\psi_0+\psi_2\alpha^2+\psi_4\alpha^4+\dots$, $w(\alpha)=\psi_1\alpha+\psi_3\alpha^3+\dots$.

nodes.name: Image relation u(Phi-1)=w(Phi+1)
nodes.statement: Then $u(\alpha)\Phi(\alpha)-w(\alpha)\Phi(\alpha)=u(\alpha)+w(\alpha)$. Therefore, \begin{equation} u(\alpha)\left(\Phi(\alpha)-1\right)=w(\alpha)\left(\Phi(\alpha)+1\right). \end{equation}

nodes.name: Relation (18)
nodes.statement: u(\alpha)\left(\Phi(\alpha)-1\right)=w(\alpha)\left(\Phi(\alpha)+1\right).
nodes.label: X10

nodes.name: Same image condition over Z[1/2]
nodes.statement: Consider the Hopf algebra $\mathcal{D}\otimes\mathbb Z[\frac{1}{2}]$. Then for the graded dual over $\mathbb Z[\frac{1}{2}]$ Hopf algebra we have: $(\mathcal{D}\otimes \mathbb Z[\frac{1}{2}])^*\simeq\mathcal{D}^*\otimes\mathbb Z[\frac{1}{2}]$. The condition that describes the image of the ring $\mathcal{P}\otimes\mathbb Z[\frac{1}{2}]$ in $\mathcal{D}^*\otimes\mathbb Z[\frac{1}{2}][\alpha]$ is the same, namely relation (\ref{X10}).

nodes.name: Proposition 7.11 (w = u (Phi-1)/(Phi+1) over Z[1/2])
nodes.statement: In the ring $\mathcal{D}^*\otimes\mathbb Z[\frac{1}{2}][\alpha]$ relation (\ref{X10}) is equivalent to the relation: \begin{equation} w(\alpha)=u(\alpha)\frac{\Phi(\alpha)-1}{\Phi(\alpha)+1}=u(\alpha)\frac{\frac{\Phi(\alpha)-1}{2}}{1+\frac{\Phi(\alpha)-1}{2}}=u(\alpha)\sum\limits_{k=1}^{\infty}(-1)^{k-1}\left(\frac{\Phi(\alpha)-1}{2}\right)^k. \end{equation}

nodes.name: Relation (19)
nodes.statement: w(\alpha)=u(\alpha)\frac{\Phi(\alpha)-1}{\Phi(\alpha)+1}=u(\alpha)\frac{\frac{\Phi(\alpha)-1}{2}}{1+\frac{\Phi(\alpha)-1}{2}}=u(\alpha)\sum\limits_{k=1}^{\infty}(-1)^{k-1}\left(\frac{\Phi(\alpha)-1}{2}\right)^k.
nodes.label: X11

nodes.name: Remark 7.12 (w is odd when u is even)
nodes.statement: In fact, equation (\ref{X11}) implies that the function $w(\alpha)$ is odd, if the function $u(\alpha)$ is even. Indeed, \begin{gather*} w(-\alpha)=u(-\alpha)\frac{\Phi(-\alpha)-1}{\Phi(-\alpha)+1}=u(\alpha)\frac{\frac{1}{\Phi(\alpha)}-1}{\frac{1}{\Phi(\alpha)}+1}=u(\alpha)(1-\Phi(\alpha))\Phi(\alpha)^{-1}(1+\Phi(\alpha))^{-1}\Phi(\alpha)=\\ =-u(\alpha)\frac{\Phi(\alpha)-1}{\Phi(\alpha)+1}=-w(\alpha). \end{gather*} Therefore for any even function $u(\alpha)$ the function $\psi(\alpha)=u(\alpha)+u(\alpha)\frac{\Phi(\alpha)-1}{\Phi(\alpha)+1}=u(\alpha)\frac{2\Phi(\alpha)}{\Phi(\alpha)+1}$ belongs to the image of $\varphi_{\alpha}$

nodes.name: Remark 7.13 (rational version)
nodes.statement: The same relation is valid in $\mathcal{D}^*\otimes\mathbb Q[\alpha]$.
nodes.label: uvQ

nodes.name: Classical map varphi_0
nodes.statement: Let us take $\varphi_{\alpha}(p)$ with $\alpha=0$. Then we obtain the classical map $$ \varphi_0:\mathcal{P}\to\mathcal{D}^*:\quad p\to\varphi_{0}(p)\quad\langle\varphi_0(p), D\rangle=\xi_{0}Dp,\;\forall p\in\mathcal{P},\;D\in\mathcal{D} $$

nodes.name: Proposition 7.14 (varphi_0 surjective over Z[1/2])
nodes.statement: The mapping $\varphi_0\otimes 1:\mathcal{P}\otimes\mathbb Z[\frac{1}{2}]\to\mathcal{D}^*\otimes\mathbb Z[\frac{1}{2}]$ is a surjection.

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 7.14
nodes.statement: Let $\psi_0\in\mathcal{D}^*\otimes\mathbb Z[\frac{1}{2}]$. Consider the element $\psi(\alpha)=u(\alpha)+w(\alpha)$, $u(\alpha)=\psi_0$, $w(\alpha)=\psi_0\frac{\Phi(\alpha)-1}{\Phi(\alpha)+1}$. According to $\mathbb Z[\frac{1}{2}]$-version of Corollary \ref{Im} we obtain that $\psi(\alpha)=\varphi_{\alpha}(p)\in\varphi_{\alpha}\otimes 1(\mathcal{P}\otimes\mathbb Z[\frac{1}{2}])$. Then $\psi_0=\psi(0)=\varphi_0(p)$.
nodes.statement_short: Lift psi_0 to psi(alpha)=psi_0 + psi_0 (Phi-1)/(Phi+1), which lies in the image.

nodes.name: Construct psi(alpha) from psi_0.
nodes.statement: Let $\psi_0\in\mathcal{D}^*\otimes\mathbb Z[\frac{1}{2}]$. Consider the element $\psi(\alpha)=u(\alpha)+w(\alpha)$, $u(\alpha)=\psi_0$, $w(\alpha)=\psi_0\frac{\Phi(\alpha)-1}{\Phi(\alpha)+1}$.
nodes.statement_short: Construct psi(alpha) from psi_0.

nodes.name: Corollary 7.10 puts psi(alpha) in the image.
nodes.statement: According to $\mathbb Z[\frac{1}{2}]$-version of Corollary \ref{Im} we obtain that $\psi(\alpha)=\varphi_{\alpha}(p)\in\varphi_{\alpha}\otimes 1(\mathcal{P}\otimes\mathbb Z[\frac{1}{2}])$.
nodes.statement_short: Corollary 7.10 puts psi(alpha) in the image.

nodes.name: Set alpha=0.
nodes.statement: Then $\psi_0=\psi(0)=\varphi_0(p)$.
nodes.statement_short: Set alpha=0.

nodes.name: Question 7.15 (integral image of varphi_0)
nodes.statement: What is the image of the map $\varphi_0$ over the integers?

nodes.name: Remark 7.16 (varphi_0 is not injective on P/Ker varphi_alpha)
nodes.statement: Let us note, that the space $\mathcal{P}/\mathrm{Ker}{\varphi_{\alpha}}$ consists of the equivalence classes of integer combinations of polytopes under the equivalence relation: $p\sim q$ if and only if $p$ and $q$ have equal flag $f$-vectors. Rank of the $(2n)$-th graded component of the group $\mathcal{P}/\mathrm{Ker}{\varphi_{\alpha}}$ is equal to $c_n$ (\cite{BB}, see also Section 2.5). On the other hand, by Corollary \ref{Fib} rank of the $(2n)$-th graded component of the ring $\mathcal{D}^*$ is equal to $c_{n-1}$ , so the mapping $\varphi_0:\mathcal{P}/\mathrm{Ker}\varphi_{\alpha}\to\mathcal{D}^*$ is not injective.

nodes.name: Example 7.17 (varphi_0 in small dimensions)
nodes.statement: Let us consider small dimensions. \begin{itemize} \item $n=1$. $\mathcal{P}/\mathrm{Ker}\varphi_{\alpha}$ is generated by $CC=I$. The ring $\mathcal{D}$ in this graduation is generated by $d$. Then $\varphi_0(I)=2d^*$. \item $n=2$. $\mathcal{P}/\mathrm{Ker}\varphi_{\alpha}$ is generated by $CCC=\Delta^2$ and $BCC=I^2$. $\mathcal{D}$ has one generator $d_2$. Then $\varphi_0(\Delta^2)=3d_2^*$, $\varphi_0(I^2)=4d_2^*$. Therefore, $d_2^*=\varphi_0(I^2-\Delta^2)$, $\mathrm{Ker}\varphi_0$ is generated by $3I^2-4\Delta^2$ \item $n=3$. $\mathcal{P}/\mathrm{Ker}\varphi_{\alpha}$ is generated by $BCCC, CBCC=CI^2, CCCC=\Delta^3$, while $\mathcal{D}$ is generated by $d_3,d_2d$. Then $$ \varphi_0(BC^3)=5d_3^*+18(d_2d)^*,\quad\varphi_0(CBC^2)=5d_3^*+16(d_2d)^*,\quad \varphi_0(C^4)=4d_3^*+12(d_2d)^* $$ So $\mathrm{Im} \varphi_0$ has the basis $d_3^*,\,2(d_2d)^*$ and $\mathrm{Ker}\varphi_0$ is generated by $2BC^3-6CBC^2+5C^4$. \end{itemize} Here by $D_{\omega}^*$ we denote the element of the dual basis: $\langle D_{\omega}^*,D_{\sigma}\rangle=\delta_{\omega,\,\sigma}$

nodes.name: Theorem 8.1 (f(P) tensor Q is a free polynomial algebra)
nodes.statement: The ring $f(\mathcal{P})\otimes\mathbb Q$ is a free polynomial algebra.

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 8.1
nodes.statement: According to Proposition \ref{DFM} we have: $$ \mathcal{D}^*\otimes\mathbb Q\simeq\mathbb Q[\mathrm{LYN}_{odd}], $$ where $\mathrm{LYN}_{odd}$ are Lyndon words consisting of odd positive integers. This is a free polynomial algebra. Therefore $\mathcal{D}^*\otimes\mathbb Q[\alpha]$ is a free polynomial algebra in the generators $\mathrm{LYN}_{odd}$ and $\alpha$. Let $\{f_{\lambda}\}$ be the functions in $\mathcal{D}^*\otimes\mathbb Q$ corresponding to the Lyndon words. Consider the polynomials $f_{\lambda}(\alpha)$ defined as $$ f_{\lambda}(\alpha)=u_{\lambda}(\alpha)+w_{\lambda}(\alpha);\quad u_{\lambda}(\alpha)=f_{\lambda},\quad w_{\lambda}(\alpha)=f_{\lambda}\frac{\Phi(\alpha)-1}{\Phi(\alpha)+1}=f_{\lambda}\frac{e^{s(\alpha)}-1}{e^{s(\alpha)}+1} $$ Each polynomial $f_{\lambda}(\alpha)$ is a homogeneous element of degree $\deg f_{\lambda}$. Let us identify $\mathcal{D}^*$ with its image in $\mathrm{Qsym}[t_1,t_2,\dots]$ under the embedding $\EuScript{R}^*$. Then according to Remark \ref{uvQ} we have: $f_{\lambda}(\alpha)\in f(\mathcal{P}\otimes\mathbb Q)=f(\mathcal{P})\otimes\mathbb Q$. \begin{lemma} $f(\mathcal{P})\otimes\mathbb Q=\mathbb Q[f_{\lambda}(\alpha),\alpha^2]$. \end{lemma} \begin{proof} At first let us proof that the polynomials $\{f_{\lambda}(\alpha)\},\,\alpha^2$ are algebraically independent. Let $g\in\mathbb Q[x,y_1,y_2,\dots,y_s]$ be a polynomial such that $g(\alpha^2,f_1(\alpha),\dots,f_s(\alpha))=0$. We can write this equality as $$ g_0(f_1(\alpha),\dots,f_s(\alpha))+g_2(f_1(\alpha),\dots,f_s(\alpha))\alpha^2+\dots+g_{2t}(f_1(\alpha),\dots,f_s(\alpha))\alpha^{2t}=0 $$ for some integers $s,t$. Let us set $\alpha=0$. Then we obtain $$ g_0(f_1,\dots,f_s)=0 $$ Since $\{f_{\lambda}\}$ are algebraically independent, $g_0\equiv 0$. Since $\mathcal{D}^*[\alpha]$ is a polynomial ring, we can divide the equality by $\alpha^2$ to obtain $$ g_2(f_1(\alpha),\dots,f_s(\alpha))+g_4(f_1(\alpha),\dots,f_s(\alpha))\alpha^2+\dots+g_{2t}(f_1(\alpha),\dots,f_s(\alpha))\alpha^{2t-2}=0 $$ Iterating this step in the end we obtain that all the polynomials $g_{2i}\equiv 0$, $i=0,1,\dots,2t$, so $g\equiv0$. Now let us prove that the polynomials $\{f_{\lambda}(\alpha)\},\alpha^2$ generate $f(\mathcal{P})\otimes \mathbb Q$. Let $\psi(\alpha)=\psi_0+\psi_1\alpha+\dots+\psi_n\alpha^n\in f(\mathcal{P})\otimes\mathbb Q$ be a homogeneous element of degree $2n$. The functions $\{f_{\lambda}\}$ generate $\mathcal{D}^*\otimes\mathbb Q$, so we can find a homogeneous polynomial $g_0\in\mathbb Q[y_1,\dots,y_s]$ such that $$ g_0(f_1,\dots,f_s)=\psi_0,\quad \deg f_i\leqslant 2n $$ Let us consider the element $\psi(\alpha)-g_0(f_1(\alpha),\dots,f_s(\alpha))\in f(\mathcal{P})\otimes \mathbb Q$. Since $\theta_1=\theta_0\frac{d}{2}$ for any $$ \theta(\alpha)=\theta_0+\theta_1\alpha+\theta_2\alpha^2+\dots+\theta_r\alpha^r\in f(\mathcal{P})\otimes \mathbb Q, $$ we obtain that $$ \psi(\alpha)-g_0(f_1(\alpha),\dots,f_s(\alpha))=\hat\psi(\alpha)\alpha^2. $$ is a homogeneous element of degree $2n$. $\hat\psi(\alpha)\alpha^2\in f(\mathcal{P})\otimes\mathbb Q$, so $\hat\psi(-\alpha)\alpha^2\Phi(\alpha)=\hat\psi(\alpha)\alpha^2$. Since $\mathcal{D}^*\otimes\mathbb Q[\alpha]$ is a polynomial ring, $\hat\psi(-\alpha)\Phi(\alpha)=\hat\psi(\alpha)$, so $\hat\psi(\alpha)\in f(\mathcal{P})\otimes \mathbb Q$ is a homogeneous element of degree $2(n-2)$. Iterating this argument in the end we obtain the expression of $\psi(\alpha)$ as a polynomial in $\{f_{\lambda}(\alpha)\}$ and $\alpha^2$. \end{proof} This lemma proves the theorem.
nodes.statement_short: Lift Lyndon generators f_lambda of D^* to f_lambda(alpha)=f_lambda 2Phi/(Phi+1); Lemma 8.2 shows these and alpha^2 freely generate f(P) tensor Q.

nodes.name: Goal 1: algebraic independence.
nodes.statement: At first let us proof that the polynomials $\{f_{\lambda}(\alpha)\},\,\alpha^2$ are algebraically independent.
nodes.statement_short: Goal 1: algebraic independence.

nodes.name: Take a relation g and split by powers of alpha^2.
nodes.statement: Let $g\in\mathbb Q[x,y_1,y_2,\dots,y_s]$ be a polynomial such that $g(\alpha^2,f_1(\alpha),\dots,f_s(\alpha))=0$. We can write this equality as $$ g_0(f_1(\alpha),\dots,f_s(\alpha))+g_2(f_1(\alpha),\dots,f_s(\alpha))\alpha^2+\dots+g_{2t}(f_1(\alpha),\dots,f_s(\alpha))\alpha^{2t}=0 $$ for some integers $s,t$.
nodes.statement_short: Take a relation g and split by powers of alpha^2.

nodes.name: At alpha=0 the relation forces g_0=0.
nodes.statement: Let us set $\alpha=0$. Then we obtain $$ g_0(f_1,\dots,f_s)=0 $$ Since $\{f_{\lambda}\}$ are algebraically independent, $g_0\equiv 0$.
nodes.statement_short: At alpha=0 the relation forces g_0=0.

nodes.name: Divide by alpha^2 and iterate.
nodes.statement: Since $\mathcal{D}^*[\alpha]$ is a polynomial ring, we can divide the equality by $\alpha^2$ to obtain $$ g_2(f_1(\alpha),\dots,f_s(\alpha))+g_4(f_1(\alpha),\dots,f_s(\alpha))\alpha^2+\dots+g_{2t}(f_1(\alpha),\dots,f_s(\alpha))\alpha^{2t-2}=0 $$ Iterating this step in the end we obtain that all the polynomials $g_{2i}\equiv 0$, $i=0,1,\dots,2t$, so $g\equiv0$.
nodes.statement_short: Divide by alpha^2 and iterate.

nodes.name: Goal 2: generation.
nodes.statement: Now let us prove that the polynomials $\{f_{\lambda}(\alpha)\},\alpha^2$ generate $f(\mathcal{P})\otimes \mathbb Q$.
nodes.statement_short: Goal 2: generation.

nodes.name: Match psi_0 by a polynomial in the f_lambda.
nodes.statement: Let $\psi(\alpha)=\psi_0+\psi_1\alpha+\dots+\psi_n\alpha^n\in f(\mathcal{P})\otimes\mathbb Q$ be a homogeneous element of degree $2n$. The functions $\{f_{\lambda}\}$ generate $\mathcal{D}^*\otimes\mathbb Q$, so we can find a homogeneous polynomial $g_0\in\mathbb Q[y_1,\dots,y_s]$ such that $$ g_0(f_1,\dots,f_s)=\psi_0,\quad \deg f_i\leqslant 2n $$

nodes.name: The difference is divisible by alpha^2.
nodes.statement: Let us consider the element $\psi(\alpha)-g_0(f_1(\alpha),\dots,f_s(\alpha))\in f(\mathcal{P})\otimes \mathbb Q$. Since $\theta_1=\theta_0\frac{d}{2}$ for any $$ \theta(\alpha)=\theta_0+\theta_1\alpha+\theta_2\alpha^2+\dots+\theta_r\alpha^r\in f(\mathcal{P})\otimes \mathbb Q, $$ we obtain that $$ \psi(\alpha)-g_0(f_1(\alpha),\dots,f_s(\alpha))=\hat\psi(\alpha)\alpha^2. $$ is a homogeneous element of degree $2n$.
nodes.statement_short: The difference is divisible by alpha^2.

nodes.name: The quotient is again in f(P) tensor Q.
nodes.statement: $\hat\psi(\alpha)\alpha^2\in f(\mathcal{P})\otimes\mathbb Q$, so $\hat\psi(-\alpha)\alpha^2\Phi(\alpha)=\hat\psi(\alpha)\alpha^2$. Since $\mathcal{D}^*\otimes\mathbb Q[\alpha]$ is a polynomial ring, $\hat\psi(-\alpha)\Phi(\alpha)=\hat\psi(\alpha)$, so $\hat\psi(\alpha)\in f(\mathcal{P})\otimes \mathbb Q$ is a homogeneous element of degree $2(n-2)$.
