nodes.name: Remark 10.14 (type I equations imply (23) for f_RP)
nodes.statement: Let us mention that in the case of $f_{\mathcal{RP},\,r}$ and $\mathrm{F}^*_r$ the equations of type (\ref{I}) contain all the generalized Dehn-Sommerville relations, and these equations for $f_{\mathcal{RP},\,r}$ imply the equation (\ref{I2}). This follows from the fact that $a_1$ can be equal to $-1$, which is not possible in the case of the generalized $f$-polynomial.

nodes.name: Proposition 10.15 (f_RP(RP) = F^*(RP))
nodes.statement: The correspondence $f_{\mathcal{RP}}\to\left.f_{\mathcal{RP}}\right|_{\alpha=0}=\mathrm{F}^*$ is an isomorphism of the images $f_{\mathcal{RP}}(\mathcal{RP})$ and $\mathrm{F}^*(\mathcal{RP})$.

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 10.15
nodes.statement: Indeed, it is clear that this mapping is an epimorphism. On the other hand, let $\mathrm{F}^*(P)=0$. Then all the flag numbers of the element $P\in\mathcal{RP}$ are equal to $0$. Therefore, $f_{\mathcal{RP}}(P)=0$, so the mapping is a monomorphism.
nodes.statement_short: Surjective by definition; F^*(P)=0 forces all flag numbers to vanish.

nodes.name: Corollary 10.16 (F^* onto R^*(D^*); rational structure)
nodes.statement: \begin{enumerate} \item The ring homomorphism $\mathrm{F}^*:\mathcal{RP}\to\EuScript{R}^*(\mathcal{D}^*)\subset\mathcal{Q}sym$ is an epimorphism, \item $\mathrm{F}^*(\mathcal{RP})\otimes\mathbb Q$ is a free polynomial algebra with dimension of the $(2n)$-th graded component equal to the $(n-1)$-th Fibonacci number $c_{n-1}$ ($c_0=c_1=1$, $c_{n+1}=c_{n}+c_{n-1}$, $n\geqslant 1$). \end{enumerate}

nodes.name: Proof of Corollary 10.16
nodes.statement: \begin{enumerate} \item Let $g\in\EuScript{R}^*(\mathcal{D}^*)$ be a quasi-symmetric function of degree $2n$. Then according to Theorem \ref{D*} $g_n(t_1,\dots,t_n)=g(t_1,\dots,t_n,0,0,\dots)$ satisfies the relations of type (\ref{I}). Therefore $g_n(t_1,\dots,t_n)=\mathrm{F}^*_n(P)$ for some $P\in\mathcal{RP}^{2n}$. Since the mapping $\mathcal{Q}sym\to\mathrm{Qsym}[t_1,\dots,t_n], t_j \to 0, j>n$ is injective on the graduation $(2n)$, we see that $g=\mathrm{F}^*(P)$. \item We see that $\mathrm{F}^*(\mathcal{RP})=\EuScript{R}^*(\mathcal{D}^*)$. Therefore, $$ \mathrm{F}^*(\mathcal{RP})\otimes\mathbb Q\simeq\mathcal{D}^*\otimes\mathbb Q\simeq\mathbb Q[\mathrm{LYN}_{odd}], $$ and $\dim \mathrm{F}^*(\mathcal{RP}^{2n})\otimes \mathbb Q=c_{n-1}$ according to Proposition \ref{DFM}. \end{enumerate}
nodes.statement_short: Use Theorem 7.3 and Theorem 10.12 for surjectivity, then Proposition 7.7.

nodes.name: Item 1: g restricts to an F^*_n image.
nodes.statement: Let $g\in\EuScript{R}^*(\mathcal{D}^*)$ be a quasi-symmetric function of degree $2n$. Then according to Theorem \ref{D*} $g_n(t_1,\dots,t_n)=g(t_1,\dots,t_n,0,0,\dots)$ satisfies the relations of type (\ref{I}). Therefore $g_n(t_1,\dots,t_n)=\mathrm{F}^*_n(P)$ for some $P\in\mathcal{RP}^{2n}$. Since the mapping $\mathcal{Q}sym\to\mathrm{Qsym}[t_1,\dots,t_n], t_j \to 0, j>n$ is injective on the graduation $(2n)$, we see that $g=\mathrm{F}^*(P)$.
nodes.statement_short: Item 1: g restricts to an F^*_n image.

nodes.name: Item 2: apply Proposition 7.7.
nodes.statement: We see that $\mathrm{F}^*(\mathcal{RP})=\EuScript{R}^*(\mathcal{D}^*)$. Therefore, $$ \mathrm{F}^*(\mathcal{RP})\otimes\mathbb Q\simeq\mathcal{D}^*\otimes\mathbb Q\simeq\mathbb Q[\mathrm{LYN}_{odd}], $$ and $\dim \mathrm{F}^*(\mathcal{RP}^{2n})\otimes \mathbb Q=c_{n-1}$ according to Proposition \ref{DFM}.
nodes.statement_short: Item 2: apply Proposition 7.7.

nodes.name: Remark 10.17 (rank comparison)
nodes.statement: Let us mention that $\deg L(P^n)=2(n+1)$, therefore, $\mathrm{rank} \mathrm{F}^*(\mathcal{RP}^{2(n+1)})=c_n=\mathrm{rank} f(\mathcal{P}^{2n})$

nodes.name: Proposition 10.18 (natural Hopf comodule structure of P over RP)
nodes.statement: Formula $$ \Delta_{\mathcal{RP}} P=\sum\limits_{F\subseteq P}F\otimes(P/F) $$ defines a natural graded right Hopf comodule structure $\Delta_{\mathcal{RP}}\colon\mathcal{P}\to\mathcal{P}\otimes\mathcal{RP}$ on the ring $\mathcal{P}$ over the Hopf algebra $\mathcal{RP}$.
nodes.statement_short: Delta_RP P = sum F (x) P/F is a ring homomorphism making P a right Hopf comodule over RP.

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 10.18
nodes.statement: We should proof that the following two diagrams commute $$ \xymatrix{ \mathcal{P}\ar[d]^{\Delta_{\mathcal{RP}}}\ar[rr]^{\Delta_{\mathcal{RP}}}&&\mathcal{P}\otimes\mathcal{RP}\ar[d]^{\mathrm{id}\otimes\Delta}\\ \mathcal{P}\otimes\mathcal{RP}\ar[rr]^{\Delta_{\mathcal{RP}}\otimes\mathrm{id}}&&\mathcal{P}\otimes\mathcal{RP}\otimes\mathcal{RP}\\ } \hspace{2cm} \xymatrix{ \mathcal{P}\ar[d]_{\Delta_{\mathcal{RP}}}\ar[dr]^{\mathrm{id}\otimes 1}&\\ \mathcal{P}\otimes \mathcal{RP}\ar[r]^{\mathrm{id}\otimes \varepsilon}&\mathcal{P}\otimes\mathbb Z\\ } $$ and that $\Delta_{\mathcal{RP}}$ is a ring homomorphism. Indeed, we have \begin{multline*} (\Delta_{\mathcal{RP}}\otimes\mathrm{id})\circ\Delta_{\mathcal{RP}} P=(\Delta_{\mathcal{RP}}\otimes\mathrm{id})\left(\sum\limits_{F\subseteq P}F\otimes P/F\right)=\sum\limits_{F\subseteq P}\left(\sum\limits_{G\subseteq F}G\otimes F/G\right)\otimes P/F=\\ =\sum\limits_{G\subseteq P}G\otimes\left(\sum\limits_{G\subseteq F\subseteq P}F/G\otimes P/F\right)=\sum\limits_{G\subseteq P}G\otimes\Delta (P/G) =(\mathrm{id}\otimes\Delta)\circ\Delta_{\mathcal{RP}} P, \end{multline*} and $$ (\mathrm{id}\otimes\varepsilon)\circ\Delta_{\mathcal{RP}}(P)=\sum\limits_{F\subseteq P}F\otimes\varepsilon(P/F)=P\otimes 1, $$ Let us check that $\Delta_{\mathcal{RP}}$ is a homomorphism of rings $\mathcal{P}\to\mathcal{P}\otimes\mathcal{RP}$: \begin{multline*} \Delta_{\mathcal{RP}}(P\times Q)=\sum\limits_{F\times G\subseteq P\times Q}(F\times G)\otimes \left(P\times Q/ F\times G\right)= \sum\limits_{F\subseteq P,\,G\subseteq Q}(F\times G)\otimes \left(P/F\divideontimes Q/G\right)=\\ =\left(\sum\limits_{F\subseteq P}F\otimes P/F\right)\cdot\left(\sum\limits_{G\subseteq Q}G\otimes Q/G\right)=\Delta_{\mathcal{RP}}(P)\cdot\Delta_{\mathcal{RP}}(Q) \end{multline*} $$ \Delta_{\mathcal{RP}}(\mathrm{pt})=\mathrm{pt}\otimes (\mathrm{pt}/\mathrm{pt})=\mathrm{pt}\otimes \varnothing=1\otimes 1. $$
nodes.statement_short: Check coassociativity, counit and multiplicativity using face polytopes of products.

nodes.name: State what must be verified.
nodes.statement: We should proof that the following two diagrams commute $$ \xymatrix{ \mathcal{P}\ar[d]^{\Delta_{\mathcal{RP}}}\ar[rr]^{\Delta_{\mathcal{RP}}}&&\mathcal{P}\otimes\mathcal{RP}\ar[d]^{\mathrm{id}\otimes\Delta}\\ \mathcal{P}\otimes\mathcal{RP}\ar[rr]^{\Delta_{\mathcal{RP}}\otimes\mathrm{id}}&&\mathcal{P}\otimes\mathcal{RP}\otimes\mathcal{RP}\\ } \hspace{2cm} \xymatrix{ \mathcal{P}\ar[d]_{\Delta_{\mathcal{RP}}}\ar[dr]^{\mathrm{id}\otimes 1}&\\ \mathcal{P}\otimes \mathcal{RP}\ar[r]^{\mathrm{id}\otimes \varepsilon}&\mathcal{P}\otimes\mathbb Z\\ } $$ and that $\Delta_{\mathcal{RP}}$ is a ring homomorphism.
nodes.statement_short: State what must be verified.

nodes.name: Coassociativity and counit.
nodes.statement: Indeed, we have \begin{multline*} (\Delta_{\mathcal{RP}}\otimes\mathrm{id})\circ\Delta_{\mathcal{RP}} P=(\Delta_{\mathcal{RP}}\otimes\mathrm{id})\left(\sum\limits_{F\subseteq P}F\otimes P/F\right)=\sum\limits_{F\subseteq P}\left(\sum\limits_{G\subseteq F}G\otimes F/G\right)\otimes P/F=\\ =\sum\limits_{G\subseteq P}G\otimes\left(\sum\limits_{G\subseteq F\subseteq P}F/G\otimes P/F\right)=\sum\limits_{G\subseteq P}G\otimes\Delta (P/G) =(\mathrm{id}\otimes\Delta)\circ\Delta_{\mathcal{RP}} P, \end{multline*} and $$ (\mathrm{id}\otimes\varepsilon)\circ\Delta_{\mathcal{RP}}(P)=\sum\limits_{F\subseteq P}F\otimes\varepsilon(P/F)=P\otimes 1, $$
nodes.statement_short: Coassociativity and counit.

nodes.name: Multiplicativity and unit.
nodes.statement: Let us check that $\Delta_{\mathcal{RP}}$ is a homomorphism of rings $\mathcal{P}\to\mathcal{P}\otimes\mathcal{RP}$: \begin{multline*} \Delta_{\mathcal{RP}}(P\times Q)=\sum\limits_{F\times G\subseteq P\times Q}(F\times G)\otimes \left(P\times Q/ F\times G\right)= \sum\limits_{F\subseteq P,\,G\subseteq Q}(F\times G)\otimes \left(P/F\divideontimes Q/G\right)=\\ =\left(\sum\limits_{F\subseteq P}F\otimes P/F\right)\cdot\left(\sum\limits_{G\subseteq Q}G\otimes Q/G\right)=\Delta_{\mathcal{RP}}(P)\cdot\Delta_{\mathcal{RP}}(Q) \end{multline*} $$ \Delta_{\mathcal{RP}}(\mathrm{pt})=\mathrm{pt}\otimes (\mathrm{pt}/\mathrm{pt})=\mathrm{pt}\otimes \varnothing=1\otimes 1. $$
nodes.statement_short: Multiplicativity and unit.

nodes.name: Corollary 10.19 (induced homomorphisms)
nodes.statement: \begin{itemize} \item Any ring homomorphism $\mathcal{P}\to\mathcal{A}$, where $\mathcal{A}$ is a ring, induces the ring homomorphism $\mathcal{P}\to\mathcal{A}\otimes\mathcal{RP}$ \item Any linear homomorphism $\psi\colon\mathcal{RP}\to\mathbb Z$ induces the linear operator $\mathcal{P}\to\mathcal{P}$, which is a ring homomorphism, if $\psi$ is a ring homomorphism. \end{itemize}

nodes.name: Example 10.20 (homomorphism l_alpha)
nodes.statement: The homomorphism $\xi_{\alpha}\colon\mathcal{P}\to\mathbb Z[\alpha]$ defines the ring homomorphism $l_{\alpha}\colon\mathcal{P}\to\mathcal{RP}[\alpha]$: $$ l_{\alpha}(P^n)=\sum\limits_{F\subseteq P}\alpha^{\dim F}P/F. $$ Let us recall that in the case of a simple $n$-polytope a face polytope of an $i$-dimensional face is a simplex $\Delta^{n-i-1}=x^{n-i}$. Therefore, $$ l_{\alpha}(P^n)=\sum\limits_{i=0}^nf_i\alpha^ix^{n-i}=f_1(\alpha,x). $$ This is a homogeneous $f$-polynomial in two variables defined in \cite{Buch}.
nodes.statement_short: l_alpha(P)=sum alpha^{dim F} P/F; for simple polytopes it is f_1(alpha,x).

nodes.name: Proposition 10.21 (Delta_RP of a join)
nodes.statement: \begin{equation} \Delta_{\mathcal{RP}}(P\divideontimes Q)=(1\otimes P)\cdot\Delta_{\mathcal{RP}}(Q)+\Delta_{\mathcal{RP}}(P)\cdot (1\otimes Q)+\Delta_{\mathcal{RP}}(P)(\divideontimes\otimes\divideontimes) \Delta_{\mathcal{RP}}(Q) \end{equation}
nodes.label: DPQ

nodes.name: Join formula for Delta_RP (24)
nodes.statement: \Delta_{\mathcal{RP}}(P\divideontimes Q)=(1\otimes P)\cdot\Delta_{\mathcal{RP}}(Q)+\Delta_{\mathcal{RP}}(P)\cdot (1\otimes Q)+\Delta_{\mathcal{RP}}(P)(\divideontimes\otimes\divideontimes) \Delta_{\mathcal{RP}}(Q)
nodes.label: FDPQ

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 10.21
nodes.statement: \begin{multline*} \Delta_{\mathcal{RP}}(P\divideontimes Q)=\sum\limits_{G\subseteq Q} \left(\varnothing\divideontimes G\right)\otimes \left(P\divideontimes Q/\varnothing \divideontimes G\right)+\sum\limits_{F\subseteq P} \left(F\divideontimes\varnothing\right)\otimes \left(P\divideontimes Q/F \divideontimes \varnothing\right)+\\ +\sum\limits_{F\subseteq P,\,G\subseteq Q}(F\divideontimes G)\otimes \left(P\divideontimes Q/F\divideontimes G\right)=\sum\limits_{G\subseteq Q} G\otimes \left(P\divideontimes (Q/G)\right)+ \sum\limits_{F\subseteq P} F\otimes \left((P/F)\divideontimes Q\right)+\\ +\sum\limits_{F\subseteq P,\,G\subseteq Q}\left(F\divideontimes G\right)\otimes\left(P/F\divideontimes Q/G\right)=(1\otimes P)\Delta_{\mathcal{RP}}(Q)+\Delta_{\mathcal{RP}}(P)(1\otimes Q)+\Delta_{\mathcal{RP}}(P)(\divideontimes\otimes\divideontimes) \Delta_{\mathcal{RP}}(Q) \end{multline*}
nodes.statement_short: Split the faces of a join into those with an empty factor and the rest.

nodes.name: Proof of Corollary 10.22
nodes.statement: Now if we apply $\xi_{\alpha}\otimes 1$ to the formula (\ref{FDPQ}), then we obtain the corollary:
nodes.statement_short: Apply xi_alpha (x) 1 to formula (24).

nodes.name: Corollary 10.22 (l_alpha of a join)
nodes.statement: $$ l_{\alpha}(P\divideontimes Q)=P\divideontimes l_{\alpha}(Q)+l_{\alpha}(P)\divideontimes Q+\alpha\; l_{\alpha}(P)\cdot l_{\alpha}(Q) $$
nodes.label: lPQ

nodes.name: Proposition 10.23 (Delta_L = (1 x F) Delta_RP)
nodes.statement: The following diagram commutes: $$ \xymatrix{ \mathcal{P}\ar[dr]_-{\Delta_{\EuScript{L}}}\ar[r]^-{\Delta_{\mathcal{RP}}}&\mathcal{P}\otimes\mathcal{RP}\ar[d]^{1\otimes \mathrm{F}}\\ &\mathcal{P}\otimes\mathcal{Q}sym } $$

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 10.23
nodes.statement: Let $P$ be an $n$-dimensional polytope. Then \begin{multline*} \Delta_{\EuScript{L}}(P)=\sum\limits_{k=0}^n\sum\limits_{(j_1,\,\dots,\,j_k)}(d_{j_1}\dots d_{j_k}P)\otimes M_{(j_1,\,\dots,\,j_k)}=\\ \sum\limits_{k=0}^n\sum\limits_{(j_1,\,\dots,\,j_k)}\sum\limits_{F^{n-(j_1+\dots+j_k)}}\left(F^{n-(j_1+\dots+j_k)}\sum\limits_{F^{n-(j_1+\dots+j_k)}\subset F^{n-(j_2+\dots+j_k)}\subset\dots\subset F^{n-j_k}\subset P}1\right)\otimes M_{(j_1,\,\dots,\,j_k)}=\\ =\sum\limits_{r=0}^n\sum\limits_{F^r\subseteq P}F^r\otimes \left(\sum\limits_{k=0}^{n-r}\sum\limits_{(j_1,\,\dots,\, j_k):j_1+\dots+j_k=n-r}\sum\limits_{F^r\subset F^{r+j_1}\subset\dots\subset F^{n-j_k}\subset P}M_{(j_1,\,\dots,\,j_k)}\right)=\\ =\sum\limits_{F\subseteq P}F\otimes \mathrm{F}(P/F)=(1\otimes\mathrm{F})\circ\Delta_{RP}(P) \end{multline*}
nodes.statement_short: Group chains by their bottom face and recognize Ehrenborg's F of P/F.

nodes.name: Corollary 10.24 (F^* o l_alpha = f)
nodes.statement: For any polytope $P\in\mathcal{P}$ we have $$ \mathrm{F}^*(l_{\alpha}P)=f(P) $$
nodes.label: Fl

nodes.name: Proof of Corollary 10.24
nodes.statement: We have $(\xi_{\alpha}\otimes1)\circ\Delta_{\EuScript{L}}P=f(P)^*$. So if we apply the homomorphism $\xi_{\alpha}\otimes 1$ to the diagram above, we obtain $\mathrm{F}\circ\, l_{\alpha}=(\xi_{\alpha}\otimes 1)\circ\Delta_{\EuScript{L}}=f^*$. Therefore, $\mathrm{F}^*\circ\, l_{\alpha}=f$.
nodes.statement_short: Apply xi_alpha (x) 1 to the diagram of Proposition 10.23.

nodes.name: xi_alpha applied to Delta_L gives f^*.
nodes.statement: We have $(\xi_{\alpha}\otimes1)\circ\Delta_{\EuScript{L}}P=f(P)^*$.
nodes.statement_short: xi_alpha applied to Delta_L gives f^*.

nodes.name: Apply to the diagram of Proposition 10.23.
nodes.statement: So if we apply the homomorphism $\xi_{\alpha}\otimes 1$ to the diagram above, we obtain $\mathrm{F}\circ\, l_{\alpha}=(\xi_{\alpha}\otimes 1)\circ\Delta_{\EuScript{L}}=f^*$.
nodes.statement_short: Apply to the diagram of Proposition 10.23.

nodes.name: Dualize.
nodes.statement: Therefore, $\mathrm{F}^*\circ\, l_{\alpha}=f$.
nodes.statement_short: Dualize.

nodes.name: Corollary 10.25 (f^* intertwines Delta_RP and Delta)
nodes.statement: The following diagram commutes: $$ \begin{CD} \mathcal{P}@>{f^*}>>\mathcal{Q}sym[\alpha]\\ @V{\Delta_{\mathcal{RP}}}VV @V{\Delta}VV\\ \mathcal{P}\otimes\mathcal{RP}@>{f^*\otimes F}>>\mathcal{Q}sym[\alpha]\otimes\mathcal{Q}sym \end{CD} $$

nodes.name: Proof of Corollary 10.25
nodes.statement: \begin{enumerate} \item Consider the commutative diagram $$ \xymatrix{ \mathcal{P}\ar[dr]_-{\Delta_{\EuScript{L}}}\ar[r]^-{\Delta_{\mathcal{RP}}}&\mathcal{P}\otimes\mathcal{RP}\ar[d]^{1\otimes \mathrm{F}}\ar[r]^-{\Delta_{\EuScript{L}}\otimes 1}& P\otimes\mathcal{Q}sym\otimes \mathcal{RP}\ar[d]^{1\otimes 1\otimes F}\\ &\mathcal{P}\otimes\mathcal{Q}sym\ar[dr]\ar[r]^-{\Delta_{\EuScript{L}}\otimes 1}& P\otimes \mathcal{Q}sym\otimes\mathcal{Q}sym\ar[d]^{\xi_{\alpha}\otimes 1\otimes 1}\\ &&\mathbb Z[\alpha]\otimes\mathcal{Q}sym\otimes\mathcal{Q}sym } $$ Then $$ \left(\xi_{\alpha}\otimes 1\otimes 1\right) \circ \left(\Delta_{\EuScript{L}}\otimes 1\right)\circ\Delta_{\EuScript{L}}= \left(\xi_{\alpha}\otimes 1\otimes 1\right)\circ\left(1\otimes\Delta\right)\circ\Delta_{\EuScript{L}}=\Delta\circ f^* $$ while $$ \left(\xi_{\alpha}\otimes 1\otimes 1\right)\circ\left(1\otimes 1\otimes \mathrm{F}\right)\circ\left(\Delta_{\EuScript{L}}\otimes 1\right)\circ \Delta_{\mathcal{RP}}= \left(f^*\otimes\mathrm{F}\right)\circ\Delta_{\mathcal{RP}} $$ Since these two compositions correspond to two pathes in the diagram, they are equal. \item Let us consider also a direct proof. We know that $$ \Delta(M_{(b_1,\,\dots,\,b_k)})=1\otimes M_{(b_1,\,\dots,\,b_k)}+M_{(b_1)}\otimes M_{(b_2,\,\dots,\,b_k)}+\dots+M_{(b_1,\,\dots,\,b_{k-1})}\otimes M_{(b_k)}+M_{(b_1,\,\dots,\,b_k)}\otimes 1 $$ and $$ f(\alpha,t_1,t_2,\dots)(P^n)^*=\alpha^n+\sum\limits_{F^{a_1}\subset\dots\subset F^{a_k}}\alpha^{a_1}M_{(a_2-a_1,\,\dots,\,n-a_k)}=\sum\limits_{F^{a_1}\subset\dots\subset F^{a_k}\subset P^n}\alpha^{a_1}M_{(a_2-a_1,\,\dots,\,n-a_k)} $$ Then \begin{multline*} \Delta(f(P^n)^*)=\sum\limits_{F^{a_1}\subset\dots\subset G^{a_s}\subset\dots\subset F^{a_k}\subset P^n}\alpha^{a_1}M_{(a_2-a_1,\,\dots,\,a_s-a_{s-1})}\otimes M_{(a_{s+1}-a_s,\,\dots,\,n-a_k)}=\\ =\sum\limits_{G^{a_s}\subseteq P^n}\left(\sum\limits_{F^{a_1}\subset\dots\subset F^{a_{s-1}}\subset G^{a_s}}\alpha^{a_1}M_{(a_2-a_1,\,\dots,\,a_s-a_{s-1})}\right)\otimes\left(\sum\limits_{G^{a_s}\subset F^{a_{s+1}}\subset\dots\subset F^{a_k}\subset P^n}M_{(a_{s+1}-a_s,\,\dots,\,n-a_k)}\right)=\\ =\sum\limits_{G\subseteq P^n}f^*(G)\otimes \mathrm{F}(P^n/G)=(f^*\otimes \mathrm{F})\circ\Delta_{\mathcal{RP}} (P^n). \end{multline*} \end{enumerate}
nodes.statement_short: Diagram chase via Proposition 10.23, and a direct computation with chains.

nodes.name: Item 1: diagram chase.
nodes.statement: Consider the commutative diagram $$ \xymatrix{ \mathcal{P}\ar[dr]_-{\Delta_{\EuScript{L}}}\ar[r]^-{\Delta_{\mathcal{RP}}}&\mathcal{P}\otimes\mathcal{RP}\ar[d]^{1\otimes \mathrm{F}}\ar[r]^-{\Delta_{\EuScript{L}}\otimes 1}& P\otimes\mathcal{Q}sym\otimes \mathcal{RP}\ar[d]^{1\otimes 1\otimes F}\\ &\mathcal{P}\otimes\mathcal{Q}sym\ar[dr]\ar[r]^-{\Delta_{\EuScript{L}}\otimes 1}& P\otimes \mathcal{Q}sym\otimes\mathcal{Q}sym\ar[d]^{\xi_{\alpha}\otimes 1\otimes 1}\\ &&\mathbb Z[\alpha]\otimes\mathcal{Q}sym\otimes\mathcal{Q}sym } $$ Then $$ \left(\xi_{\alpha}\otimes 1\otimes 1\right) \circ \left(\Delta_{\EuScript{L}}\otimes 1\right)\circ\Delta_{\EuScript{L}}= \left(\xi_{\alpha}\otimes 1\otimes 1\right)\circ\left(1\otimes\Delta\right)\circ\Delta_{\EuScript{L}}=\Delta\circ f^* $$ while $$ \left(\xi_{\alpha}\otimes 1\otimes 1\right)\circ\left(1\otimes 1\otimes \mathrm{F}\right)\circ\left(\Delta_{\EuScript{L}}\otimes 1\right)\circ \Delta_{\mathcal{RP}}= \left(f^*\otimes\mathrm{F}\right)\circ\Delta_{\mathcal{RP}} $$ Since these two compositions correspond to two pathes in the diagram, they are equal.
nodes.statement_short: Item 1: diagram chase.

nodes.name: Item 2: direct computation with chains.
nodes.statement: Let us consider also a direct proof. We know that $$ \Delta(M_{(b_1,\,\dots,\,b_k)})=1\otimes M_{(b_1,\,\dots,\,b_k)}+M_{(b_1)}\otimes M_{(b_2,\,\dots,\,b_k)}+\dots+M_{(b_1,\,\dots,\,b_{k-1})}\otimes M_{(b_k)}+M_{(b_1,\,\dots,\,b_k)}\otimes 1 $$ and $$ f(\alpha,t_1,t_2,\dots)(P^n)^*=\alpha^n+\sum\limits_{F^{a_1}\subset\dots\subset F^{a_k}}\alpha^{a_1}M_{(a_2-a_1,\,\dots,\,n-a_k)}=\sum\limits_{F^{a_1}\subset\dots\subset F^{a_k}\subset P^n}\alpha^{a_1}M_{(a_2-a_1,\,\dots,\,n-a_k)} $$ Then \begin{multline*} \Delta(f(P^n)^*)=\sum\limits_{F^{a_1}\subset\dots\subset G^{a_s}\subset\dots\subset F^{a_k}\subset P^n}\alpha^{a_1}M_{(a_2-a_1,\,\dots,\,a_s-a_{s-1})}\otimes M_{(a_{s+1}-a_s,\,\dots,\,n-a_k)}=\\ =\sum\limits_{G^{a_s}\subseteq P^n}\left(\sum\limits_{F^{a_1}\subset\dots\subset F^{a_{s-1}}\subset G^{a_s}}\alpha^{a_1}M_{(a_2-a_1,\,\dots,\,a_s-a_{s-1})}\right)\otimes\left(\sum\limits_{G^{a_s}\subset F^{a_{s+1}}\subset\dots\subset F^{a_k}\subset P^n}M_{(a_{s+1}-a_s,\,\dots,\,n-a_k)}\right)=\\ =\sum\limits_{G\subseteq P^n}f^*(G)\otimes \mathrm{F}(P^n/G)=(f^*\otimes \mathrm{F})\circ\Delta_{\mathcal{RP}} (P^n). \end{multline*}
nodes.statement_short: Item 2: direct computation with chains.

nodes.name: Commutation of d_k with the cone in P
nodes.statement: For $k\geqslant 2$ we have the similar situation. $$ d_kCP^n=\begin{cases} Cd_kP^n+d_{k-1}P^n,&k<n+1,\\ 1+d_{k-1}P^n=C\varnothing+d_{k-1}P^n,&k=n+1 \end{cases} $$ So we have $[d_{k+1},C]=d_k+\frac{1}{k!}\left.\frac{\partial^k}{\partial \alpha^k}\right|_{\alpha=0}\xi_{\alpha}$, $k\geqslant 0$.

nodes.name: Proposition 11.1 (Phi(t)C)
nodes.statement: We have $$ \Phi(t)C=(C+t)\Phi(t)+t\xi_t $$
nodes.label: PC

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 11.1
nodes.statement: Let $P$ be an $n$-polytope. Then $$ \Phi(t)CP=CP+(CdP+P)t+\dots+(Cd_nP+d_{n-1}P)t^n+(1+d_nP)t^{n+1}=C\Phi(t)P+t\Phi(t)P+t\xi_{t}P $$
nodes.statement_short: Expand Phi(t)CP term by term.

nodes.name: Commutation of d_k with the bipyramid in P
nodes.statement: $dBP=2CdP$ for any polytope of positive dimension, while $dB\mathrm{pt}=dI=2\mathrm{pt}$, and $2Cd\mathrm{pt}=0$. So $dBP=2CdP+2\xi_0$. For $k\geqslant 2$ we have $$ d_kBP^n=\begin{cases}2Cd_kP^n+d_{k-1}P^n,&k<n+1;\\ 2+d_{k-1}P^n=2C\varnothing+d_{k-1}P^n,&k=n+1; \end{cases} $$ So $d_{k+1}B=2Cd_{k+1}+d_k+\frac{2}{k!}\left.\frac{\partial^k}{\partial \alpha^k}\right|_{\alpha=0}\xi_{\alpha}$, $k\geqslant 1$.

nodes.name: Proposition 11.2 (Phi(t)B)
nodes.statement: $$ \Phi(t)B=(B-2C-t)+(2C+t)\Phi(t)+2t\xi_{t} $$
nodes.label: PB

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 11.2
nodes.statement: For a point we have: $\Phi(t)B\mathrm{pt}=\Phi(t)I=I+(2\mathrm{pt})t$, and $$ \left((B-2C-t)+(2C+t)\Phi(t)+2t\xi_t\right)\mathrm{pt}=I-2I-(\mathrm{pt})t+2I+(\mathrm{pt}) t+2(\mathrm{pt})t=I+(2\mathrm{pt}) t $$ Let $P$ be an $n$-polytope, $n>0$. Then \begin{multline*} \Phi(t)BP=BP+(2CdP)t+(2Cd_2P+dP)t^2+\dots+(2Cd_nP+d_{n-1}P)t^n+(2+d_n P)t^{n+1}=\\ =(B-2C-t)P+2C\Phi(t)P+t\Phi(t)P+2t\xi_tP \end{multline*}
nodes.statement_short: Check the point separately, then expand for positive dimension.

nodes.name: Case of a point.
nodes.statement: For a point we have: $\Phi(t)B\mathrm{pt}=\Phi(t)I=I+(2\mathrm{pt})t$, and $$ \left((B-2C-t)+(2C+t)\Phi(t)+2t\xi_t\right)\mathrm{pt}=I-2I-(\mathrm{pt})t+2I+(\mathrm{pt}) t+2(\mathrm{pt})t=I+(2\mathrm{pt}) t $$
nodes.statement_short: Case of a point.

nodes.name: Positive-dimensional case.
nodes.statement: Let $P$ be an $n$-polytope, $n>0$. Then \begin{multline*} \Phi(t)BP=BP+(2CdP)t+(2Cd_2P+dP)t^2+\dots+(2Cd_nP+d_{n-1}P)t^n+(2+d_n P)t^{n+1}=\\ =(B-2C-t)P+2C\Phi(t)P+t\Phi(t)P+2t\xi_tP \end{multline*}
nodes.statement_short: Positive-dimensional case.

nodes.name: Operator A = 2C - B
nodes.statement: Let us denote $A=2C-B$.

nodes.name: Phi(t)A = A + t + t Phi(t)
nodes.statement: Then from Propositions \ref{PC} and \ref{PB} we have $$ \Phi(t)A=A+t+t\Phi(t) $$

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 11.3
nodes.statement: \begin{multline*} \Phi(t)[B,C]=\Phi(t)(BC-CB)=\left(B-2C-t+(2C+t)\Phi(t)+2t\xi_t\right)C-\left((C+t)\Phi(t)+t\xi_t\right)B=\\ =(B-2C-t)C+(2C+t)\left((C+t)\Phi(t)+t\xi_t\right)+2t^2\xi_t-(C+t)\left(B-2C-t+(2C+t)\Phi(t)+2t\xi_t\right)-t^2\xi_t=\\ =(BC-CB)-t(B-2C-t)+2Ct\xi_t+t^2\xi_t+2t^2\xi_t-2Ct\xi_t-2t^2\xi_t-t^2\xi_t=[B,C]+At+t^2 \end{multline*}
nodes.statement_short: Substitute Propositions 11.1 and 11.2 and simplify.

nodes.name: Proposition 11.4 (operators C, A on Qsym[alpha] intertwined by f)
nodes.statement: Mappings $C,A\colon\mathcal{Q}sym[\alpha]\to\mathcal{Q}sym[\alpha]$ defined by the formulas \begin{gather*} Cg=(\alpha+\sigma_1)g+\sum\limits_{n=1}^{\infty}t_n g(t_n,t_1,\dots,t_{n-1},0,0,\dots)\\ Ag=\alpha g(\alpha,0,0,\dots)+t_1g(\alpha,t_1,t_2,\dots)+\sum\limits_{n=2}^{\infty}(t_n+t_{n-1})g(\alpha,t_n,t_{n+1},\dots) \end{gather*} satisfy the relations $$ f(CP)=Cf(P),\quad f(AP)=Af(P) $$ for all $P\in\mathcal{P}$.
nodes.statement_short: Explicit operators C and A on Qsym[alpha] satisfy f(CP)=Cf(P) and f(AP)=Af(P).
nodes.label: AC

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 11.4
nodes.statement: At first let us prove that this mappings are correctly defined, that is for any $g\in\mathcal{Q}sym[\alpha]$ its images $Cg$, and $Ag$ belong to $\mathcal{Q}sym[\alpha]$. We will use the criterion obtained in Proposition \ref{Crn} and Remark \ref{cr}. It is easy to see that if $g$ has bounded degree, then $Cg$ and $Ag$ have bounded degree. Let $i\geqslant 1$. Then \begin{multline*} (Cg)(\alpha,t_1,\dots,t_{i-1},0,t_{i+1},\dots)=(\alpha+\sum\limits_{j\ne i}t_j)g(\alpha,t_1,\dots,t_{i-1},0,t_{i+1},\dots)+\sum\limits_{n=1}^{i-1}t_n g(t_n,t_1,\dots,t_{n-1},0,0,\dots)+\\ +\sum\limits_{n=i+1}^{\infty} t_n g(t_n,t_1,\dots,t_{i-1},0,t_{i+1},\dots,t_{n-1},0,0,\dots)=\\ =(\alpha+\sigma_1(t_1,\dots,t_{i-1},t_{i+1},\dots))g(\alpha,t_1,\dots,t_{i-1},t_{i+1},\dots)+\sum\limits_{n=1}^{i-1}t_n g(t_n,t_1,\dots,t_{n-1},0,0,\dots)+\\ +t_{i+1}g(t_{i+1},t_1,\dots,t_{i-1},0,0,\dots)+\sum\limits_{n=i+2}^{\infty} t_n g(t_n,t_1,\dots,t_{i-1},t_{i+1},\dots,t_{n-1},0,0,\dots)=(Cg)(\alpha,t_1,\dots,t_{i-1},t_{i+1},\dots) \end{multline*} Now consider $A$. For $i=1$ the relation is clear. Let $i>1$. Then \begin{multline*} (Ag)(\alpha,t_1,\dots,t_{i-1},0,t_{i+1},\dots)=\alpha g(\alpha,0,0,\dots)+\sum\limits_{n=1}^{i-1}(t_n+t_{n-1})g(\alpha,t_n,\dots,t_{i-1},0,t_{i+1},\dots)+\\ +(0+t_{i-1})g(\alpha,0,t_{i+1},\dots)+(t_{i+1}+0)g(\alpha,t_{i+1},t_{i+2},\dots)+\sum\limits_{n=i+2}^{\infty}(t_n+t_{n-1})g(\alpha,t_n,t_{n+1},\dots)=\\ =\alpha g(\alpha,0,0,\dots)+\sum\limits_{n=1}^{i-1}(t_n+t_{n-1})g(\alpha,t_n,\dots,t_{i-1},t_{i+1},\dots)+(t_{i+1}+t_{i-1})g(\alpha,t_{i+1},t_{i+2},\dots)+\\ +\sum\limits_{n=i+2}^{\infty}(t_n+t_{n-1})g(\alpha,t_n,t_{n+1},\dots)= (Ag)(\alpha,t_1,\dots,t_{i-1},t_{i+1},\dots) \end{multline*} On the other hand, we have \begin{gather*} \Phi(t_1)C=(C+t_1)\Phi(t_1)+t_1\xi_{t_1}\\ \Phi(t_2)\Phi(t_1)C=(C+t_2+t_1)\Phi(t_2)\Phi(t_1)+t_2\xi_{t_2}\Phi(t_1)+t_1\xi_{t_1}\\ \dots\\ \Phi(t_n)\Phi(t_{n-1})\dots\Phi(t_1)C=(C+t_n+\dots+t_1)\Phi(t_n)\Phi(t_{n-1})\dots\Phi(t_1)+t_n\xi_{t_n}\Phi(t_{n-1})\dots\Phi(t_1)+\dots+t_1\xi_{t_1}\\ \dots\\ \Phi_{\infty}C=(C+\sigma_1)\Phi_{\infty}+\sum\limits_{n=1}^{\infty}t_nf(t_n,t_1,\dots,t_{n-1},0,\dots)\\ f(CP)=\xi_{\alpha}\Phi_{\infty}CP=(\alpha+\sigma_1)\xi_{\alpha}\Phi_{\infty}P+\sum\limits_{n=1}^{\infty}t_nf(t_n,t_1,\dots,t_{n-1},0,\dots)=Cf(P) \end{gather*} \begin{gather*} \Phi(t_1)A=A+t_1+t_1\Phi(t_1)\\ \Phi(t_2)\Phi(t_1)A=A+t_2+(t_2+t_1)\Phi(t_2)+t_1\Phi(t_2)\Phi(t_1)\\ \dots\\ \Phi(t_n)\Phi(t_{n-1})\dots\Phi(t_1)A=A+t_n+(t_n+t_{n-1})\Phi(t_n)+(t_{n-1}+t_{n-2})\Phi(t_n)\Phi(t_{n-1})+\dots+t_1\Phi(t_n)\dots\Phi(t_1)\\ \dots\\ \Phi_{\infty}A=A+t_1\Phi_{\infty}(t_1,t_2,\dots)+\sum\limits_{n=2}^{\infty}(t_n+t_{n-1})\Phi_{\infty}(t_n,t_{n+1},\dots)\\ f(AP)=\xi_{\alpha}\Phi_{\infty}AP=\alpha f(\alpha,0,0,\dots)+t_1f(\alpha,t_1,t_2,\dots)+\sum\limits_{n=2}^{\infty}(t_n+t_{n-1})f(\alpha,t_n,t_{n+1},\dots)=Af(P) \end{gather*}
nodes.statement_short: Check well-definedness by the zero-insertion criterion, then iterate Prop 11.1 and the A-relation through Phi_infty.

nodes.name: Well-definedness via Proposition 3.3 and Remark 3.4.
nodes.statement: At first let us prove that this mappings are correctly defined, that is for any $g\in\mathcal{Q}sym[\alpha]$ its images $Cg$, and $Ag$ belong to $\mathcal{Q}sym[\alpha]$. We will use the criterion obtained in Proposition \ref{Crn} and Remark \ref{cr}. It is easy to see that if $g$ has bounded degree, then $Cg$ and $Ag$ have bounded degree.
nodes.statement_short: Well-definedness via Proposition 3.3 and Remark 3.4.

nodes.name: Zero-insertion check for C.
nodes.statement: Let $i\geqslant 1$. Then \begin{multline*} (Cg)(\alpha,t_1,\dots,t_{i-1},0,t_{i+1},\dots)=(\alpha+\sum\limits_{j\ne i}t_j)g(\alpha,t_1,\dots,t_{i-1},0,t_{i+1},\dots)+\sum\limits_{n=1}^{i-1}t_n g(t_n,t_1,\dots,t_{n-1},0,0,\dots)+\\ +\sum\limits_{n=i+1}^{\infty} t_n g(t_n,t_1,\dots,t_{i-1},0,t_{i+1},\dots,t_{n-1},0,0,\dots)=\\ =(\alpha+\sigma_1(t_1,\dots,t_{i-1},t_{i+1},\dots))g(\alpha,t_1,\dots,t_{i-1},t_{i+1},\dots)+\sum\limits_{n=1}^{i-1}t_n g(t_n,t_1,\dots,t_{n-1},0,0,\dots)+\\ +t_{i+1}g(t_{i+1},t_1,\dots,t_{i-1},0,0,\dots)+\sum\limits_{n=i+2}^{\infty} t_n g(t_n,t_1,\dots,t_{i-1},t_{i+1},\dots,t_{n-1},0,0,\dots)=(Cg)(\alpha,t_1,\dots,t_{i-1},t_{i+1},\dots) \end{multline*}
nodes.statement_short: Zero-insertion check for C.

nodes.name: Zero-insertion check for A.
nodes.statement: Now consider $A$. For $i=1$ the relation is clear. Let $i>1$. Then \begin{multline*} (Ag)(\alpha,t_1,\dots,t_{i-1},0,t_{i+1},\dots)=\alpha g(\alpha,0,0,\dots)+\sum\limits_{n=1}^{i-1}(t_n+t_{n-1})g(\alpha,t_n,\dots,t_{i-1},0,t_{i+1},\dots)+\\ +(0+t_{i-1})g(\alpha,0,t_{i+1},\dots)+(t_{i+1}+0)g(\alpha,t_{i+1},t_{i+2},\dots)+\sum\limits_{n=i+2}^{\infty}(t_n+t_{n-1})g(\alpha,t_n,t_{n+1},\dots)=\\ =\alpha g(\alpha,0,0,\dots)+\sum\limits_{n=1}^{i-1}(t_n+t_{n-1})g(\alpha,t_n,\dots,t_{i-1},t_{i+1},\dots)+(t_{i+1}+t_{i-1})g(\alpha,t_{i+1},t_{i+2},\dots)+\\ +\sum\limits_{n=i+2}^{\infty}(t_n+t_{n-1})g(\alpha,t_n,t_{n+1},\dots)= (Ag)(\alpha,t_1,\dots,t_{i-1},t_{i+1},\dots) \end{multline*}
nodes.statement_short: Zero-insertion check for A.

nodes.name: Iterate Proposition 11.1 to get f(CP)=Cf(P).
nodes.statement: On the other hand, we have \begin{gather*} \Phi(t_1)C=(C+t_1)\Phi(t_1)+t_1\xi_{t_1}\\ \Phi(t_2)\Phi(t_1)C=(C+t_2+t_1)\Phi(t_2)\Phi(t_1)+t_2\xi_{t_2}\Phi(t_1)+t_1\xi_{t_1}\\ \dots\\ \Phi(t_n)\Phi(t_{n-1})\dots\Phi(t_1)C=(C+t_n+\dots+t_1)\Phi(t_n)\Phi(t_{n-1})\dots\Phi(t_1)+t_n\xi_{t_n}\Phi(t_{n-1})\dots\Phi(t_1)+\dots+t_1\xi_{t_1}\\ \dots\\ \Phi_{\infty}C=(C+\sigma_1)\Phi_{\infty}+\sum\limits_{n=1}^{\infty}t_nf(t_n,t_1,\dots,t_{n-1},0,\dots)\\ f(CP)=\xi_{\alpha}\Phi_{\infty}CP=(\alpha+\sigma_1)\xi_{\alpha}\Phi_{\infty}P+\sum\limits_{n=1}^{\infty}t_nf(t_n,t_1,\dots,t_{n-1},0,\dots)=Cf(P) \end{gather*}
nodes.statement_short: Iterate Proposition 11.1 to get f(CP)=Cf(P).

nodes.name: Iterate the A-relation to get f(AP)=Af(P).
nodes.statement: \begin{gather*} \Phi(t_1)A=A+t_1+t_1\Phi(t_1)\\ \Phi(t_2)\Phi(t_1)A=A+t_2+(t_2+t_1)\Phi(t_2)+t_1\Phi(t_2)\Phi(t_1)\\ \dots\\ \Phi(t_n)\Phi(t_{n-1})\dots\Phi(t_1)A=A+t_n+(t_n+t_{n-1})\Phi(t_n)+(t_{n-1}+t_{n-2})\Phi(t_n)\Phi(t_{n-1})+\dots+t_1\Phi(t_n)\dots\Phi(t_1)\\ \dots\\ \Phi_{\infty}A=A+t_1\Phi_{\infty}(t_1,t_2,\dots)+\sum\limits_{n=2}^{\infty}(t_n+t_{n-1})\Phi_{\infty}(t_n,t_{n+1},\dots)\\ f(AP)=\xi_{\alpha}\Phi_{\infty}AP=\alpha f(\alpha,0,0,\dots)+t_1f(\alpha,t_1,t_2,\dots)+\sum\limits_{n=2}^{\infty}(t_n+t_{n-1})f(\alpha,t_n,t_{n+1},\dots)=Af(P) \end{gather*}
nodes.statement_short: Iterate the A-relation to get f(AP)=Af(P).

nodes.name: Operator B on Qsym[alpha]
nodes.statement: Now the mapping $B:\mathcal{Q}sym[\alpha]\to\mathcal{Q}sym[\alpha]$ can be defined as $B=2C-A$.

nodes.name: f(BP) = Bf(P)
nodes.statement: Then $f(BP)=Bf(P)$.

nodes.name: Cone in RP is multiplication by x
nodes.statement: In this ring $CP$ is just the multiplication by the element $x=\mathrm{pt}$. So \begin{gather*} \Phi(t)CP=\Phi(t)(xP)=(\Phi(t)x)\divideontimes(\Phi(t)P)=(x+t)\Phi(t)P=(C+t)\Phi(t)P\\ \Phi_{\infty}(CP)=\Phi_{\infty}(xP)=\Phi_{\infty}(x)\divideontimes\Phi_{\infty}(P)=(x+\sigma_1)\Phi_{\infty}(P)=(C+\sigma_1)\Phi_{\infty}(P)\\ f_{\mathcal{RP}}(CP)=f_{\mathcal{RP}}(xP)=f_{\mathcal{RP}}(x)f_{\mathcal{RP}}(P)=(\alpha+\sigma_1)f_{\mathcal{RP}}(P)\\ \mathrm{F}^*(CP)=\mathrm{F}^*(xP)=\mathrm{F}^*(x)\mathrm{F}^*(P)=\sigma_1\mathrm{F}^*(P)\\ \end{gather*}

nodes.name: Commutators of C, B with d_k in RP
nodes.statement: In fact, the existence of the empty polytope $\varnothing$ such that $d_{n+1}P^n=\varnothing$ for any $n$-polytope $P^n$ makes the formulas connecting $C,B$, and $d_k$ simpler. We have: \begin{align*} [C,d]=1,& \quad [C,d_{k+1}]=d_k,\, k\geqslant 1\\ dB=2Cd+\varepsilon_0,&\quad d_{k+1}B=2Cd_{k+1}+d_k,\, k\geqslant 1 \end{align*}

nodes.name: Proposition 11.5 (Phi(t)B in RP)
nodes.statement: $$ \Phi(t)B=(B-2C-t)+(2C+t)\Phi(t)+\varepsilon_0t $$

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 11.5
nodes.statement: Indeed, \begin{multline*} \Phi(t)BP=BP+(2CdP+\varepsilon_0(P))t+(2Cd_2P+dP)t^2+\sum\limits_{k\geqslant 3}(2Cd_kP+d_{k-1}P)t^k=\\ =(B-2C-t)P+2C\Phi(t)P+t\Phi(t)P+\varepsilon_0(P)t \end{multline*}
nodes.statement_short: Expand Phi(t)BP term by term.

nodes.name: Phi(t)A in RP
nodes.statement: Then $$ \Phi(t)A=A+t+t\Phi(t)-\varepsilon_0t $$

nodes.name: Proposition 11.6 (operators A_RP, A_0)
nodes.statement: The mappings $A_{\mathcal{RP}}\colon\mathcal{Q}sym[\alpha]\to\mathcal{Q}sym[\alpha]$, $A_{0}\colon\mathcal{Q}sym\to\mathcal{Q}sym$ defined by the formulas \begin{gather*} A_{\mathcal{RP}}g=\alpha g(\alpha,0,0,\dots)+t_1g(\alpha,t_1,t_2,\dots)+\sum\limits_{n=2}^{\infty}(t_n+t_{n-1})g(\alpha,t_n,t_{n+1},\dots)-\sigma_1g(0,0,\dots)\\ A_{0}g=t_1g(t_1,t_2,\dots)+\sum\limits_{n=2}^{\infty}(t_n+t_{n-1})g(t_n,t_{n+1},\dots)-\sigma_1g(0,0,\dots) \end{gather*} satisfy the relations $$ f_{\mathcal{RP}}(AP)=A_{\mathcal{RP}}f_{\mathcal{RP}}(P),\quad \mathrm{F}^*(AP)=A_{0}\mathrm{F}^*(P) $$ for all $P\in\mathcal{RP}$.

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 11.6
nodes.statement: From the proof of Proposition \ref{AC} we see that both mappings $A_{\mathcal{RP}}$ and $A_{0}$ are correctly defined. Then \begin{gather*} \Phi(t_1)A=A+t_1+t_1\Phi(t_1)-\varepsilon_0 t_1\\ \Phi(t_2)\Phi(t_1)A=A+t_2+(t_2+t_1)\Phi(t_2)+t_1\Phi(t_2)\Phi(t_1)-\varepsilon_0(t_2+t_1)\\ \dots\\ \Phi(t_n)\Phi(t_{n-1})\dots\Phi(t_1)A=A+t_n+(t_n+t_{n-1})\Phi(t_n)+(t_{n-1}+t_{n-2})\Phi(t_n)\Phi(t_{n-1})+\dots\\ +t_1\Phi(t_n)\dots\Phi(t_1)-\varepsilon_0(t_n+\dots+t_1)\\ \dots\\ \Phi_{\infty}A=A+t_1\Phi_{\infty}(t_1,t_2,\dots)+\sum\limits_{n=2}^{\infty}(t_n+t_{n-1})\Phi_{\infty}(t_n,t_{n+1},\dots)-\varepsilon_0\sigma_1\\ f_{\mathcal{RP}}(AP)=\varepsilon_{\alpha}\Phi_{\infty}A=\varepsilon_{\alpha}(AP)+t_1\varepsilon_{\alpha}\Phi_{\infty}(t_1,t_2,\dots)+\sum\limits_{n=2}^{\infty}(t_n+t_{n-1})\varepsilon_{\alpha}\Phi_{\infty}(t_n,t_{n+1},\dots)-\varepsilon_0(P)\sigma_1=\\ =\alpha f_{\mathcal{RP}}(\alpha,0,0,\dots)+t_1f_{\mathcal{RP}}(\alpha,t_1,t_2,\dots)+\sum\limits_{n=2}^{\infty}(t_n+t_{n-1})f_{\mathcal{RP}}(\alpha,t_n,t_{n+1},\dots)-\sigma_1f_{\mathcal{RP}}(0,0,\dots)=A_{\mathcal{RP}}f_{\mathcal{RP}}(P)\\ \mathrm{F}^*(AP)=\varepsilon_{0}\Phi_{\infty}A=\varepsilon_{0}(AP)+t_1\varepsilon_{0}\Phi_{\infty}(t_1,t_2,\dots)+\sum\limits_{n=2}^{\infty}(t_n+t_{n-1})\varepsilon_0\Phi_{\infty}(t_n,t_{n+1},\dots)-\varepsilon_0(P)\sigma_1=\\ =t_1\mathrm{F}^*(t_1,t_2,\dots)+\sum\limits_{n=2}^{\infty}(t_n+t_{n-1})\mathrm{F}^*(t_n,t_{n+1},\dots)-\sigma_1\mathrm{F}^*(0,0,\dots)=A_{0}\mathrm{F}^*(P) \end{gather*}
nodes.statement_short: As in Proposition 11.4, iterating the RP relation for Phi(t)A.

nodes.name: Operators B_RP and B_0
nodes.statement: As before $B_{\mathcal{RP}}$ and $B_{0}$ are defined as $B_{\mathcal{RP}}=2C_{\mathcal{RP}}-A_{\mathcal{RP}}$, $B_0=2C_0-A_0$, where $C_{\mathcal{RP}}g=(\alpha+\sigma_1)g$, $C_{0}g=\sigma_1g$, and $$ f_{\mathcal{RP}}(BP)=B_{\mathcal{RP}}f_{\mathcal{RP}}(P),\quad \mathrm{F}^*(BP)=B_0\mathrm{F}^*(B) $$

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 11.7
nodes.statement: At last \begin{multline*} \Phi(t)(BC-CB)=\left(B-2C-t+(2C+t)\Phi(t)+\varepsilon_0t\right)C-(C+t)\Phi(t)B=\\ =BC-(2C+t)C+(2C+t)(C+t)\Phi(t)-(C+t)\left(B-2C-t+(2C+t)\Phi(t)+\varepsilon_0t\right)=\\ =BC-CB+(2C-B)t+t^2-(C+t)\varepsilon_0t=BC-CB+At+t^2-(x+t)t\varepsilon_0 \end{multline*} So we obtain the following proposition.
nodes.statement_short: Substitute the RP formulas for Phi(t)B and Phi(t)C and simplify.

nodes.name: Proposition 11.7 (Phi(t)[B,C] in RP)
nodes.statement: In the ring $\mathcal{RP}$ $$ \Phi(t)[B,C]=[B,C]+At+t^2-(x+t)t\varepsilon_0 $$

nodes.name: Image of simple polytopes characterized by one relation
nodes.statement: In fact, for the polynomial $g=g(\alpha,\sigma_1)\in\mathrm{Qsym}[t_1,t_2,\dots][\alpha]$ this condition is necessary and sufficient to be an image of an integer combination of simple polytopes.
nodes.section: 12 Problem of the Description of Flag Vectors of Polytopes

nodes.name: h-polynomial of a simple polytope
nodes.statement: For an $n$-dimensional simple polytope $P^n$ let us define an {\itshape $h$-polynomial}: $$ h(\alpha,t)(P^n)=h_0\alpha^n+h_1\alpha^{n-1}t+\dots+h_{n-1}\alpha t^{n-1}+h_nt^n=f_1(\alpha-t,t)(P^n) $$
nodes.section: 12 Problem of the Description of Flag Vectors of Polytopes

nodes.name: Symmetry of the h-polynomial
nodes.statement: Since $f_1(-\alpha,\alpha+t)=f_1(\alpha,t)$, the $h$-polynomial is symmetric: $h(\alpha,t)=h(t,\alpha)$. So $h_i=h_{n-i}$.
nodes.section: 12 Problem of the Description of Flag Vectors of Polytopes

nodes.name: g-vector of a simple polytope
nodes.statement: A {\itshape $g$-vector} of a simple polytope $P^n$ is the set of numbers $g_0=1$, $g_i=h_i-h_{i-1}, 1\leqslant i\leqslant [\frac{n}{2}]$.
nodes.section: 12 Problem of the Description of Flag Vectors of Polytopes

nodes.name: Binomial i-decomposition
nodes.statement: For any positive integers $a$ and $i$ there exists a unique ''binomial $i$-decomposition'' of $a$: $$a=\binom{a_i}{i}+\binom{a_{i-1}}{i-1}+\dots+\binom{a_j}{j},$$ where $a_i>a_{i-1}>\dots>a_j\geqslant j\geqslant 1.$
nodes.section: 12 Problem of the Description of Flag Vectors of Polytopes

nodes.name: Pseudo-power a^<i>
nodes.statement: Let us define $$a^{\langle i\rangle}=\binom{a_i+1}{i+1}+\binom{a_{i-1}+1}{i}+\dots+\binom{a_j+1}{j+1}, \quad 0^{\langle i\rangle}=0.$$
nodes.section: 12 Problem of the Description of Flag Vectors of Polytopes

nodes.name: g-theorem
nodes.statement: Integer numbers $(g_0,g_1,\dots,g_{[\frac{n}{2}]})$ form the $g$-vector of some simple $n$-dimensional polytope if and only if they satisfy the following conditions: $$ g_0=1,\;0\leqslant g_1,\;0\leqslant g_{i+1}\leqslant g_i^{\langle i\rangle},\; i=1,2,\dots, \left[\frac{n}{2}\right]-1. $$
nodes.section: 12 Problem of the Description of Flag Vectors of Polytopes
nodes.statement_short: McMullen's conditions g_0=1, 0<=g_1, 0<=g_{i+1}<=g_i^<i> characterize g-vectors of simple polytopes.
conclusions: $$ g_0=1,\;0\leqslant g_1,\;0\leqslant g_{i+1}\leqslant g_i^{\langle i\rangle},\; i=1,2,\dots, \left[\frac{n}{2}\right]-1. $$

nodes.name: Question 12.2 (images of single polytopes)
nodes.statement: Find a criterion when the polynomial $\psi\in\mathrm{Qsym}[t_1,t_2,\dots][\alpha]$ is the image of an $n$-dimensional polytope.
nodes.section: 12 Problem of the Description of Flag Vectors of Polytopes

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 2.14 (Appendix A)
nodes.statement: The formula for dimension of $P^{n_1}\divideontimes Q^{n_2}$ follows from Remark \ref{Join}. The nonempty faces of a polytope are exactly the subsets of the polytope that minimize some linear function on it. Let $\ib{c}=(\ib{c}_1,\ib{c}_2)$ be a linear function in $(\mathbb R^{n_1+1}\times\mathbb R^{n_2+1})^*=(\mathbb R^{n_1+1})^*\times(\mathbb R^{n_2+1})^*$. Then $\ib{c}_1$ has its minimum $c_1$ on the face $F$ of $P^{n_1}$, and $\ib{c}_2$ has its minimum $c_2$ on the face $G$ of $Q^{n_2}$. Since any point of $P^{n_1}\divideontimes Q^{n_2}$ has the form $t_1\ib{p}+t_2\ib{q}$, where $\ib{p}\in P^{n_1},\, \ib{q}\in Q^{n_2},\,t_1,t_2\geqslant 0, t_1+t_2=1$, we have \begin{itemize} \item if $c_1<c_2$, then $\ib{c}$ has its minimum on the face $F\divideontimes\varnothing$ of $P^{n_1}\divideontimes Q^{n_2}$; \item if $c_1>c_2$, then $\ib{c}$ has its minimum on $\varnothing\divideontimes G$; \item if $c_1=c_2$, then $\ib{c}$ has its minimum on the set $$ X=\{t_1\ib{p}+t_2\ib{q},\;\ib{p}\in F,\,\ib{q}\in G,\; t_1,t_2\geqslant 0,\,t_1+t_2=1\}. $$ Let $F$ lie in the $k$-simplex $\mathrm{conv}\{\ib{p}_1,\dots,\ib{p}_{k+1}\}\subset \mathrm{aff}(F)$, and $G$ lie in the $l$-simplex\linebreak $\mathrm{conv}\{\ib{q}_1,\dots,\ib{q}_{l+1}\}\subset\mathrm{aff}(G)$. Now let $\{\overrightarrow{O\ib{p}_i},\,i=1,\dots,k+1\}$ be a basis in $\mathbb R^{k+1}=\mathrm{aff}\{O,\,\ib{p}_i,\,i=1,\dots, k+1\}$ and $\{\overrightarrow{O\ib{q}_j},\,j=1,\dots,l+1\}$ be a basis in $\mathbb R^{l+1}=\mathrm{aff}\{O,\,\ib{q}_j,\,j=1,\dots, l+1\}$. Then $X=F\divideontimes G$. \end{itemize} Note that $\ib{c}_1$ can have the constant value on $P^{n_1}$, or $\ib{c}_2$ can have the constant value on $Q^{n_2}$. In these cases $F=P^{n_1}$, or $G=Q^{n_2}$. Let $\lambda_P$ be the linear function equal to the sum of all the coordinates in $\mathbb R^{n_1+1}$, and $\lambda_Q$ be the linear function equal to the sum of all the coordinates in $\mathbb R^{n_2+1}$. Then \begin{gather*} \lambda_P(\ib{p})=1,\quad\lambda_Q(\ib{p})=0\quad\mbox{for any }\ib{p}\in P^{n_1}=P^{n_1}\divideontimes \varnothing\\ \lambda_P(\ib{q})=0,\quad\lambda_Q(\ib{q})=1\quad\mbox{for any }\ib{q}\in Q^{n_2}=\varnothing\divideontimes Q^{n_2} \end{gather*} Now let $F\ne\varnothing$, $F\subseteq P^{n_1}$ be a face of $P^{n_1}$, and let $\ib{c}_1\in(\mathbb R^{n_1+1})^*$ be a linear function that has its minimum $c_1$ exactly on $F$. Similarly, let $(G,\ib{c}_2,c_2)$ be the corresponding data for $Q^{n_2}$. Then let $\ib{c}=(\ib{c}_1,\ib{c}_2)\in \left(\mathbb R^{n_1+1}\times\mathbb R^{n_2+1}\right)^*$. By an addition or a subtraction of $\lambda_P$ and $\lambda_Q$ with coefficients we can obtain any of the cases $c_1<c_2$, $c_1=c_2$, or $c_1>c_2$, so $F\divideontimes\varnothing$, $F\divideontimes G$, $\varnothing\divideontimes G$ are faces of $P^{n_1}\divideontimes Q^{n_2}$. Thus faces of the polytope $P^{n_1}\divideontimes Q^{n_2}$ up to an affine equivalence have the form $$ F\divideontimes G,\; \varnothing\subseteq F\subseteq P^{n_1},\; \varnothing\subseteq G\subseteq Q^{n_2}. $$
nodes.statement_short: Faces are minimizers of linear functionals; compare minima c_1, c_2 on P and Q, and use lambda_P, lambda_Q to realize every F*G.

nodes.name: Dimension from Remark 2.13.
nodes.statement: The formula for dimension of $P^{n_1}\divideontimes Q^{n_2}$ follows from Remark \ref{Join}.
nodes.statement_short: Dimension from Remark 2.13.

nodes.name: Minimize a split linear functional c=(c_1,c_2).
nodes.statement: The nonempty faces of a polytope are exactly the subsets of the polytope that minimize some linear function on it. Let $\ib{c}=(\ib{c}_1,\ib{c}_2)$ be a linear function in $(\mathbb R^{n_1+1}\times\mathbb R^{n_2+1})^*=(\mathbb R^{n_1+1})^*\times(\mathbb R^{n_2+1})^*$. Then $\ib{c}_1$ has its minimum $c_1$ on the face $F$ of $P^{n_1}$, and $\ib{c}_2$ has its minimum $c_2$ on the face $G$ of $Q^{n_2}$. Since any point of $P^{n_1}\divideontimes Q^{n_2}$ has the form $t_1\ib{p}+t_2\ib{q}$, where $\ib{p}\in P^{n_1},\, \ib{q}\in Q^{n_2},\,t_1,t_2\geqslant 0, t_1+t_2=1$, we have
nodes.statement_short: Minimize a split linear functional c=(c_1,c_2).

nodes.name: Case c_1<c_2.
nodes.statement: if $c_1<c_2$, then $\ib{c}$ has its minimum on the face $F\divideontimes\varnothing$ of $P^{n_1}\divideontimes Q^{n_2}$;
nodes.statement_short: Case c_1<c_2.

nodes.name: Case c_1>c_2.
nodes.statement: if $c_1>c_2$, then $\ib{c}$ has its minimum on $\varnothing\divideontimes G$;
nodes.statement_short: Case c_1>c_2.

nodes.name: Case c_1=c_2: minimum set is F*G.
nodes.statement: if $c_1=c_2$, then $\ib{c}$ has its minimum on the set $$ X=\{t_1\ib{p}+t_2\ib{q},\;\ib{p}\in F,\,\ib{q}\in G,\; t_1,t_2\geqslant 0,\,t_1+t_2=1\}. $$ Let $F$ lie in the $k$-simplex $\mathrm{conv}\{\ib{p}_1,\dots,\ib{p}_{k+1}\}\subset \mathrm{aff}(F)$, and $G$ lie in the $l$-simplex\linebreak $\mathrm{conv}\{\ib{q}_1,\dots,\ib{q}_{l+1}\}\subset\mathrm{aff}(G)$. Now let $\{\overrightarrow{O\ib{p}_i},\,i=1,\dots,k+1\}$ be a basis in $\mathbb R^{k+1}=\mathrm{aff}\{O,\,\ib{p}_i,\,i=1,\dots, k+1\}$ and $\{\overrightarrow{O\ib{q}_j},\,j=1,\dots,l+1\}$ be a basis in $\mathbb R^{l+1}=\mathrm{aff}\{O,\,\ib{q}_j,\,j=1,\dots, l+1\}$. Then $X=F\divideontimes G$.
nodes.statement_short: Case c_1=c_2: minimum set is F*G.

nodes.name: Constant functionals give F=P or G=Q.
nodes.statement: Note that $\ib{c}_1$ can have the constant value on $P^{n_1}$, or $\ib{c}_2$ can have the constant value on $Q^{n_2}$. In these cases $F=P^{n_1}$, or $G=Q^{n_2}$.
nodes.statement_short: Constant functionals give F=P or G=Q.

nodes.name: Coordinate-sum functionals lambda_P, lambda_Q.
nodes.statement: Let $\lambda_P$ be the linear function equal to the sum of all the coordinates in $\mathbb R^{n_1+1}$, and $\lambda_Q$ be the linear function equal to the sum of all the coordinates in $\mathbb R^{n_2+1}$. Then \begin{gather*} \lambda_P(\ib{p})=1,\quad\lambda_Q(\ib{p})=0\quad\mbox{for any }\ib{p}\in P^{n_1}=P^{n_1}\divideontimes \varnothing\\ \lambda_P(\ib{q})=0,\quad\lambda_Q(\ib{q})=1\quad\mbox{for any }\ib{q}\in Q^{n_2}=\varnothing\divideontimes Q^{n_2} \end{gather*}
nodes.statement_short: Coordinate-sum functionals lambda_P, lambda_Q.

nodes.name: Every F*G is realized as a face.
nodes.statement: Now let $F\ne\varnothing$, $F\subseteq P^{n_1}$ be a face of $P^{n_1}$, and let $\ib{c}_1\in(\mathbb R^{n_1+1})^*$ be a linear function that has its minimum $c_1$ exactly on $F$. Similarly, let $(G,\ib{c}_2,c_2)$ be the corresponding data for $Q^{n_2}$. Then let $\ib{c}=(\ib{c}_1,\ib{c}_2)\in \left(\mathbb R^{n_1+1}\times\mathbb R^{n_2+1}\right)^*$. By an addition or a subtraction of $\lambda_P$ and $\lambda_Q$ with coefficients we can obtain any of the cases $c_1<c_2$, $c_1=c_2$, or $c_1>c_2$, so $F\divideontimes\varnothing$, $F\divideontimes G$, $\varnothing\divideontimes G$ are faces of $P^{n_1}\divideontimes Q^{n_2}$.
nodes.statement_short: Every F*G is realized as a face.

nodes.name: Faces are exactly F*G.
nodes.statement: Thus faces of the polytope $P^{n_1}\divideontimes Q^{n_2}$ up to an affine equivalence have the form $$ F\divideontimes G,\; \varnothing\subseteq F\subseteq P^{n_1},\; \varnothing\subseteq G\subseteq Q^{n_2}. $$
nodes.statement_short: Faces are exactly F*G.

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 2.22 (Appendix B)
nodes.statement: We will show that any polytope $P^n$ of positive dimension can be represented in a unique up to the order of factors way as a product of indecomposable polytopes of positive dimensions $P=P_1\times\dots\times P_k$. It is clear that such a decomposition exists. Now let $$ P_1\times\dots\times P_k=Q_1\times\dots\times Q_s, $$ where $$ 1\leqslant \dim P_1\leqslant\dim P_2\leqslant\dots\leqslant\dim P_k,\quad\mbox{and }1\leqslant \dim Q_1\leqslant\dim Q_2\leqslant\dots\leqslant \dim Q_s. $$ Let us consider a face $F$ of the form $\ib{v}_1\times\dots\times\ib{v}_{k-1}\times P_k\simeq P_k$, where $\ib{v}_i$ are vertices. Then we have $F=G_1\times \dots\times G_s$, where $G_i$ is a face of $Q_i$. Since $P_k$ is indecomposable, we see that all $G_j$ but one are points, and $P_k$ is combinatorially equivalent to a face of some $Q_r$. Similarly $Q_r$ is combinatorially equivalent to a face of some $P_t$. Then $\dim P_k\leqslant\dim Q_r\leqslant\dim P_t\leqslant\dim P_k$, therefore, $P_k=Q_r$. Similarly $Q_s\simeq P_l$ for some $l$. So $\dim P_k=\dim Q_s$ and without loss of generality we can set $P_k=Q_s$. If $P_k=I$ then $P_i=Q_j=I$ for all $i,j$, so the statement is true. Let $P_k\ne I$. We know that $$ \ib{v}_1\times\dots\times\ib{v}_{k-1}\times P_k=\ib{w}_1\times\dots\times\ib{w}_{s-1}\times P_k $$ Let us consider a face $G$ of the form $\ib{v}_1\times\dots\times \ib{v}_{i-1}\times I\times \ib{v}_{i+1}\times\dots\times \ib{v}_{k-1}\times P_k$, where $I$ is the edge that joins the vertices $\ib{v}_i$ and $\ib{v}_i'$ of the polytope $P_i$. Then $G=\ib{w}_1\times\dots\times\ib{w}_{j-1}\times J\times\ib{w}_{j+1}\times\dots\times\ib{w}_{s-1}\times P_k$, where $J$ is the edge that joins the vertices $\ib{w}_j$ and $\ib{w}_j'$ of some polytope $Q_j$. Since $\ib{v}_1\times\dots\times\ib{v}_i'\times\dots\times P_k\subset G$, $P_k$ is indecomposable, and $P_k\ne J$, we have $$ \ib{v}_1\times\dots\times\ib{v}_i'\times\dots\times P_k=\ib{w}_1\times\dots\times\ib{w}_j'\times\dots\times P_k. $$ Changing the edges we can achieve any vertex $\ib{v}_1'\times\dots\times\ib{v}_{k-1}'$ of $P_1\times\dots\times P_{k-1}$, so for any such a vertex we have $\ib{v}_1'\times\dots\times\ib{v}_{k-1}'\times P_k=\ib{w}_1'\times\dots\times \ib{w}_{s-1}'\times P_k$. Therefore for any face $F_1\times \dots\times F_{k-1}\times P_k$ $$ F_1\times \dots\times F_{k-1}\times P_k=G_1\times\dots\times G_{s-1}\times P_k $$ Thus for any face $F$ of the polytope $P_1\times\dots\times P_{k-1}$ there is a face $G$ of the polytope $Q_1\times\dots\times Q_{s-1}$ such that $F\times P_k=G\times P_k$, and vice versa. Moreover, $F\subset F'$ if and only if $G\subset G'$. Thus $$ P_1\times\dots\times P_{k-1}=Q_1\times\dots\times Q_{s-1} $$ Iterating this step in the end we obtain that $k=s$, and up to the order of the polytopes $P_i=Q_i$, $i=1,\dots,k$.
nodes.statement_short: Unique factorization into indecomposables: identify the largest factor via faces of the form v x P_k, then peel it off and iterate.

nodes.name: Reduce to unique factorization.
nodes.statement: We will show that any polytope $P^n$ of positive dimension can be represented in a unique up to the order of factors way as a product of indecomposable polytopes of positive dimensions $P=P_1\times\dots\times P_k$.
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to unique factorization.

nodes.name: Existence; take two factorizations.
nodes.statement: It is clear that such a decomposition exists. Now let $$ P_1\times\dots\times P_k=Q_1\times\dots\times Q_s, $$ where $$ 1\leqslant \dim P_1\leqslant\dim P_2\leqslant\dots\leqslant\dim P_k,\quad\mbox{and }1\leqslant \dim Q_1\leqslant\dim Q_2\leqslant\dots\leqslant \dim Q_s. $$
nodes.statement_short: Existence; take two factorizations.

nodes.name: Largest factors coincide.
nodes.statement: Let us consider a face $F$ of the form $\ib{v}_1\times\dots\times\ib{v}_{k-1}\times P_k\simeq P_k$, where $\ib{v}_i$ are vertices. Then we have $F=G_1\times \dots\times G_s$, where $G_i$ is a face of $Q_i$. Since $P_k$ is indecomposable, we see that all $G_j$ but one are points, and $P_k$ is combinatorially equivalent to a face of some $Q_r$. Similarly $Q_r$ is combinatorially equivalent to a face of some $P_t$. Then $\dim P_k\leqslant\dim Q_r\leqslant\dim P_t\leqslant\dim P_k$, therefore, $P_k=Q_r$. Similarly $Q_s\simeq P_l$ for some $l$. So $\dim P_k=\dim Q_s$ and without loss of generality we can set $P_k=Q_s$.
nodes.statement_short: Largest factors coincide.

nodes.name: Case P_k = I.
nodes.statement: If $P_k=I$ then $P_i=Q_j=I$ for all $i,j$, so the statement is true.
nodes.statement_short: Case P_k = I.

nodes.name: Case P_k != I: edges of the remaining factors.
nodes.statement: Let $P_k\ne I$. We know that $$ \ib{v}_1\times\dots\times\ib{v}_{k-1}\times P_k=\ib{w}_1\times\dots\times\ib{w}_{s-1}\times P_k $$ Let us consider a face $G$ of the form $\ib{v}_1\times\dots\times \ib{v}_{i-1}\times I\times \ib{v}_{i+1}\times\dots\times \ib{v}_{k-1}\times P_k$, where $I$ is the edge that joins the vertices $\ib{v}_i$ and $\ib{v}_i'$ of the polytope $P_i$. Then $G=\ib{w}_1\times\dots\times\ib{w}_{j-1}\times J\times\ib{w}_{j+1}\times\dots\times\ib{w}_{s-1}\times P_k$, where $J$ is the edge that joins the vertices $\ib{w}_j$ and $\ib{w}_j'$ of some polytope $Q_j$.
nodes.statement_short: Case P_k != I: edges of the remaining factors.

nodes.name: Faces F x P_k correspond.
nodes.statement: Since $\ib{v}_1\times\dots\times\ib{v}_i'\times\dots\times P_k\subset G$, $P_k$ is indecomposable, and $P_k\ne J$, we have $$ \ib{v}_1\times\dots\times\ib{v}_i'\times\dots\times P_k=\ib{w}_1\times\dots\times\ib{w}_j'\times\dots\times P_k. $$ Changing the edges we can achieve any vertex $\ib{v}_1'\times\dots\times\ib{v}_{k-1}'$ of $P_1\times\dots\times P_{k-1}$, so for any such a vertex we have $\ib{v}_1'\times\dots\times\ib{v}_{k-1}'\times P_k=\ib{w}_1'\times\dots\times \ib{w}_{s-1}'\times P_k$. Therefore for any face $F_1\times \dots\times F_{k-1}\times P_k$ $$ F_1\times \dots\times F_{k-1}\times P_k=G_1\times\dots\times G_{s-1}\times P_k $$
nodes.statement_short: Faces F x P_k correspond.

nodes.name: Cancel the common factor P_k.
nodes.statement: Thus for any face $F$ of the polytope $P_1\times\dots\times P_{k-1}$ there is a face $G$ of the polytope $Q_1\times\dots\times Q_{s-1}$ such that $F\times P_k=G\times P_k$, and vice versa. Moreover, $F\subset F'$ if and only if $G\subset G'$. Thus $$ P_1\times\dots\times P_{k-1}=Q_1\times\dots\times Q_{s-1} $$
nodes.statement_short: Cancel the common factor P_k.

nodes.name: Iterate.
nodes.statement: Iterating this step in the end we obtain that $k=s$, and up to the order of the polytopes $P_i=Q_i$, $i=1,\dots,k$.
nodes.statement_short: Iterate.

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 2.33 (Appendix B)
nodes.statement: Let $P_1\divideontimes P_2\dots\divideontimes P_k=Q_1\divideontimes Q_2\divideontimes\dots\divideontimes Q_s$, where $P_i, Q_j$ are polytopes, $$ 0\leqslant\dim P_1\leqslant \dim P_2\leqslant \dots\leqslant \dim P_k,\quad 0\leqslant\dim Q_1\leqslant \dim Q_2\leqslant\dots\leqslant \dim Q_s $$ and each polytope $P_i $ and $Q_j$ can not be decomposed as a join of polytopes of lower dimensions. Let $\dim P_k\geqslant \dim Q_s$. Consider the face $\varnothing\divideontimes\varnothing\divideontimes\dots\divideontimes P_k$. It can be represented in the form $G_1\divideontimes G_2\divideontimes\dots\divideontimes G_s$, where $G_j$ is a face of $Q_j$. Since $P_k$ is join-indecomposable, all $G_j$ but one should be equal to $\varnothing$, and one of them should be equal to $P_k$. Let $P_k=G_r$. Then $P_k$ is a face of $Q_r$, so $P_k=Q_r$, since $\dim P_k\geqslant\dim Q_s\geqslant\dim Q_r$. Without loss of generality we can take $r=s$. We have $P'\divideontimes P_k=Q'\divideontimes P_k$, and the combinatorial equivalence identifies the face $\varnothing\divideontimes P_k$ of the first polytope with the same face $\varnothing\divideontimes P_k$ of the second. Consider the face $P'\divideontimes\varnothing$. It should have the form $G_1\divideontimes G_2$ where $G_1$ is a face of $Q'$ and $G_2$ is a face of $P_k$. Then $\varnothing\divideontimes G_2$ should be a face of $\varnothing\divideontimes P_k$ and $P'\divideontimes \varnothing$, therefore $G_2=\varnothing$ and $G_1=P'$. Since $\dim P'=\dim Q'$, we see that $P'=Q'$. So $P_1\divideontimes P_2\divideontimes\dots\divideontimes P_{k-1}=Q_1\divideontimes Q_2\divideontimes\dots Q_{s-1}$. Let $s\geqslant k$. Iterating this step in the end we obtain $P_1=Q_1\divideontimes Q_2\divideontimes\dots\divideontimes Q_{s-k+1}$. Therefore $k=s$ and $P_1=Q_1$. Thus each polytope can be decomposed in a unique up to permutations way as $P_1\divideontimes\dots\divideontimes P_k$, where $P_j$ are join-indecomposable. Since $\mathcal{RP}$ additively is a free abelian group generated by combinatorial polytopes and $\varnothing$, it is a ring of polynomials generated by all join-indecomposable polytopes.
nodes.statement_short: Unique factorization into join-indecomposables: the largest join factor appears as a face, then cancel it and iterate.

nodes.name: Two join factorizations.
nodes.statement: Let $P_1\divideontimes P_2\dots\divideontimes P_k=Q_1\divideontimes Q_2\divideontimes\dots\divideontimes Q_s$, where $P_i, Q_j$ are polytopes, $$ 0\leqslant\dim P_1\leqslant \dim P_2\leqslant \dots\leqslant \dim P_k,\quad 0\leqslant\dim Q_1\leqslant \dim Q_2\leqslant\dots\leqslant \dim Q_s $$ and each polytope $P_i $ and $Q_j$ can not be decomposed as a join of polytopes of lower dimensions.
nodes.statement_short: Two join factorizations.

nodes.name: The largest factor appears in both.
nodes.statement: Let $\dim P_k\geqslant \dim Q_s$. Consider the face $\varnothing\divideontimes\varnothing\divideontimes\dots\divideontimes P_k$. It can be represented in the form $G_1\divideontimes G_2\divideontimes\dots\divideontimes G_s$, where $G_j$ is a face of $Q_j$. Since $P_k$ is join-indecomposable, all $G_j$ but one should be equal to $\varnothing$, and one of them should be equal to $P_k$. Let $P_k=G_r$. Then $P_k$ is a face of $Q_r$, so $P_k=Q_r$, since $\dim P_k\geqslant\dim Q_s\geqslant\dim Q_r$. Without loss of generality we can take $r=s$.
nodes.statement_short: The largest factor appears in both.

nodes.name: Cancel the common factor.
nodes.statement: We have $P'\divideontimes P_k=Q'\divideontimes P_k$, and the combinatorial equivalence identifies the face $\varnothing\divideontimes P_k$ of the first polytope with the same face $\varnothing\divideontimes P_k$ of the second. Consider the face $P'\divideontimes\varnothing$. It should have the form $G_1\divideontimes G_2$ where $G_1$ is a face of $Q'$ and $G_2$ is a face of $P_k$. Then $\varnothing\divideontimes G_2$ should be a face of $\varnothing\divideontimes P_k$ and $P'\divideontimes \varnothing$, therefore $G_2=\varnothing$ and $G_1=P'$. Since $\dim P'=\dim Q'$, we see that $P'=Q'$.
nodes.statement_short: Cancel the common factor.

nodes.name: Iterate.
nodes.statement: So $P_1\divideontimes P_2\divideontimes\dots\divideontimes P_{k-1}=Q_1\divideontimes Q_2\divideontimes\dots Q_{s-1}$. Let $s\geqslant k$. Iterating this step in the end we obtain $P_1=Q_1\divideontimes Q_2\divideontimes\dots\divideontimes Q_{s-k+1}$. Therefore $k=s$ and $P_1=Q_1$.
nodes.statement_short: Iterate.

nodes.name: Unique factorization gives the polynomial ring.
nodes.statement: Thus each polytope can be decomposed in a unique up to permutations way as $P_1\divideontimes\dots\divideontimes P_k$, where $P_j$ are join-indecomposable. Since $\mathcal{RP}$ additively is a free abelian group generated by combinatorial polytopes and $\varnothing$, it is a ring of polynomials generated by all join-indecomposable polytopes.
nodes.statement_short: Unique factorization gives the polynomial ring.

nodes.name: Proposition C.1 (monomials in the image of F)
nodes.statement: Any monomial $M_{\omega}$ such that $M_{\omega}\in \mathrm{F}(\mathcal{RP})$ has the form $M_{(2k+1)},\;k\geqslant 0$.

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition C.1
nodes.statement: Indeed, for the monomial $M_{(a_1,\,\dots,\,a_k)}$ we have \begin{multline*} M_{(a_1,\,\dots,\,a_k)}(t,-t,t_1,t_2,\dots)=M_{(a_1,\,\dots,\,a_k)}(t_1,t_2,\dots)+\left(t^{a_1}+(-t)^{a_1}\right)M_{(a_2,\,\dots,\,a_k)}(t_1,t_2,\dots)+\\ +(-1)^{a_2}t^{a_1+a_2}M_{(a_3,\,\dots,\,a_k)} \end{multline*} If $k\geqslant 2$ the last summand does not cancel, so $k=1$. For $M_{(n)}$ with $n=2l+1$ we have $$ M_{(2l+1)}(t_1,\dots,t_{i-1},t,-t,t_{i},\dots)=t_1^{2l+1}+\dots+t_{i-1}^{2l+1}+t^{2l+1}-t^{2l+1}+t_i^{2l+1}+\dots=M_{(2l+1)}(t_1,\dots,t_{i-1},t_i,\dots), $$ while for $n=2l$ the term containing $t^{2l}+(-t)^{2l}$ does not cancel.
nodes.statement_short: Substitute t,-t and check which monomials are invariant.

nodes.name: Proposition C.2 (antisymmetrized odd pair in the image of F)
Proof of Proposition C.2
nodes.statement: Indeed, \begin{multline*} M_{(2k+1,\,2l+1)}(t_1,\dots,t_{i-1},t,-t,t_i,\dots)=M_{(2k+1,\,2l+1)}(t_1,\dots,t_{i-1},t_i,\dots)+\\ +\sum\limits_{j<i}t_j^{2k+1}(t^{2l+1}+(-t)^{2l+1})+\sum\limits_{j\geqslant i}(t^{2k+1}+(-t)^{2k+1})t_j^{2l+1}+(-1)^{2l+1}t^{2k+2l+2} \end{multline*} Then \begin{multline*} \left(M_{(2k+1,\,2l+1)}-M_{(2l+1,\,2k+1)}\right)(t_1,\dots,t_{i-1},t,-t,t_i,\dots)=\\ \left(M_{(2k+1,\,2l+1)}-M_{(2l+1,\,2k+1)}\right)(t_1,\dots,t_{i-1},t_i,\dots) \end{multline*}
nodes.statement_short: Substitute t,-t; the extra terms cancel in the difference.

nodes.name: Proposition C.3 (antisymmetrized odd monomials in the image of F)
nodes.statement: Let $(j_1,\dots,j_k)$ be the set of odd positive integer numbers. Then the quasi-symmetric polynomial $$ \sum\limits_{\sigma\in S_k}(-1)^{\sigma}M_{(j_{\sigma(1)},\,\dots,\,j_{\sigma(k)})} $$ belongs to the image of $\mathrm{F}$.
assumptions: Let $(j_1,\dots,j_k)$ be the set of odd positive integer numbers.

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition C.3
nodes.statement: Indeed, since $j_l$ are odd, we have \begin{multline*} M_{(j_1,\,\dots,\,j_k)}(t_1,\dots,t_{i-1},t,-t,t_i,\dots)=M_{(j_1,\,\dots,\,j_k)}(t_1,\dots, t_{i-1},t_i,\dots)-\\ -\sum\limits_{l_1<\dots<l_s<i\leqslant l_{s+3}<\dots<l_k}t_{l_1}^{j_1}\dots t_{l_s}^{j_s}t^{j_{s+1}+j_{s+2}}t_{l_{s+3}}^{j_{s+3}}\dots t_{l_k}^{j_k} \end{multline*} For any pair $(j_{s+1},j_{s+2})$ there exists a unique monomial $M_{(j_1,\,\dots,\,j_s,\,j_{s+2},\,j_{s+1},\,j_{s+3},\,\dots,\,j_k)}$, and this monomial has the opposite sign. Therefore all the monomials of the form $t_{l_1}^{j_{\sigma(1)}}\dots t_{l_s}^{j_{\sigma(s)}}t^{j_{\sigma(s+1)}+j_{\sigma(s+2)}}t_{l_{s+3}}^{j_{\sigma(s+3)}}\dots t_{l_k}^{j_{\sigma(k)}}$ vanish.
nodes.statement_short: Pair each defect term with the transposed composition of opposite sign.

nodes.name: Image of the Ehrenborg transformation in small dimensions
nodes.statement: Let us calculate the image of the Ehrenborg transformation $\mathrm{F}$ in small dimensions. \begin{itemize} \item[$n=0$] The image of the point $x=\mathrm{pt}$ is $M_{(1)}=\sigma_1$. So $$ \mathrm{F}(\mathcal{RP}^2)=\EuScript{R}^*((\mathcal{D}^*)^2)=\mathbb Z\langle \sigma_1\rangle. $$ \item[$n=1$] The image of the segment $I=\mathrm{pt}*\mathrm{pt}$ is $M_{(2)}+2M_{(1,\,1)}=\sigma_1^2$. So $$ \mathrm{F}(\mathcal{RP}^4)=\EuScript{R}^*((\mathcal{D}^*)^4)=\mathbb Z\langle \sigma_1^2\rangle. $$ \item[$n=2$] The image of the $m$-gon $M_m^2$ is $$ M_{(3)}+mM_{(2,\,1)}+mM_{(1,\,2)}+2mM_{(1,\,1,\,1)}=M_{(3)}+m(\sigma_1\sigma_2-\sigma_3) $$ Therefore, $$ \mathrm{F}(\mathcal{RP}^6)=\EuScript{R}^*((\mathcal{D}^*)^6)=\mathbb Z\langle M_{(3)},\sigma_1\sigma_2-\sigma_3\rangle, $$ where $$ M_{(3)}=\mathrm{F}(4\Delta^2-3I^2),\quad \sigma_1\sigma_2-\sigma_3=\mathrm{F}(I^2-\Delta^2), $$ \item[$n=3$] The image of a $3$-dimensional polytope is $$ M_{(4)}+f_0M_{(1,\,3)}+f_1M_{(2,\,2)}+f_2M_{(3,\,1)}+f_{01}M_{(1,\,1,\,2)}+f_{02}M_{(1,\,2,\,1)}+f_{12}M_{(2,\,1,\,1)}+f_{012}M_{(1,\,1,\,1,\,1)} $$ Since $f_0-f_1+f_2=2$, $f_{01}=f_{02}=f_{12}=2f_1$, and $f_{012}=4f_1$, we obtain $$ \left(M_{(4)}+2M_{(3,\,1)}\right)+f_0\left(M_{(1,\,3)}-M_{(3,\,1)}\right)+f_1\left(M_{(2,\,2)}+M_{(3,\,1)}+2\left(\sigma_1\sigma_3-2\sigma_4\right)\right), $$ Then $$ \mathrm{F}(\mathcal{RP}^8)=\EuScript{R}^*((\mathcal{D}^*)^8)=\mathbb Z\langle M_{(4)}+2M_{(3,\,1)},M_{(1,\,3)}-M_{(3,\,1)}, M_{(2,\,2)}+M_{(3,\,1)}+2\left(\sigma_1\sigma_3-2\sigma_4\right)\rangle, $$ where \begin{gather*} M_{(4)}+2M_{(3,\,1)}=\mathrm{F}(5\Delta^3-6CI^2+2B\Delta^2),\quad M_{(1,\,3)}-M_{(3,\,1)}=\mathrm{F}(-\Delta^3+3CI^2-2B\Delta^2)\\ M_{(2,\,2)}+M_{(3,\,1)}+2\left(\sigma_1\sigma_3-2\sigma_4\right)=\mathrm{F}(-CI^2+B\Delta^2) \end{gather*} \end{itemize}
nodes.statement_short: Explicit bases of F(RP^{2n+2}) = R^*(D^*) for n=0..3 and their preimages.
